blurbs.800m Men:
**Predicted finish — Men’s 800m, Lausanne Diamond League, 21 August 2026:**

1. **Marco Arop (CAN)** — **1:41.82**  
2. **Brandon Miller (USA)** — **1:42.05**  
3. **Emmanuel Wanyonyi (KEN)** — **1:42.28**  
4. **Djamel Sedjati (ALG)** — **1:42.61**  
5. **David Barroso (ESP)** — **1:43.47**  
6. **Francesco Pernici (ITA)** — **1:43.73**  
7. **Marino Bloudek (CRO)** — **1:43.95**  
8. **Gabriel Tual (FRA)** — **1:44.37**  
9. **Patryk Sieradzki (POL)** — **1:46.83**

---

**Why this order?**

This is a seriously deep field, but the top end separates fairly clearly on 2026 form.

**Marco Arop** gets the nod for the win. His 1:41.84 in Paris on 28 June is the fastest 800m run by anyone in this field all season, and he followed it with another confident 1:42.13 in Edmonton. At 27, he is at his physical peak, and as the 2023 world champion and 2024 Olympic silver medallist, he has the big-race pedigree. Arop’s 2025 was solid but not spectacular; his 2026 has been a clear step back up, and he looks ready to beat the man who beat him in Paris 2024.

**Brandon Miller** is the most obvious threat. His London victory on 18 July was the standout result of his career: 1:42.19, ahead of Emmanuel Wanyonyi, who finished fourth in 1:43.31. Miller also won at Prefontaine in 1:43.68 and ran a sharp 1:14.08 for 600m in mid-August, showing his speed is still there. At 23, he’s still improving. The only reason he isn’t first is that Arop has run faster twice in 2026 and has a longer history of world-class consistency.

**Emmanuel Wanyonyi** is the most decorated athlete in the field — Olympic champion, world champion, and 2026 world record holder at 1000m with 2:11.83 in Monaco. That 1000m performance was extraordinary and shows he’s in superb shape overall. In the 800m specifically, he has run 1:42.09 in Oslo. But his 4th place in London, behind Miller, was a warning sign. He was beaten by over a second, and he has not yet matched Arop’s 1:41.84 this season. On talent alone he could win, but based on head-to-head evidence in 2026, third is the right call.

**Djamel Sedjati** is the toughest to place. His 2025 credentials are excellent — world silver in Tokyo and multiple Diamond League wins — and he opened his 2026 800m account with a strong 1:43.19 win in Budapest. But he has raced sparingly over 800m in 2026, and in Monaco over 1000m he was well behind Wanyonyi. Sedjati’s lack of consistent 2026 racing and lack of a sub-1:42 mark this season puts him just behind the top three, though he’s clearly the best of the rest.

The battle behind the top four is really for the “best of the Europeans” spot, and **David Barroso** takes it. Barroso ran 1:43.60 in Budapest, 1:43.83 in Nancy, and finished 4th in the European Championship final. He’s been consistently in the 1:43-mid range all summer, which gives him a clear edge over the next group. At 24, he’s also still developing.

**Francesco Pernici** has very similar numbers: 1:43.60 in Nancy, 1:43.84 in the European semi-final, and an Italian title. But he faded to 5th in the Euro final, while Barroso was 4th, and Pernici has been slightly less reliable in the biggest races. Still, he should be right in the mix and can run comfortably in the 1:43-lows.

**Marino Bloudek** is a European silver medallist and a proven championship performer, which explains his strong result in Birmingham. But his 2026 outdoor 800m times have been mostly 1:44.6–1:45.0, and he hasn’t shown the 1:43-low speed that Barroso and Pernici have mustered. On a fast Lausanne track, he could be closer, but the ceiling is slightly lower.

**Gabriel Tual** is the most difficult to judge. He has a 1:41.61 personal best and won the European title in 2024, so his talent is real. But his 2026 form has been poor: 8th in Paris in 1:44.92, 7th in Budapest in 1:43.97, and then elimination in the European Championship semi-final. That is not the profile of a man ready to challenge a world-class Diamond League field. He’ll need a major turnaround to finish higher than 8th.

**Patryk Sieradzki** rounds out the field. He has struggled with a long string of DNFs throughout 2025 and 2026, and even when he finishes, his times have been around 1:46–1:47. Against this level of opposition, he is unlikely to be competitive. The prediction is more about survival than victory for him.
blurbs.Long Jump Men:
### Predicted Finish – Men’s Long Jump, Lausanne Diamond League (21 Aug 2026)

1. **Miltiadis Tentoglou** – **8.56 m**  
2. **Simon Ehammer** – **8.43 m**  
3. **Bozhidar Sarâboyukov** – **8.38 m**  
4. **Jorge A. Hodelín** – **8.35 m**  
5. **Tajay Gayle** – **8.24 m**  
6. **Gerson Baldé** – **8.19 m**  
7. **Wayne Pinnock** – **8.12 m**  
8. **Anvar Anvarov** – **8.06 m**  
9. **Luka Bošković** – **8.01 m**

---

### Why This Order?

**1. Miltiadis Tentoglou**  
Tentoglou is the clear favourite. His 2026 season has been exceptional: **8.46 m in Xiamen**, **8.49 m in Limassol**, **8.61 m in Monaco**, **8.66 m at the Greek Championships**, and a dominant **8.44 m (-1.1)** to win the European title in Birmingham. He has already beaten most of this exact field at Monaco, where he jumped 8.61 against Pinnock, Hodelín, Sarâboyukov, Ehammer, Baldé, and Gayle. With two Olympic golds and a World Championship gold in his career, he is both the most talented and the most reliable jumper in the field. The only slight question is post-European Championship fatigue, but even so, 8.56 m is a realistic winning mark.

**2. Simon Ehammer**  
Ehammer is the best of the rest, especially on home soil in Lausanne. He won the European silver medal behind Tentoglou with **8.29 m (-2.7)** in a very difficult headwind. Earlier in 2026, he produced a huge **8.51 m (+1.0)** long jump within his 8778-point decathlon at Götzis, and he also jumped 8.32 m in Monaco. His decathlon background gives him elite runway rhythm and contest toughness. At the same Lausanne meeting in 2025 the conditions were poor, but Ehammer has improved significantly since then. Expect him to feed off the home crowd and finish clearly second, possibly around 8.43 m.

**3. Bozhidar Sarâboyukov**  
Sarâboyukov has been remarkably consistent throughout 2026. He beat Tentoglou head-to-head in Rome with **8.26 m (-0.1)**, jumped **8.36 m in Monaco**, **8.49 m in Plovdiv**, **8.48 m at the Bulgarian Championships**, and took European bronze with **8.26 m (-1.7)**. At 21, he is rising fast and has proven he can win big senior competitions, as shown by his 2025 European Indoor title. He was just behind Ehammer at the European Championships, and Hodelín edged him by 0.02 in Monaco, but Sarâboyukov’s overall consistency and multiple 8.40+ jumps this year give him the edge for third.

**4. Jorge A. Hodelín**  
At only 18, Hodelín is the most exciting young jumper in the field. He set the world U20 record in 2026 with **8.46 m (+1.9)** at Pierre-Bénite, finished third in Monaco with **8.38 m (+0.5)**, took bronze in Rome with **8.18 m (-0.1)**, and won the CAC Games with **8.23 m**. He has already beaten several established stars, including Pinnock, Baldé, and even Sarâboyukov at Monaco. However, he is still young and less reliable than the athletes above him. His 2025 World Championships qualifying effort of 7.50 m shows that he can still have off days. Fourth place with 8.35 m seems right for this stage of his development, though he could threaten the podium on a good day.

**5. Tajay Gayle**  
Gayle is the 2019 World Champion and won silver at the 2025 World Championships in Tokyo. In 2026, he won the Jamaican title with **8.37 m (+1.6)**, took second in Xiamen with **8.32 m**, and won the Commonwealth Games title with **8.15 m**. His ceiling remains high, but his season has also included disappointing jumps of **8.04 m in Monaco** and **6.80 m in Budapest**. He is more proven than Baldé and Pinnock, but not as consistently sharp as Tentoglou, Ehammer, Sarâboyukov, or Hodelín. A 8.24 m result in Lausanne would put him in the top five without quite matching the front group.

**6. Gerson Baldé**  
Baldé is the reigning World Indoor Champion after his **8.46 m** victory in Toruń in March. Outdoors, though, he has been a step below the top group: **8.00 m in Rome**, **8.20 m in Monaco**, and **8.18 m in the European final**. He also produced a wind-aided **8.42 m (+3.8)** in Lisbon, which shows he has more in him. But his legal outdoor best this season is still only 8.20 m. Gayle has been more explosive outdoors and has a stronger championship pedigree, so Baldé slots in just behind him. Sixth seems fair, but a clean technical day could lift him a place or two.

**7. Wayne Pinnock**  
Pinnock has the talent to win any meeting. He is a former Olympic silver medallist and World silver medallist, and his **8.39 m (+0.3)** in Monaco was the best non-Tentoglou jump of that meeting. But his 2026 season has been wildly inconsistent: **7.93 m in Xiamen**, **7.75 m in Rome**, **8.08 m in Budapest**, and a strange low-key **7.53 m (+8.6)** performance in Istanbul. If he recaptures his Monaco form, he could finish second, but that version of Pinnock has not appeared often enough this year. At Lausanne, he is more likely to land mid-pack around 8.12 m than to challenge the podium.

**8. Anvar Anvarov**  
Anvarov is a solid, consistent international jumper and the Uzbek national record holder. He won in Zagreb with **8.29 m (+0.7)**, took second in Budapest with **8.12 m**, and was fifth in Xiamen with **8.01 m**. He does not have the same ceiling as the leading Jamaicans, Cubans, or Europeans, but he rarely embarrasses himself. In the weaker 2025 Lausanne field he won with 7.84 m, but this 2026 field is much deeper. A mark around 8.06 m is realistic for him.

**9. Luka Bošković**  
Bošković is only 19 but already has serious credentials: World U20 silver in 2024, European U20 bronze in 2025, and a senior European final appearance in 2026. He jumped a wind-aided **8.33 m (+2.4)** in qualifying at the European Championships and a legal **8.23 m (+0.8)** in Zagreb. However, his final in Birmingham was just **8.08 m (-1.4)**, and he has not shown the consistency to compete with the very best seniors yet. He is a genuine future star, but in this loaded Diamond League field, ninth place with around 8.01 m seems the most likely outcome.
blurbs.100m Hurdles Women:
Predicted result (legal, near-ideal conditions):

1. Masai Russell (USA, 25) – 12.18  
2. Alia Armstrong (USA, 25) – 12.36  
3. Alaysha Johnson (USA, 29) – 12.38  
4. Nadine Visser (NED, 30) – 12.44  
5. Pia Skrzyszowska (POL, 24) – 12.48  
6. Rayniah Jones (USA, 24) – 12.51  
7. Demisha Roswell (JAM, 27) – 12.57  
8. Ditaji Kambundji (SUI, 23) – 12.65  

---

**Why this order:**

Masai Russell is the clear favourite. The Olympic champion and American record holder has been untouchable outdoors in 2026: 12.14 in Xiamen, 12.20 in Monaco, 12.24 at Prefontaine, and 12.25 in Shaoxing. She has won every major 100m hurdles final she has contested this season, and her combination of pure speed and technical consistency puts her in a different tier from the rest of this field. Lausanne should simply be another Russell coronation.

Behind her, the battle for second is between the two Americans who have traded wins this summer. Alia Armstrong gets the nod over Alaysha Johnson because of head-to-head form: Armstrong beat Johnson at the 2026 US Championships (12.38 to 12.42) and also finished ahead of Johnson at Hengelo (12.60 to 12.72). Armstrong’s late-season peak has been real, and winning the US title in 12.38 shows she can deliver under pressure. Johnson has been more consistent overall, with 12.38 in Monaco and 12.39 in Paris, but she has twice come off second-best to Armstrong in direct meetings. In a fast Diamond League race, Armstrong’s championship confidence gives her a slight edge.

Nadine Visser is the best of the rest. The reigning European champion ran 12.41 at Paris and won the European title in Birmingham, but she has not quite matched the top Americans’ speed this season. She lost to both Armstrong and Johnson in their common races, and her 12.54 at Budapest showed she is still a step off the 12.3-range athletes. Still, Visser’s 2026 consistency, indoor silver at Worlds, and Euro gold make her a clear fourth ahead of the next group.

Pia Skrzyszowska and Rayniah Jones project as the next two. Skrzyszowska has the better head-to-head record against Jones, having beaten her at Paris (12.46 to 12.60) and at Monaco, where both ran 12.54. She also has a 12.44 season best from Tomblaine and a European silver medal. Jones, meanwhile, has had a genuine breakthrough year with 12.43 in Zagreb and 12.47 in Budapest, but she faded to 12.59 at the US Championships. That inconsistency in her biggest recent race pushes her just behind Skrzyszowska.

Demisha Roswell is difficult to trust despite her Jamaican title. She ran a superb 12.40 to win the Jamaican Championships, but her Diamond League finals have fallen apart: 12.78 at Paris and 12.56 at Monaco. She is clearly capable of a top-five finish, but her pattern of fading in loaded finals drops her to seventh here. Ditaji Kambundji, despite being the reigning world champion and having a 12.24 personal best, has had a miserable 2026 outdoor season. Her season best is just 12.62, and she could only finish fourth at the European Championships in 12.75. The home crowd in Lausanne may lift her slightly, but it should not be enough to overcome her poor form relative to this deep field.
blurbs.5000m Men:
**Predicted Finish — Men’s 5000m, Lausanne Diamond League, 21 August 2026**

1. **Grant Fisher (USA)** — 12:46.35  
2. **Birhanu Balew (BRN)** — 12:47.10  
3. **Jacob Krop (KEN)** — 12:47.85  
4. **Parker Wolfe (USA)** — 12:48.50  
5. **Graham Blanks (USA)** — 12:49.30  
6. **Dominic Lokinyomo Lobalu (SUI)** — 12:50.05  
7. **Nico Young (USA)** — 12:51.20  
8. **Mezgebu Sime (ETH)** — 12:52.10  
9. **Mathew Kipchumba Kipsang (KEN)** — 12:53.05  
10. **Egide Ntakarutimana (BDI)** — 12:53.75  
11. **Cornelius Kemboi (KEN)** — 12:54.55  
12. **Laban Kiptoo Kosgei (KEN)** — 12:55.40  
13. **Eduardo Herrera (MEX)** — 13:00.20  
14. **Santiago Catrofe (URU)** — 13:01.15  
15. **Khairi Bejiga (ETH)** — 13:03.30  
16. **Getnet Wale (ETH)** — 13:05.50  
17. **Tim Verbaandert (NED)** — 13:08.80  
18. **Charles Kiboino (KEN)** — 13:12.30  
19. **Kuma Girma (ETH)** — 13:15.60  
20. **Shimelis Niguse (ETH)** — 13:18.90  
21. **Abderezak Suleman (ERI)** — 13:26.40  
22. **Žan Rudolf (SLO)** — 13:47.20  

---

**Why this order**

**Grant Fisher** gets the nod for the win. He has the strongest overall pedigree in the field — Olympic bronze medalist, world record holder in the indoor short-track 3000m and 5000m, and American record holder outdoors. His 2026 season is exactly what you want from a favourite: he won the Paris Diamond League 5000m in 12:54.80 over a loaded field, and he was only fifth in Oslo in 12:49.61 in a blazing race. That Oslo run actually shows he can handle championship-style depth, while his Paris win shows he can close when it matters. He should be the man to beat in Lausanne.

**Birhanu Balew** is the logical second pick. His 12:47.73 in Oslo was the fastest 5000m by any athlete in this field in 2026, and he followed it with 12:52.91 in Monaco. He has been remarkably consistent on the Diamond League circuit all summer, and his World Championships final experience gives him an edge over the younger Americans. The only question is whether Fisher’s finishing kick is better on a fast night — I think it is.

**Jacob Krop** rounds out the top three. The 2022 World silver medalist and 2023 World bronze medalist has rediscovered his best form in 2026. His Paris runner-up finish in 12:55.22 and Monaco fourth in 12:53.71 put him right in the mix. His Oslo race was poor by his standards — 13:01.51 — but he has shown enough in the more recent races to suggest he is peaking for the late-summer circuit. He is the strongest pure 5000m pedigree among the Kenyans in this field.

**Parker Wolfe** is the most exciting young American in the race. He ran 12:49.45 in Oslo, actually beating Fisher in that race, and then crushed the field at the Prefontaine 2 Miles in 8:10.13. He is a former NCAA champion with serious range, and his 2026 form suggests he is not intimidated by the big names. I still put him behind Fisher, Balew, and Krop because he lacks their international medal hardware, but he is knocking on the door.

**Graham Blanks** is incredibly reliable. A two-time NCAA champion and Olympian, he has run 12:49.99 in Oslo, 12:52.60 in Monaco, and 12:57.12 in Paris in 2026. He does not always win, but he almost always puts himself in the conversation. The gap between him and Wolfe is small, but Wolfe’s Prefontaine win and faster Oslo time give him the edge.

**Dominic Lokinyomo Lobalu** is a dangerous floater. He won Monaco in 12:52.54 and took silver in the 10,000m at the European Championships just six days before Lausanne. That European 10,000m effort shows brilliant stamina, but it also raises fatigue concerns for a 5000m six days later. His Oslo 5000m was poor — 13:08.78 — and his European 5000m final was only seventh in 13:18.24. On pure Monaco form he could win, but the recent championship workload drops him to sixth.

**Nico Young** is the hardest athlete to place. He owns the American outdoor 5000m record at 12:45.27 from Oslo in 2025 and was sixth in the World Championships final that year. But in 2026 he has no outdoor 5000m results listed before Lausanne. He has shown strong fitness in shorter races — 7:33.32 for 3000m and 3:34.56 for 1500m — but a 5000m off just those races is a different ask. I still expect him to be in the mix because of his class, but he is a slight unknown. Seventh feels fair.

**Mezgebu Sime** has been quietly excellent. He ran 12:50.17 in Oslo in 2026 and was seventh in that deep race, ahead of several better-known names. He lacks the championship medals of the top group, but his 5000m consistency in Diamond League settings is solid. He slots in just ahead of the Kenyan pack.

**Mathew Kipchumba Kipsang** is the Commonwealth Games champion from August 2026 and won in Budapest over 3000m in 7:31.90. His Paris 5000m in 12:58.95 was solid, and he has a strong cross-country background that makes him durable. The Commonwealth final was slow and tactical, but he won it, which shows he can handle pressure. He edges Ntakarutimana for ninth.

**Egide Ntakarutimana** deserves a top-ten projection. He was fourth in Paris in 12:56.06 and third in Turku in 12:59.45, and he has represented Burundi at multiple World Championships. He does not have the flashy PRs of some rivals, but his 2026 Diamond League form is excellent. He should be right in the fight for the back end of the top ten.

**Cornelius Kemboi** is a consistent 12:56–12:58 runner in 2026. He was fourth at the Commonwealth Games, albeit in a slow 13:24.99, and he has multiple Diamond League sub-13 efforts this season. He lacks the top-end kick to climb much higher, but he is too reliable to drop far.

**Laban Kiptoo Kosgei** is the clear “young gun” of the field. He is only 19, but he ran 12:57.32 at IFAM Oordegem in August 2026 and has improved throughout the year. He is not quite ready to beat the established Diamond League regulars, but he is ahead of the next group.

**Eduardo Herrera** has a fast 13:00.69 from Xiamen, but his Paris race was disappointing at 13:16.18, and his Central American and Caribbean Games 5000m win was slow. He is a national record holder and clearly classy, but the 2026 form is too inconsistent to rank higher.

**Santiago Catrofe** is a consistent 13:01–13:09 performer in 2026, with a 13:02.57 in Paris. He is a multiple Uruguayan record holder and a strong road runner, but he lacks the track footspeed of the men directly above him. He should still be in the top fifteen.

**Khairi Bejiga** is another promising young Ethiopian. He ran 13:06.45 in Xiamen and 13:07.06 in Monaco, and he has elite U20 road credentials. At 19, he is still finding his feet at this level, but he should beat the more specialised or out-of-form runners behind him.

**Getnet Wale** is primarily a steeplechaser. His 13:03.95 in Turku shows he has flat ability, but his 13:15.68 in Paris shows that he is not a genuine 5000m Diamond League contender. He will compete hard but likely loses contact with the main pack.

**Tim Verbaandert** has had an up-and-down 2026: a 13:13.34 in Oslo, a DNF in Paris, and tenth in the European Championships 5000m. He is a Dutch record holder and a solid professional, but this is a deep field. He should be the best of the non-elite tier.

**Charles Kiboino** has no significant 5000m results in 2026, only 10,000m races, including 27:22.80 in Ostrava. That suggests he has the engine, but a 5000m at Lausanne against this calibre is a big ask. He lands near the back.

**Kuma Girma** is the biggest form concern of the Ethiopians. He ran 12:46.41 in 2025 and looked like a future star, but his 2026 season has fallen apart: a DNF in Xiamen and a poor 13:33.07 in Paris. I cannot put him any higher than 19th on current form.

**Shimelis Niguse** has only a 13:33.80 5000m and a 28:16.57 10,000m to his name in 2026. He is outclassed here.

**Abderezak Suleman** has focused on 1500m and 3000m, with nothing close to a competitive 5000m in 2026. He should be near the back.

**Žan Rudolf** is a Slovenian 800m specialist with a long list of DNFs in 2026 at 1500m races. This 5000m is completely outside his comfort zone, and I expect him to be the last finisher by a wide margin.
blurbs.800m Women:
Predicted finish — Women’s 800m, Lausanne Diamond League, 21 August 2026:

1. Audrey Werro (SUI) — 1:54.42  
2. Femke Broeders-Bol (NED) — 1:55.31  
3. Lilian Odira (KEN) — 1:56.08  
4. Oratile Nowe (BOT) — 1:57.14  
5. Prudence Sekgodiso (RSA) — 1:57.39  
6. Addison Wiley (USA) — 1:57.71  
7. Saida Tsehaye (ETH) — 1:57.98  
8. Valentina Rosamilia (SUI) — 1:58.43  
9. Veronica Vancardo (SUI) — 1:58.67  
10. Sage Hurta-Klecker (USA) — 1:59.92  
11. Myrte van der Schoot (NED) — 2:04.15  

Why this order:

Audrey Werro is the clear favourite. Her 1:53.80 in Paris makes her the third-fastest woman in history, and she confirmed her major-race strength by winning the European title in 1:54.81 just a week before Lausanne. At 21, she is also the most complete 800m runner in this field right now — strong from the front, fast at the end, and racing in Switzerland in front of a home crowd.

Femke Broeders-Bol is the most credible challenger. Her transition from 400m hurdles to the 800m has been remarkably quick, and her 1:55.54 European final put her firmly ahead of everyone else here except Werro. She has both the 400m speed and the growing aerobic strength to run consistently in 1:55-low. She still lacks Werro’s specialist 800m depth over a full season, so she slots into second rather than threatening the win.

Lilian Odira is the reigning world champion and cannot be dismissed, but her 2026 outdoor form has not matched her 2025 title-winning level. Her best this season is 1:56.19, and she was only second in the Commonwealth final in 2:00.58. That shows she can still compete, but she has not produced the same sub-1:55 spark as Werro or even Broeders-Bol. I still put her third because her 1:56.19 at the Prefontaine Classic is better than anything the rest of the field has managed this year.

Oratile Nowe gets fourth on consistency. She has run 1:57.32 in Rabat and 1:57.46 in Paris, made Commonwealth finals, and avoided the kind of major championship collapse that has hurt some others. She lacks the finishing gear to beat the top three, but she is reliably in the 1:57 range.

Prudence Sekgodiso is difficult to rank because her best — 1:56.83 in Paris — is better than Nowe’s best this season. But her results after Paris fall away badly: 1:58.79 at Prefontaine and then a shock semifinal exit at the Commonwealth Games in 2:01.57. That inconsistency is why I have her behind Nowe. If she rediscovers her Paris form, she could move up, but the evidence from July suggests she is not arriving in Lausanne in peak shape.

Addison Wiley has had a solid but not spectacular season. She won in Doha in 1:57.98, ran 1:57.70 at Prefontaine, and took silver at US Championships, but she also ran 2:00.01 in London and 1:59.40 at USAs. She is competitive, but she has not shown enough sustained sub-1:57 speed to break into the top five here.

Saida Tsehaye is the wildcard — only 17 years old, but she ran 1:57.96 in Oordegem in early August. That is a genuine breakthrough performance. However, she also ran 2:04.22 in Doha and has very little top-level Diamond League experience. I expect her to be competitive but slightly inconsistent, so seventh.

Valentina Rosamilia and Veronica Vancardo are both in good national-team form after the European Championships. Rosamilia’s 1:58.16 semifinal in Birmingham is slightly better than Vancardo’s 1:58.20 heat, and Rosamilia also finished ahead of Vancardo in the European final. They are capable of running 1:58-low, but not quite enough to crack the top seven.

Sage Hurta-Klecker is the hardest to place because her last meaningful outdoor result this season was a 1:59.80 in mid-June. She has the pedigree — including a 1:55.89 World Championships final in 2025 — but her 2026 season has stalled around 1:58-low, with no recent evidence of top form. I have her tenth.

Myrte van der Schoot is a 400m specialist dipping into the 800m. Her only 800m attempt this season ended in a DNF in Paris, and while she is an excellent relay runner, she does not have the specific 800m strength yet. She should be a clear last if she finishes at all.
blurbs.200m Men:
**Predicted finish – Men’s 200m, Lausanne Diamond League, 21 August 2026:**

1. Letsile Tebogo (BOT) – **19.76**  
2. Sinesipho Dambile (RSA) – **19.83**  
3. José Figueroa (PUR) – **19.90**  
4. Makanakaishe Charamba (ZIM) – **19.96**  
5. Zharnel Hughes (GBR) – **20.05**  
6. Timothé Mumenthaler (SUI) – **20.14**  
7. Brandon Hicklin (USA) – **20.22**  
8. Courtney Lindsey (USA) – **20.28**

---

**Why this order:**

**Letsile Tebogo** remains the clear favourite. The Olympic 200m champion and 2025 World Championships finalist has the best blend of top-end speed and championship pedigree in this field. His 19.65 at the 2025 World final showed his ceiling, and in 2026 he has been consistently fast: 19.96 in Rabat, 19.84 in Oslo, and 19.93 in Eugene. He has also beaten Dambile head-to-head at both Rabat and Oslo this summer. At 22, he is the most complete 200m runner in the race and should control the bend before powering away late.

**Sinesipho Dambile** is the biggest threat to Tebogo. The new Commonwealth Games 200m champion ran 19.74 in Doha and 19.77 in Nairobi in 2026, and his 19.96 Commonwealth final win confirmed his ability to deliver under pressure. He has improved enormously from his 2025 World final appearance, where he finished 8th. However, in direct Diamond League meetings this season, Tebogo has had the edge. Dambile will push him hard, but Tebogo’s superior consistency against elite international fields gives him the narrow advantage.

**José Figueroa** is the most exciting young sprinter in the field. At 21, he has already won the Pan American Championships in 19.87 and followed it with a CAC Games title in 19.98. He also ran 19.76 with a legal? wind in the CAC heats, though his fully legal best is 19.87. His 2026 trajectory is remarkable, but a 20.34 at the Prefontaine Classic shows he can still be inconsistent at the highest Diamond League level. Still, his recent senior championship wins and rapid progression put him ahead of the rest of the chasing pack.

**Makanakaishe Charamba** has been excellent but not quite at the level of the top three in 2026. He has run 19.88 twice this season, in College Station and Doha, and reached the 2025 World Championships semifinal/final rounds. He was also third at the Prefontaine Classic behind Tebogo in 20.11. Dambile beat him convincingly in Doha, and Figueroa’s late-season peak looks stronger. Charamba’s consistency gives him 4th, but he will need a personal best to break into the medals.

**Zharnel Hughes** remains a classy, experienced competitor. The British record holder was European 200m silver medallist in 2026, running a windy 20.16 in the final and a legal 20.09 in the semi-final. His 2026 best legal time is 20.04, which is solid, but the top four have all run faster this season. At 30, Hughes can still beat almost anyone on his day, but he no longer has the raw speed to consistently challenge the younger 19.7/19.8 men. He gets 5th ahead of Mumenthaler based on his superior senior resume and his head-to-head win over Mumenthaler at the European final.

**Timothé Mumenthaler** is a genuine home-region favourite in Lausanne and a former European 200m champion. He ran a big 20.09 personal best in the European semi-final in 2026 before taking bronze. However, his 2026 season has been uneven: a DQ in Stockholm, 20.58 in Oslo, and a modest 20.51 at the Swiss Championships. He should be motivated by the Swiss crowd in Lausanne, but he still lacks the consistent fast times of those above him. A 20.1 performance seems likely.

**Brandon Hicklin** has had a strong year, most notably finishing 2nd in the 200m at the US Championships in 20.29. He also ran 19.92 at the Star Athletics meet, showing he has sub-20 ability on paper. But his Diamond League form in 200m this year has been less convincing, and his recent US final time of 20.29 suggests he still needs a faster, cleaner race to beat the international specialists. He edges Lindsey based on that 19.92 legal run and his national-level silver medal.

**Courtney Lindsey** rounds out the field. He was outstanding in 2025, including a 19.82 in the US Championships 200m final and a World Athletics Relay gold, but in 2026 he has largely focused on the 100m. His 200m marks this year are all in the 20.19–20.28 range, and he was behind Tebogo, Charamba, Hughes, and Figueroa at the Prefontaine Classic. His 100m form is still strong, but he has not yet shown the 200m sharpness needed to threaten the top group. A low-20.2 clocking is the realistic projection.

blurbs.High Jump Women:
Predicted finish – Women’s High Jump, Silesia Diamond League, 23 August 2026  
*Predicted bar progression: 1.80m, 1.84m, 1.88m, 1.92m, 1.96m, 1.98m, 2.00m, 2.02m, 2.04m*

1. Yaroslava Mahuchikh – 2.02m  
2. Nicola Olyslagers – 2.02m  
3. Eleanor Patterson – 2.00m  
4. Yuliia Levchenko – 2.00m  
5. Marija Vuković – 1.98m  
6. Maria Żodzik – 1.98m  
7. Angelina Topić – 1.96m  
8. Iryna Gerashchenko – 1.96m  
9. Lamara Distin – 1.92m  
10. Louise Ekman – 1.92m  
11. Vashti Cunningham – 1.92m  

---

**Why this order?**

This is a stacked field, but the top two pick themselves: Mahuchikh vs Olyslagers. Mahuchikh is the world record holder, the Olympic champion, and 2026 World Indoor champion. She also won this exact Silesia meeting in 2025 with 2.00m, and her 2026 season has been consistently strong: 2.01m at London, 2.00m at the Ukrainian Championships, and Euro gold in Birmingham. Olyslagers, the 2025 world champion and reigning Diamond League champion, beat Mahuchikh in London on countback at 2.01m and has the pedigree to win anywhere. But her 2026 Commonwealth Games was a red flag: she only managed 1.93m and lost to Patterson. Mahuchikh, by contrast, followed London with a European title. I give Mahuchikh the edge on a cleaner countback at 2.02m, with both failing at 2.04m.

Patterson and Levchenko are the best of the rest. Patterson is a former world champion and won Commonwealth gold in 2026, plus had 2.00m wins in Essen and Budapest. She has been the most consistent non-Mahuchikh/Olyslagers jumper outdoors this year. Levchenko has the high ceiling — 1.99m at the World Indoor Championships and 1.99m in Xiamen — but also had a 1.91m blip in Rabat. Both clearing 2.00m is realistic, but Patterson gets bronze on fewer misses.

The 1.98m group is the competitive heart of the field. Vuković is 33 but having a wonderful late-career revival: 1.98m in Athina and 1.98m in Budapest, plus Euro bronze in 2026. Żodzik has world and European silver medals in the last two years and will have a strong Polish crowd behind her in Silesia; she gets sixth only because Vuković has been more consistent at 1.98m outdoors. Topić has the biggest talent upside — a 2.00m indoor national record and 1.99m to share silver at the World Indoor Championships — but her 12th-place Euro finish at just 1.83m shows she is still very inconsistent outdoors. She clears 1.96m but fails 1.98m.

Gerashchenko is a solid but not spectacular 1.96m/1.97m jumper in 2026; her Xiamen 1.97m was good, but she was only 1.92m at the Euro final. Distin and Ekman are both capable of 1.92m, but neither has shown top-level outdoor form in 2026. Distin has the better overall résumé — Commonwealth champion and Jamaican record holder — so she gets ninth. Ekman’s big 1.96m indoor breakthrough hasn’t fully transferred to a high outdoor mark.

Cunningham, despite being a 2026 US champion, has struggled badly against this class of field all season: 1.83m in Rabat and 1.92m at US Champs is simply not enough to compete with the world-record holder and three world champions at the pointy end. She finishes last, clearing 1.92m but failing at 1.96m.

Predicted finish — Women’s Triple Jump, Silesia Diamond League, 23 August 2026 (all marks legal distances):

1. Leyanis Pérez Hernández (CUB) — 15.01 m  
2. Saly Sarr (SEN) — 14.97 m  
3. Davisleydi Velazco (CUB) — 14.91 m  
4. Thea Lafond (DMA) — 14.86 m  
5. Dariya Derkach (ITA) — 14.63 m  
6. Liadagmis Povea (CUB) — 14.57 m  
7. Aleksandra Nacheva (BUL) — 14.28 m  
8. Ackelia Smith (JAM) — 14.21 m  
9. Ivana Španović (SRB) — 14.12 m  
10. Saliyya Guisse (BEL) — 14.04 m  

---

Why this order?

**1. Leyanis Pérez Hernández** is the clear favourite. She is the reigning outdoor world champion and the 2025 and 2026 world indoor champion, and her 2026 outdoor form has been outstanding. She won Monaco with 15.06 m into a −0.1 headwind, and also produced a legal 14.93 m in Doha. Even when she underperformed in Oslo with 14.51 m, she immediately bounced back with 14.93 m and 15.06 m. In a head-to-head against the other top three, she has the best combination of peak and consistency.

**2. Saly Sarr** gets the edge for second because she has the strongest upward curve in the field. The 23-year-old Senegalese athlete has gone from 14.57 m in early June to 14.75 m in Oslo, 14.86 m in Doha, and 14.99 m in Monaco. That last mark was only 7 cm behind Pérez, and she beat both Lafond and Velazco in Monaco. She has also beaten Lafond in every shared meeting this season. She has not yet broken 15 m legally, but this meeting looks like the moment she could threaten it.

**3. Davisleydi Velazco** has the standout Diamond League result of the year with 15.13 m in Doha, where she finished ahead of Pérez and Sarr. She also beat Lafond in Oslo and Doha, and she has multiple 14.8 m-plus marks. However, she followed her Doha peak with 14.56 m in Essen and 14.66 m in Monaco. That inconsistency — and losing badly to Sarr in Monaco — keeps her just behind Sarr but clearly ahead of Lafond.

**4. Thea Lafond** is the biggest wildcard. Her 15.25 m in Zagreb is the best legal mark of the entire 2026 season and shows she can still beat anyone. But she did not back it up at Diamond League level: she jumped 14.49 m in Oslo, 14.52 m in Doha, and 14.79 m in Monaco. Sarr has beaten her in every meeting they shared this summer, and Velazco has beaten her more often than not. I still put her fourth because of her Olympic pedigree and that huge Zagreb result, but I am not predicting a repeat here.

**5. Dariya Derkach** is the European champion after winning with 14.60 m in Birmingham. She has been building through the season: 14.39 m, 14.51 m, 14.42 m, then 14.60 m in the European final. That championship consistency gives her the edge over the next group. She does not have the raw power of the top four, but she is in the best competitive form of her career.

**6. Liadagmis Povea** has the higher ceiling of the next group — her 14.71 m at the Central American and Caribbean Games was strong, and she jumped 14.58 m in Doha. But she has also been very inconsistent, including a poor 14.03 m in Zagreb and several 14.2 m-level jumps. Derkach gets the nod because of recent championship momentum and fewer poor outings.

**7. Aleksandra Nacheva** is the best of the remaining Europeans. She won in Istanbul with a legal 14.35 m and then took bronze at the European Championships, even if that 14.40 m was wind-assisted. She has shown she can post 14.2–14.4 m consistently, which should be enough to beat the final three.

**8. Ackelia Smith** is difficult to rank because of her 14.50 m in Oslo. That was a genuine standout result, placing her right with the top group that day. But after Oslo she produced 13.95 m, 14.02 m, and 14.04 m in triple jump. With her season also focusing heavily on the long jump, I expect her to land around 14.2 m rather than reproduce the Oslo mark.

**9. Ivana Španović** is one of the greatest long jumpers in history, but as a triple jumper at age 35 she is no longer at the elite level. Her best legal outdoor triple jump this season appears to be 14.25 m in Zagreb, and she was only 14.06 m wind-assisted at the European final. She is still competitive, but the younger specialists have moved past her in this event.

**10. Saliyya Guisse** rounds out the field. Her European silver medal was a great result, but it was aided by a +2.4 m/s wind and her legal best is only 14.07 m. Without a helpful breeze, she lacks the top-end speed and power to finish higher against this international field.

---

## Race Preview and Reasoning

### The top three: Ajayi, Seville and Eseme separate themselves

This is a genuinely loaded field, but the strongest case belongs to **Kayinsola Ajayi**. Still only 21, he won the NCAA 100m title in 2026, then produced two massive legal Diamond League wins: **9.84 (+0.1) at the Prefontaine Classic** and **9.84 (-0.7) in London**. In London he beat **Oblique Seville** head-to-head, as he had done earlier in Eugene. That head-to-head record is crucial — Ajayi has now repeatedly out-kicked the reigning world champion in big professional races. His only minor blip was the Commonwealth Games final, where he ran 9.90 and took bronze, but that came after a very fast London race and a long NCAA season. With rest and a Diamond League stage, he is the most logical winner.

**Oblique Seville** is the safest pick for second. The 2025 world champion has the fastest legal time in the field this season: **9.82 (+0.6)** at the Jamaican Championships. He also won Monaco in 9.88 and ran 9.87 in London behind Ajayi. Seville is not as consistently explosive out of the blocks as Ajayi, but his top-end speed is elite. If Ajayi falters even slightly, Seville is the most likely successor.

**Emmanuel Eseme** gets third over the American cluster. At 32, he produced a season-defining win at the Commonwealth Games: **9.83 (+1.3)** in the final, with a 9.89 semi-final. That is better than anything Ronnie Baker or Kenneth Bednarek have done legally in 2026. Eseme’s London race was poor by comparison — only 9.97 — but he has now shown he can follow a bad race with a massive championship-level performance. On the Silesia track, where late-season sprinting can be quick, Eseme should be right in the medals mix.

### The American chase pack: Baker, Bednarek, Anthony, Coleman

Behind the top three, the American contingent is deep but slightly below the top trio.

**Ronnie Baker** has revived his career impressively at 32. At the 2026 US Championships he finished second in the final in **9.88 (+0.8)**, beating both Bednarek and Coleman directly. That head-to-head result gives him the edge here. His start is world-class, and at his best he can challenge 9.85. The question is whether he can produce another 9.87-level run after a long season.

**Kenneth Bednarek** is the most physically powerful sprinter in the field, and his **9.72w (+2.4)** in Los Angeles was the rawest speed anyone has shown this year. But his legal 100m results are less overwhelming: 9.88 at US Champs, 9.96 at Pre, 9.98 in Shaoxing. He is a better 200m runner, and although he finishes strongly, his 100m acceleration still costs him against pure 100m specialists. Fifth is about right, though a shock podium is not impossible if the race comes down to the final 30m.

**Jordan Anthony** is the reigning world indoor 60m champion and has elite top speed — his 6.41 indoor run is the fastest anyone has run this year. Outdoors, he has been excellent but not yet dominant: **9.92 in Monaco** and 9.99 in London. He is still only 21, and his trajectory is clearly upward, but he has not quite shown he can produce 9.85 in a stacked outdoor Diamond League race. Sixth feels fair, with room to move up.

**Christian Coleman** is the toughest former star to rank. The 2019 world champion and 60m world-record holder still has a great start, but his 2026 legal 100m best is only **9.93 (+0.8)** from US Champs, where he finished fourth behind Baker and Bednarek. Coleman’s 9.84w at the LA Grand Prix showed he still has fast legs, but he is no longer consistently breaking 9.90 in legal conditions. At 29, he remains dangerous, but the data says he is now a 9.90–9.95 sprinter rather than a 9.80 sprinter.

### Kennedy, Leotlela and the inconsistent veterans

**Lachlan Kennedy** is the most intriguing outside threat. The 22-year-old Australian won Commonwealth silver with **9.85 (+1.3)**, which is elite-level confirmation of his 60m speed. However, his Diamond League form outside that one race has been moderate: 10.01 in Shaoxing, 10.06 in Xiamen, 10.09 at Pre. If he catches a perfect race, he could challenge for the podium, but his consistency is not yet at Ajayi or Seville’s level.

**Gift Leotlela** has had a quietly good year: he won the 100m in Shaoxing with 9.97, placed second in Xiamen with 10.00, and ran 9.91 at the Commonwealth Games. At 27, he is in his prime, but he lacks the very top-end speed to beat the very best in a fast Diamond League final. Ninth is a fair projection.

**Trayvon Bromell** is the hardest to judge. On pure talent and history, he should be higher. He won the Paris Diamond League in June with **9.91 (+0.1)** and has a 9.85w from Texas. But after Paris, he essentially disappears from the competitive record — no US Championships, no Commonwealth Games, no late-season races. That suggests either injury or a carefully managed training block. At the Silesia meeting in 2025 he was only fifth in 9.97. If he is fit and race-sharp, he could finish top five; if he is rusty, he could fall even further. Tenth is a cautious but data-driven call.

**Romell Glave** became European champion in 2026 with a 10.09 wind-legal win, but his best 100m this summer is a legal **9.97 in London**. That is very good but not enough to crack the top seven here. He is a strong championship runner, but the Diamond League field is deeper than the European Championships field.

### The rest: Blake, Ansah, Simbine, Azu, Blaskowski, de Grasse, Kopeć

**Ackeem Blake** has the talent to be top five, but he has been alarmingly inconsistent in 2026. He ran 9.94 at Jamaican Championships, but then produced 10.06 at Pre, 10.04 in Budapest, and a bizarre 11.55 at the LA Track Festival. At 23, he should be more reliable, but he is not.

**Owen Ansah** is a genuine breakthrough sprinter — the first German under 10 seconds — and his 200m gold at the 2026 European Championships shows he is in great form. But in the 100m, his legal best this season is only 10.00, with a 10.01 in Monaco. He lacks the raw speed of the elite 100m men, though he could run a late-season 9.9x.

**Akani Simbine** remains a class act, and his **9.97 in Paris** shows he can still run fast at 32. But the former African record holder is no longer the consistent 9.85-level threat he was in his prime. He has finished behind the new generation repeatedly, and 14th reflects his current standing.

**Jeremiah Azu** is a proven championship sprinter — European indoor and world indoor 60m champion — but his 100m outdoors has not reached the same level. He ran 10.03 at the Commonwealth Games and 10.16 in the European final. He is competitive, but not quite a sub-9.90 contender.

**Sam Blaskowski** is fascinating because of his 9.89 (+1.5) at the Music City Track Carnival, which suggests genuine 9.85 potential. But his Diamond League results have been far less impressive: 10.06 in Monaco and 10.12 in Budapest. Until he shows he can produce that speed on the big circuit, he remains an outsider.

**Andre de Grasse** is a seven-time Olympic medallist and one of the greatest championship sprinters of his generation, but in 2026 the 100m is clearly his secondary event. He ran 9.95 in Botswana and 10.02 in Paris, but his 200m (19.95) is stronger. At 31, he can still pop a 9.9x on the right day, but a top-five finish here looks beyond him.

**Dominik Kopeć** is a solid European-level sprinter, but his 10.29 at the European final and his Polish title in 10.24 show he is not at the global elite level. In this company, he is the clear outsider.

---

Final verdict: **Ajayi** wins a tight, high-quality race from **Seville** and **Eseme**, with the American pack left fighting for places behind them. The race will likely be decided between 60 and 90 metres, where Ajayi’s late-race power and Seville’s world-class cruising speed will pull clear.

### Why this order

**Alison dos Santos over Karsten Warholm**  
Dos Santos has the strongest 2026 credentials. He ran a world-leading 46.48 at the Brazilian Championships, plus 46.72 and 46.89 in Diamond League wins in Xiamen and Oslo. In both of those races he beat Warholm head-to-head. His flat 400m speed is also excellent: 44.38 in April and 44.60 at Brazilians, which gives him a serious finish over the last 100m. Warholm remains the greatest championship hurdler of his generation — world record holder, European champion in 2026, and winner of last year’s Silesia meeting in 46.28 — but in 2026 dos Santos has simply been faster and more decisive in their direct meetings. I expect Warholm to push him hard on a fast track, but dos Santos takes it.

**Ezekiel Nathaniel third**  
Nathaniel is clearly the best of the chasing pack. He was second in Silesia in 2025 in 47.31, fourth at the 2025 World Championships in a Nigerian record 47.11, and won the 2026 Commonwealth Games. His 2026 flat 400m best of 45.32 also shows he has plenty of speed. However, his 48.30 in London and 48.47 in the Commonwealth final show he hasn’t consistently recaptured his 47.1-level form. He should still beat everyone except the big two if he runs a clean race.

**Trevor Bassitt ahead of Caleb Dean and Matheus Lima**  
Bassitt has been quietly excellent in 2026: 47.37, 47.59, 47.82. He also beat both Dean and Lima at the Budapest meeting, finishing second in 47.59 ahead of Dean’s 47.62 and Lima’s 47.74. Dean has similar speed — 47.42 and 47.62 — but his London disaster of 50.45 and 48.66 at US Championships make him less reliable. Lima has real talent and ran 47.37 in Stockholm, but his Diamond League consistency is still patchy: 48.22 in Xiamen, 48.37 in Oslo, 48.33 in London. Bassitt is the most reliable of the three and gets the nod.

**Abderrahman Samba fading but still above the Euro pair**  
Samba is not the force he once was. He was second man ever under 47 seconds and a World bronze medallist in 2025, but his 2026 season has been modest: 47.93 in Xiamen, 48.60 in Oslo, 48.31 in Budapest, 48.10 in London. At 30, he is still competitive, but he no longer looks capable of dipping near 47. He should outrun İsmail Nezir and Oskar Edlund based on experience and his better 2026 floor.

**Nezir over Edlund**  
Nezir won European bronze in 48.26 and ran 48.16 in the semi-final, while Edlund was fourth in 48.36 after a brilliant 47.81 semi-final. Nezir got the better of Edlund when it mattered in Birmingham, and he has shown more consistent global-level racing in 2026. Edlund has a higher ceiling on his best day — that 47.81 proves it — but he hasn’t yet shown he can produce that in a fast, high-pressure final. Nezir is the safer pick.

**Predicted Finish & Marks – Women’s 400m, Silesia Diamond League, 23 August 2026**

2. **Henriette Jæger (NOR)** — **49.03**

**Why this order?**

**Marileidy Paulino is the clear favourite.** Her 2026 season is simply on another level: she has multiple sub-49s — 48.48 in Paris, 48.67 in Monaco, 48.91 in Doha, 48.94 at the CAC Games, and 48.97 in London. She also won this exact Silesia meeting in 2025. She is the Olympic champion, the world No. 1, and the only athlete in this field with multiple 48-second performances in 2026. Nobody here beats her unless she makes a major error.

**Henriette Jæger gets second on momentum.** The young Norwegian is in the form of her life. She won the European title on 15 August with 49.04, and before that ran 49.15 in London, 49.52 in Oslo, and 49.60 in Roma. That is a remarkably consistent late-season progression. She also finished third at Silesia in 2025, so she knows the stadium. Her 49.04 is arguably more impressive than a one-off fast race because she has backed it up again and again.

**Aaliyah Butler is the biggest threat, but I place her third.** Butler owns the fastest non-Paulino time of 2026: her 48.84 runner-up finish in Monaco was electric. That time alone would put her second. However, her other 2026 races — 49.78, 49.83, 49.90, 49.93 — are all in the 49.7–50.0 range, not quite at Jæger’s consistent 49.0–49.6 level. Butler also hasn’t raced since the US Championships on 25 July, so there is a slight rust/unknown factor. In a fast Silesia race, she could absolutely outkick Jæger, but based on season-long consistency, I give Jæger the edge.

**Stacey Ann Williams takes fourth.** She has been quietly excellent in 2026: 49.48 in Zagreb, 49.51 in Paris, 49.52 in London, and 49.80 in Texas. She also finished third in London ahead of Pryce, Bukowiecka, and Gómez. Williams has multiple sub-49.6 performances, which puts her clearly above the next cluster.

**Nickisha Pryce is fifth.** The Jamaican is consistent — 49.56 in Monaco, 49.75 in Shaoxing, 49.80 in Roma — but she hasn’t quite matched Williams in their 2026 head-to-heads. At London, Williams beat her 49.52 to 50.09. Pryce is definitely in the 49.5–50.0 range, but Williams has the faster peak and better recent results.

**Natalia Bukowiecka just edges Lieke Klaver for sixth.** Both are coming off strong European Championships: Bukowiecka took silver with 50.04, and Klaver took bronze with 50.15. Bukowiecka also ran 49.57 in her Euro semi-final, while Klaver’s best is 49.58 from Monaco. It’s close, but Bukowiecka’s European final result and slightly faster season best put her ahead.

**Lieke Klaver is seventh.** She has been a model of consistency and ran 49.58 in Monaco and 49.71 in her Euro semi-final. But she also has several 50.6 races in 2026, and in the biggest races this summer she has been just behind Bukowiecka. Still a major relay and 400m talent, but at Silesia I expect her to be in the 49.6–49.8 range.

**Roxana Gómez is eighth.** The Cuban has been solidly in the 50.0–50.4 range all season, with a 49.99 at the CAC Games. She doesn’t have the 49.5 speed of Williams, Pryce, Bukowiecka, or Klaver in 2026. She is a tough competitor and rarely runs badly, but this field has moved past her in the last two years.

**Salwa Eid Naser is last — with a major caveat.** This is purely a form-based ranking. Naser is a former world champion and ran 48.19 at the 2025 World Championships, but her 2026 results are almost nonexistent. Her only listed 400m in 2026 is a 51.56 in Shaoxing in May. That is far below the rest of this field. If she has recovered and found her old form, she could be top three, but based on the data available, she has to be projected last.

**Why this order?**

**Top tier: el Bakkali, Edmund Serem, Godana, Bebendorf**  
Soufiane el Bakkali remains the man to beat. He is a two-time Olympic champion and has repeatedly shown he can produce lethal closing speed in fast Diamond League races. His 2026 Rabat win in 7:57.25 is the quickest anyone in this field has run this season, and even allowing for a slightly less aggressive Silesia race, he should control the pace and kick away over the final lap. His only real loss among this group was at the Tokyo World Championships in 2025, but his 2026 form suggests he has moved on.

Edmund Serem is only 18 but has already won the Commonwealth Games and taken bronze at the 2025 World Championships. His 8:01.61 in Rabat in 2026 is comfortably faster than anyone else here except el Bakkali. He was beaten by both Godana and Bebendorf in Paris in June, which is why he is not an automatic second, but his ceiling appears higher. In a clean, fast race, his youth and raw strength should carry him to second.

Gemechu Godana has had a genuine breakthrough year. He won the African Championships title and then ran 8:05.86 in Paris, only 0.31 seconds behind Karl Bebendorf. At 20, he is improving rapidly and is less likely to be flat after a major championship. I put him third ahead of Bebendorf because Silesia comes just one week after the European Championships, where Bebendorf had to race hard and took bronze. Godana has had more time to sharpen for this Diamond League race.

Karl Bebendorf deserves huge credit for his Paris win in 8:05.55, which was the standout performance of his career. He also ran consistently in Stockholm and at the European Championships. However, he is 29 and coming off a championship campaign. I expect him to be in the lead group for most of the race, but he may lack the final 200-metre surge needed to hold off the younger Africans.

**Chasing pack: Firewu, ben Yazide, Miura, Wilkinson, Tindouft, Arce**  
Samuel Firewu has been the steadiest of the next group. He won in Xiamen in 2025 with 8:05.61, and in 2026 he has produced 8:10.44 in Doha and 8:09.13 in Paris. He was disappointing in Rabat, but that race was unusually fast and he perhaps went out too hard. In Silesia, with a more controlled pace, he should be the best of the non-elite group.

Salah Eddine ben Yazide has a very similar profile to Firewu but with slightly less impressive top-end speed in 2026. He won in Ostrava in 8:09.88 and ran 8:10.64 in Rabat, but his 2025 Monaco run of 8:06.44 shows he has the talent to be higher. I still place him ahead of Miura because he has been more consistent in 2026 and is racing with confidence after a strong Moroccan season.

Ryuji Miura is the big unknown. His Japanese record of 8:03.43 in Monaco in 2025 proves he can run with the world’s best, but his 2026 season has been more uneven. A 13th-place finish in Stockholm in 8:23.97 was a warning sign, even though he bounced back with 8:10.30 in Monaco. In Silesia, I expect him to be competitive but not quite able to challenge the top five.

Matthew Wilkinson is consistently in the 8:09–8:14 range. His 8:09.56 in Rabat was strong, and he has a solid Olympic pedigree from making the Paris Games. However, he has not shown the ability to go much faster than 8:09, and he was only 10th at the US Championships, which is why he falls behind Miura and the Moroccans.

Mohamed Tindouft has run well in smaller meetings, including 8:10.04 in Ostrava and 8:10.77 in Rabat, but he has also had multiple DNFs in high-level Diamond League races. His inconsistency is a concern. Daniel Arce is reliable but lacks the raw speed of the men above him. His 8:11.42 in Rabat and 8:13.35 in Doha are respectable, but at 33, he is unlikely to find another gear in Silesia.

**Middle group: Mountain, Querinjean, Daru, Faid, Buchholz**  
Nathan Mountain is a fascinating entry. He won the US title in 8:13.81 and ran 8:11.92 earlier in the year, so he has genuine sub-8:15 ability. His inexperience on the Diamond League circuit is the main reason I do not place him higher, but his speed and momentum from the US Championships give him the edge over the Europeans.

Ruben Querinjean is a proven international performer, having won a Diamond League race in Brussels in 2025 and taken silver at the 2026 European Championships. However, his 2026 Diamond League marks have been more modest: 8:14.22 in Monaco and 8:15.45 in Paris. The Euro silver came in a tactical race, not a fast time trial, so in a quick Silesia race he may be slightly exposed.

Nicolas-Marie Daru is still capable of running 8:11 or 8:12, as he showed in Rabat and Paris, but his 8:33.15 in Monaco and 8:29.46 at the European Championships show the 37-year-old cannot produce those marks every week. Faid el Mostafa ran 8:11.64 in Rabat, which is faster than many of his rivals, but he has also failed to finish in Doha and at the Moroccan Championships in 2026. His unreliability pushes him down.

Niklas Buchholz has a solid 8:15.27 from Turku, but he was ninth at the European Championships and has not shown the ability to go under 8:15 with any regularity. He should finish midfield but not challenge the top ten.

**Final group: Amos Serem, Megier, Bouassel**  
Amos Serem’s 2021 U20 world title feels distant now. In 2026 he has run 8:21.30 at best in Monaco and struggled badly in Doha and at the African Championships. Maciej Megier is a strong European U23 champion, but he was well beaten in Stockholm and failed to make the European final this year. Abderrafia Bouassel has excellent talent on paper, but his recent record is littered with DNFs in Diamond League races. I predict he will stay upright and finish last, but his overall reliability is still a major concern.

Ultimately, Silesia should produce a fast, honest steeplechase. El Bakkali will likely take the race out quickly, Edmund Serem will try to stay with him, and the battle for the remaining podium spots should be fierce. But class and consistency point to another Diamond League win for the Moroccan master.

Ja’Kobe Tharp is the clear favourite. He arrives as the world-record holder after his 12.75 at the 2026 NCAA Championships, and he has backed that up all summer with 12.91 at Prefontaine, 12.85 in Budapest and 12.89 in London. For a 20-year-old, that level of consistency in Diamond League company is extraordinary. Unless he hits a hurdle, this is his race.

The main fight is for second. I’ve given Jamal Britt the edge based on ceiling: his 12.86 win at Prefontaine included a head-to-head victory over Tharp, and he also ran 12.89 in Paris and 12.98 in Zagreb. Britt has had bad races this season — the 13.16 in London and the 13.85 in Doha stand out as warning signs — but when his rhythm is right, he is the only man in this field who has run within a tenth of Tharp in 2026. I’m projecting a bounce-back race.

Kendry L. Menéndez has the momentum to push Britt. The 19-year-old Cuban has been superb since June, with 13.02 in Zagreb, 13.09 in Budapest and a breakthrough 13.01 behind Tharp in London. In that London race, Menéndez finished ahead of Britt, Tinch and Cunningham, which is a huge statement. I rate him third, but he wouldn’t surprise me by taking second if Britt misfires again.

Cordell Tinch is the reigning world champion and the 2026 US champion after his 13.00 in New York. He also won this meeting in 2025 in 13.03, so the Silesia track suits him. However, his 13.17 in London and 13.06 in Budapest show he has been slightly behind the very sharp end of this field this summer. His US title was strong, but it came without Tharp, Britt and Cunningham in the final, so I’m slightly hesitant to rank it above Menéndez’s London performance.

Trey Cunningham remains frustratingly consistent rather than spectacular: he won Rome in 12.98 and ran 13.03 in Los Angeles, but his 13.07 in Paris and 13.12 in London suggest he hasn’t quite found another gear. He should be in the mix for fourth or fifth, but I don’t see him jumping the Americans ahead of him based on the recent head-to-heads.

Orlando Bennett has had solid results — 13.15 at Prefontaine and 13.21 in London — but also a poor 13.40 in Budapest. He is a proven championship finalist, but in this loaded field he looks more like a mid-pack finisher than a podium threat. Just Kwaou-Mathey’s European silver medal in 13.16 shows he can deliver in a final, but his 13.76 in Rome and 13.57 in Doha remind us that his floor is still high. Jakub Szymański will have home support in Poland, and his 13.26 European bronze was a breakthrough, but outdoor 110m hurdles remains a step below his world-class indoor 60m form. Rachid Muratake ran 13.05 in Osaka in May and 13.13 in Xiamen, which would put him higher on paper, but he faded to 13.21 in Paris and has not shown the same late-summer sharpness as the others. I expect him to round out the field unless he rediscovers his spring form in Chorzów.

Why this order:

**1. Kristjan Čeh over 2. Mykolas Alekna**  
Čeh gets the nod because of his 2026 championship form. He just won the European title in Birmingham with 72.51 m, and he has multiple 72-metre throws this season: 72.61 m in Ramona, 72.26 m in Ramona, 71.86 m at the Slovenian Championships and 70.58 m in the Diamond League in China. Alekna is the world record holder and threw a huge 72.65 m at the Lithuanian Championships in July, but in the direct 2026 head-to-head that matters most — the European final — Čeh beat him decisively, 72.51 m to 69.89 m. Čeh is peaking at the right time; Alekna is slightly more vulnerable to being contained in the 69–70 m range.

**3. Henrik Janssen over 4. Daniel Ståhl**  
Janssen was the standout German in 2026 and took European bronze with 69.53 m, directly ahead of Ståhl, who finished fourth with 68.22 m. That head-to-head is the key separator. Janssen has been extremely consistent: 68.54 m in Rehlingen, 68.47 m in Wiesbaden, 68.21 m at the FBK Games, and then his big 69.53 m at the Europeans. His only major blemish in recent years was the no-mark in the 2025 World Championship final, but his 2026 profile is much more stable. Ståhl is a three-time world champion and won the 2025 world title with 70.47 m, but in 2026 he has not reached 70 m and his best results — 69.85 m at the Swedish Championships and 69.60 m in Stockholm — put him just behind Janssen on current form.

**5. Matthew Denny over 6. Roje Stona**  
Denny gets fifth because he is more reliable than Stona at this point. Denny won the 2026 Commonwealth Games title with 67.73 m, and he has a string of consistent 67–69 m competitions this year, including 69.02 m in Stockholm and 68.74 m early in the season. His April marks of 74.04 m and 73.58 m show his ceiling is still elite, even if he has not rediscovered that level recently. Stona is the Olympic champion and has serious talent — he threw 70.66 m in Ramona and 69.11 m in Oklahoma — but he has also thrown in the low-63s multiple times recently, including 63.73 m in late July. Denny’s floor is higher, and that is more valuable in a Diamond League field this deep.

**7. Ruben Rolvink over 8. Steven Richter**  
Rolvink has momentum and consistency. He set the Dutch record with 71.22 m in Ramona in May and backed it up with 70.23 m, 69.08 m, 67.88 m and a European final appearance where he threw 65.45 m. He is young, left-handed, improving and now a genuine international final-level thrower. Richter, by contrast, has a huge ceiling — his 74.00 m in Ramona in April was one of the best throws in the world this year — but he has not translated that into major meets. He failed to qualify from the European Championships with only 62.02 m, and his late-season form has been erratic. The talent is obvious, but Rolvink is the safer pick right now.

**9. Alex Rose over 10. Ralford Mullings**  
Rose edges Mullings based on recent head-to-head form. Rose was the 2025 world bronze medallist and threw 70.43 m in Ramona in April 2026. He has not been at that level lately, but he was 65.86 m at Prefontaine and fourth at the Commonwealth Games with 63.32 m. Mullings, the two-time NCAA champion, has had a quieter 2026: he won the NCAA title with 65.81 m, but was only 64.94 m at Prefontaine and fifth at the Commonwealth Games with 62.85 m. In their Commonwealth clash, Rose finished one place and almost half a metre ahead. Mullings has the higher ceiling from 2025 — 69.66 m in Brussels — but his 2026 form places him at the back of this very strong field.

---

**Why this order?**

I’ve weighted 2026 outdoor form heavily, while using 2025 championship pedigree as a tie-breaker. Silesia usually produces an honest, fast 1500m, so the athletes who have already shown they can run 3:55–3:58 this season should be the ones fighting at the front.

**Top group: Haylom, Ewoi, Hull, Duguma, Guillemot**

Birke Haylom gets the nod for the win. She has the best 2026 1500m form in the field: a clear 3:55.56 Diamond League win in Shaoxing, a strong 3:57.79 in Xiamen, and a win in Doha. That Shaoxing race is particularly valuable for comparison because she beat Duguma, Ewoi, Hull, MacKay, Billings, Hollingsworth and Hall in the same race. At 19, she is young, but her consistency this year is better than anyone else’s.

Dorcus Ewoi is my pick for second. Her 2025 World Championships silver medal in 3:54.92 is the single best championship result in this field, and she has carried that form into 2026 with 3:57.74 in Shaoxing and 3:58.91 in Xiamen. She also got the better of Jessica Hull in both of their 2026 1500m meetings, and she was second in the Prefontaine mile behind Nikki Hiltz. Ewoi’s proven ability to produce a huge race when it matters makes her the safest bet to challenge Haylom.

Jessica Hull is third. Yes, her 2026 1500m form has been slightly below her best — she was 6th in Shaoxing, 5th in Xiamen and 4th in Paris, with a 4th in the Prefontaine mile. But her overall credentials are enormous: Olympic silver, World Championships bronze, Oceanian records, and a 2026 World Indoor silver in the 1500m. Her London 3000m win in 8:24.69 and Commonwealth Games medals show she is fit and competitive. In a fast, clean race, she has more proven class than anyone except perhaps Ewoi, but Ewoi has simply had her number recently.

Tsige Duguma is fourth. Her 3:55.71 in Shaoxing was the breakthrough 1500m of her career and just behind Haylom. She is also a world-class 800m runner, as shown by her 1:56.92 in London, which gives her excellent closing speed. The concern is that she has not consistently backed up that 1500m form — she was 5th in a slower 1500m in Budapest in July. If she has a good day, she could top the podium; I think she lands just off it.

Agathe Guillemot rounds out the top five. Her 3:56.24 in Paris is the best 1500m time by any European in this field this season, and she beat Hull directly there. She is also the French record holder and a former European Indoor champion. The European Championships final in Birmingham was tactical and the time was slow, but that does not erase her Paris performance. She is genuine top-five material here.

**Middle pack: Hiltz, Kazimierska, MacKay, Hollingsworth, Billings, Silva, Hall**

Nikki Hiltz is sixth. Hiltz has been remarkably consistent and is the reigning US champion in the 1500m/mile. The Prefontaine mile win in 4:17.49 was excellent, and she has 2025 World Championship final experience, finishing 5th. But her 2026 outdoor 1500m best is only 3:59.26 in Rome, and that is a clear step behind the top five in this field.

Klaudia Kazimierska is seventh. The European silver medallist and Polish record-holder indoors, she has had a strong 2026: 2nd in Rome in 3:59.24, 4th in the Prefontaine mile, and a silver at the European Championships. With the crowd in Chorzów behind her, she could push higher, but Hiltz’s superior American record pedigree and 2025 Worlds 5th place just give her the edge.

Emily MacKay is eighth. She has been extremely consistent in 2026 with 3:58.13 in Xiamen and 3:58.54 in Shaoxing, and she was second in the World Indoor 3000m. She lacks the standout sub-3:57 performance that the athletes above her have produced, but she should be firmly in the top eight.

Claudia Hollingsworth and Sarah Billings are next. Both are versatile Australian middle-distance runners with elite 800m speed. Hollingsworth’s 3:58.84 in Shaoxing and Commonwealth Games mile bronze give her a slight edge over Billings, whose 3:58.81 was almost identical in Shaoxing but who has been more 800m-focused in 2026. Billings’ Oceanian 800m record and Commonwealth bronze are classy, but Hollingsworth’s 1500m win at the Australian Championships and stronger mile result tip the balance.

Patricia Silva is 11th. The European Championships bronze medallist ran 3:58.74 in Paris and has been very solid all season. She is a tough, tactically smart runner, but her 1500m ceiling is slightly below the group ahead of her.

Linden Hall is 12th. The 34-year-old has a fantastic 2025 Silesia reference — 6th in 3:56.39 — and has been a major force in Australian middle-distance running for years. But in 2026 she has not matched that level, with a best of 3:58.96 in Shaoxing and a heavy Commonwealth Games 5000m campaign in her legs. I expect her to be competitive but not quite at her 2025 Silesia form.

**Lower half: Berhe, Healy, Lizakowska, Johnson, Parks, Ibarzabal**

Saron Berhe is 13th. She is only 18 but has already run 4:00.32 in Xiamen and was 2nd in Doha. Her inconsistency is the issue — she has also been 13th in Shaoxing and 11th in the Prefontaine mile. Still, in a fast race she has more 2026 speed than most of the remaining field.

Sarah Healy is 14th. Healy’s 2025 season was much better than her 2026, with a 3:57.15 in Paris and European Indoor 3000m gold. This year, though, she has not gone faster than 4:01.50 in a 1500m, and she was 5th in the European final in 4:10.76. Her 3000m form is good, but the 1500m sharpness is just not there yet.

Weronika Lizakowska is 15th. The home athlete will have crowd support, and she has been consistent in European competition, but her 2026 best of 4:03.69 is below the international standard in this field. She was 12th at Silesia in 2025, and I don’t see her improving enough to crack the top 14 here.

Sinclaire Johnson is 16th. Johnson owns the North American mile record and was a genuine world 1500m finalist in 2025, but 2026 has been a difficult year. Her Sir Walter Miler performance — 4:25.15 for the mile with a 4:07.42 1500m split — is far below what she is capable of. I can’t justify putting her any higher.

Taryn Parks is 17th. She has shown flashes of 4:05-level form, including in the US Championships heats, but her 2026 record also includes multiple DNFs and a 12th-place finish in the US final. In this company, she is too unreliable to trust for a higher placing.

Lorea Ibarzabal is last. She is an Olympian and multiple Spanish champion, but she is primarily an 800m runner. Her 1500m best this season is only 4:07.28, and she also DNF’d in this exact race in 2025. Against a field this deep, that does not project beyond the back of the pack.
blurbs.400m Men:
**Predicted Finish – Men’s 400m, Silesia Diamond League (23 August 2026)**

1. **Busang Collen Kebinatshipi (BOT)** – **43.47**
2. **Rai Benjamin (USA)** – **43.92**
3. **Jacory Patterson (USA)** – **44.01**
4. **Zakithi Nene (RSA)** – **44.12**
5. **Chris Bailey (USA)** – **44.21**
6. **Jereem Richards (TTO)** – **44.48**
7. **Attila Molnár (HUN)** – **44.54**
8. **Bayapo Ndori (BOT)** – **44.72**
9. **Maksymilian Szwed (POL)** – **45.08**

---

### Why This Order

**Kebinatshipi is the clear favourite.** The reigning world champion has been the most dominant 400m runner on the planet in 2026. His season includes straight wins at Xiamen (43.92), Paris (43.54), Eugene (44.00), and Monaco (43.44). That Monaco mark is the fastest anyone in this field has run in 2026 by a significant margin. He also showed range and speed with a stunning 9.89 100m in Botswana in April, but his 400m consistency is what matters here. At 21, he is at the peak of his powers, and Silesia should be another controlled victory.

**Rai Benjamin gets the nod for second.** His 2026 flat 400m progression has been excellent: 44.69 in Tokyo, then 44.11 in Eugene, 44.13 in Monaco, and 44.05 in London. He has also beaten Patterson head-to-head twice this season, in Eugene and London, and his London 44.05 was the best flat 400m of his career. Benjamin’s 400m hurdles pedigree — he is the world champion and Olympic champion in that event — gives him elite endurance and race composure. There is a chance he threatens 43.8 here, which would make him the clear runner-up.

**Patterson is right behind Benjamin.** He has the fastest 2026 non-Kebinatshipi victory? Actually his 43.96 at Monaco is his standout result, and he also won Rabat in 44.11. He is hugely consistent at 44.0–44.3. However, he lost to Benjamin at Eugene and London, and his 44.88 in Eugene showed he can still have an off race. He is a genuine podium threat, but Benjamin has been the more reliable performer in their direct meetings.

**Nene is the biggest wildcard.** His 43.89 in Paris was the second-fastest 400m time by anyone in this field this year, only behind Kebinatshipi’s 43.54. That suggests enormous upside. But he also ran 45.21 in the Commonwealth final and 45.70 in the semi-final after a heavy season. That inconsistency is why I place him fourth rather than second. Still, his 44.24 in Monaco and 44.40 in Xiamen show he can mix with the top tier. If he finds the form he had in Paris, he could move up; on overall reliability, fourth is fair.

**Bailey rounds out the top five.** He is a proven championship performer — World Indoor champion in 2025, US champion in 2026 — and he ran 44.06 in Paris this year. He also beat Patterson at the US Championships? No, he won USAs in 44.39. But Nene has beaten Bailey in both of their 2026 meetings, including in Paris where Bailey ran 44.06 and still finished behind Nene’s 43.89. So Bailey is clearly elite, but just a step behind the top four on current form.

**Richards over Molnár is a close call.** Richards is the 2025 world silver medallist and has a 43.72 pedigree, but his 2026 season has been more modest: 44.44 at Monaco, 44.53 in Paris, 44.63 in London, and 44.82 at the Commonwealth Games. Still, he edged Molnár 44.44 to 44.47 in Monaco, and he has more big-race experience. Molnár has been excellent, running 44.47 in Monaco, 44.51 in Budapest, and 44.55 in the European final, and he is younger and improving. But Richards’s proven higher ceiling gives him the edge for sixth.

**Ndori is a little below his 2025 level.** He was brilliant at the 2025 World Championships, taking bronze in 44.20 behind Kebinatshipi and Richards. But in 2026 he has not broken 44.60, with best marks around 44.62 and 44.68. He beat Molnár earlier in the season at Rabat and Xiamen, but Molnár has since overtaken him with consistent sub-44.6 runs. Ndori also ran 45.31 in mid-August, suggesting he is not quite in the same sharp form. Eighth is appropriate.

**Szwed is likely last, but not disgraced.** The young Pole ran 44.94 this season and reached the European final, finishing sixth in 45.06. That is a strong level, but against this world-class field it is not quite enough. He does not have a 43-second or even a 44.3-second performance on the board for 2026, so he will probably be chasing the leaders from the gun. With home support in Silesia, he might find something extra, but the gap in raw 400m talent is clear.
