This is a fascinating and unusually deep 1500m field, and I’ve treated it as a genuinely fast, paced Diamond League race rather than a slow championship final.

**Phanuel Kipkosgei Koech** gets the nod for the win. He is the highest-ceiling athlete in the field after his 2025 world U20 record of 3:27.72 and his Diamond League win in London in 3:28.82. His 2026 season has not been as explosive, but his Budapest win in 3:31.09 in mid-July shows he is still rounding into form. At 19, he has the raw speed to outkick almost anyone in a true 3:29 race.

**Jakob Ingebrigtsen** is second, but not first, because the recent data is not as kind as his reputation. His 2025 World Championships ended with a shock 1500m heat exit and a modest 10th in the 5000m final. He then won the European 5000m title in 2026, and he remains the most talented runner in the world, but he has no outdoor 1500m result in 2026 to compare with Koech or Wightman. I still expect him to be right there off his class, range, and indoor 3:29.63 form from 2025.

**Jake Wightman** is third. His 3:29.95 in Paris in June 2026 is the single best outdoor 1500m time any of these men has produced this summer. He was also the 2025 world silver medallist and has proven he can deliver in big races. At 31, he may not have the same finishing kick as Koech, but his consistency makes him a clear podium threat. His Euro 6th in a tactical 3:37 race is not a concern for a fast Silesia-style affair.

**Isaac Nader** is the reigning world champion, and that alone keeps him high. His 3:30.43 in Rabat and his 2025 world title in Tokyo show he belongs in the top group. However, his 12th-place finish in the 2026 European final was a real warning sign. I think he rebounds in a cleanly paced Diamond League race, but I can’t put him above Wightman given Wightman’s better 2026 1500m clocking and more consistent championship form.

**Anass Essayi** and **Reynold Cheruiyot** are the best of the next wave. Essayi has been strikingly consistent: 3:30.17 in Paris and 3:31.54 in Budapest, though he has not won a major global race. Cheruiyot has a 3:30.28 in Paris and a 2025 world bronze medal, but his Commonwealth Games mile DNF and 11th-place Prefontaine mile make him slightly more volatile. I give Essayi the edge because Cheruiyot’s risk profile is higher.

**Vincent Ciattei** deserves a top-seven spot. He ran 3:30.90 in Rabat and 3:31.63 in Stockholm, making him one of the most reliable 1500m performers in the field in 2026. He also won the US 5000m title just weeks before this race, so he arrives with strong fitness and confidence.

**Hobbs Kessler** is next. The 2000m world record holder has world-class strength, and his 3:31.76 in Stockholm and 4th-place Prefontaine mile show he is close to the front. He still lacks the proven 3:29-level 1500m result that the top four have, but he is dangerous.

**Cole Hocker** is the hardest athlete to place. He is the Olympic champion and world 5000m champion, which gives him enormous pedigree. But his 2026 outdoor mileage has not translated into a standout 1500m or mile: he was 6th at Prefontaine in 3:47.57 and has no 1500m final to judge. In a fast Silesia race, he could easily finish top three, but based on current data I cannot put him above Kessler or Ciattei.

**Stefan Nillessen** is the European champion and deserves respect, but his Euro title came in a slow 3:35.70 final. His 3:32.45 in Paris suggests he can run faster in a paced race, but he has not yet shown the sharp 3:29-3:30 gear of the leaders.

**Jake Heyward**, **Romain Mornet**, **Nathan Green**, and **Ethan Strand** form a strong second tier. Heyward’s London mile 3rd and Euro 4th give him a slight edge over Mornet, who has similar times but was only 8th at Euros. Green is the US 1500m champion and won in Zagreb with 3:32.46. Strand ran a brilliant Prefontaine mile but his open 1500m results are not as convincing as Green’s. **Samuel Pihlström** is the European silver medallist, but his 2026 Diamond League form has been slower, so he sits just behind that group.

**Filip Ostrowski**, **Patryk Sieradzki**, and **Žan Rudolf** are the likely tail. Ostrowski is a genuine 800/1500 talent but his Euro heat exit and 3:35.80 best this summer put him behind the specialists. Sieradzki and Rudolf are primarily 800m runners with a disturbing number of recent DNFs; I expect them to be off the pace if they make it to the line at all.

Silesia should deliver an honest, quick race, and Koech’s blend of 2025 U20 record-breaking brilliance and 2026 Budapest form makes him my pick to hold off the more established names.

**Why this order?**

**Melissa Jefferson-Wooden** gets the nod for the win. She has the strongest big-race pedigree of anyone in the field: 100 m world champion in 2025 with 10.61, and she already won this exact Silesia meeting in 2025 in 10.66. In 2026, she beat Sha’Carri Richardson head-to-head at the Prefontaine Classic, 10.78 to 10.79, and her 21.69 US title run in the 200 m shows she is still carrying serious speed into the late summer. At 24, she is in her prime, and her ability to peak for high-level finals is proven.

**Sha’Carri Richardson** is the clear #2. Her 10.77 at the US Championships was the fastest legal 100 m time any of these women ran in 2026, and she has clearly recovered from her frustrating 2025 season. But she was still just 0.01 behind Jefferson-Wooden at Prefontaine, and in 2025 at Silesia she faded to 11.05 in a very similar field. She is a threat to win, but the narrow head-to-head loss and slightly less consistent seasonal résumé leave her just behind.

**Julien Alfred** is more difficult to place. Her 200 m form in 2026 has been superb: 21.51 in Monaco and 21.66 in London. That, plus a 6.99 60 m indoors, suggests she has the raw speed to dip under 10.80. However, her legal 100 m season best is only 10.87, and she has not faced Jefferson-Wooden or Richardson over 100 m in 2026. She is an enormous talent and could win if everything clicks, but I think her comparative lack of 100 m championship rounds in 2026 costs her late-race sharpness.

**Shericka Jackson** still has a superstar resume, but at 31 she is not the same force over 100 m that she was in her peak 200 m years. Her 10.81 at the Jamaican Championships was excellent, but she followed it with 11.02 at Prefontaine, losing to both Tina Clayton and the top Americans. She is still good enough to beat the younger Jamaicans on a good day, but the consistency is no longer there.

**Tina Clayton** is the most reliable of the younger Jamaicans. She was the 2025 World Championships silver medallist in 10.76 and has run 10.85 twice in 2026. She is consistent, competitive, and rarely has a bad race. The only question is whether she can find another gear against the top three; she has not broken 10.80 in 2026, so I have her leading the second pack rather than challenging for the podium.

**Zoe Hobbs** deserves the next spot. Her Commonwealth Games gold in 10.93 was a landmark result, and she has been steadily improving all season with 11.00 in Darwin, 11.02 in Zagreb, and then 10.93 in Glasgow. At 28, she is running with real confidence and should benefit from racing against a world-class field.

**Ewa Swoboda** gets a slight home-ground boost in Silesia. She ran 10.98 in Zagreb and won European silver in 11.02, so she is in the best outdoor form of her career. But her top-end ceiling is still a step below the world leaders, and even with the crowd behind her, 10.96 feels like a realistic ceiling.

**Brianna Lyston** has had a solid year: 10.94 twice and 10.99 in Hengelo. She is clearly talented, but she has not yet produced a breakthrough on the Diamond League stage against this exact level of competition. She can run 10.9x, but I think she is just behind the more seasoned Hobbs and Swoboda.

**Tia Clayton** is the hardest to rank. She ran 10.82 at this meeting in 2025 and has a 10.91 season’s best in 2026, but she also only managed 11.14 in the Prefontaine heats and has not shown the same consistency as her twin sister Tina. With Jackson, Tina, Lyston and the international sprinters all in form, I expect her to finish last unless she rediscovers her 2025 sharpness.

Predicted finish — Women’s Pole Vault, Weltklasse Zürich, 27 August 2026  
*(Marks are final clearances; ties decided on countback)*

1. **Hana Moll (USA)** — 4.85 m  
2. **Angelica Moser (SUI)** — 4.80 m  
3. **Katie Moon (USA)** — 4.80 m  
4. **Sandi Morris (USA)** — 4.75 m  
5. **Imogen Ayris (NZL)** — 4.70 m  
6. **Eliza McCartney (NZL)** — 4.70 m  
7. **Wilma Heltelä (FIN)** — 4.70 m  
8. **Marie-Julie Bonnin (FRA)** — 4.65 m  
9. **Emily Grove (USA)** — 4.65 m  
10. **Tina Šutej (SLO)** — 4.55 m  

The predicted marks fit a legal bar progression of 4.45, 4.50, 4.55, 4.60, 4.65, 4.70, 4.75, 4.80, 4.85, 4.90. I see Hana Moll clearing 4.85 for the win, then taking one unsuccessful shot at 4.90.

---

**Why this order?**

The clearest guide is the Lausanne Diamond League meeting on 21 August 2026, six days before Zürich, where most of this exact group competed. There, **Hana Moll won with 4.84 m**, ahead of **Angelica Moser at 4.74 m**, while Katie Moon and Sandi Morris both stopped at 4.64 m. Form rarely flips completely in six days, especially in a technical event like the pole vault.

**Hana Moll** is the youngest woman in the field at 20, but she is already jumping like the world leader. Her 4.88 m indoor win in Seattle and her Lausanne victory at 4.84 m are the best standalone results of anyone in this field. She also has NCAA titles and a World U20 title on her résumé. She has the highest recent ceiling and the momentum.

**Angelica Moser** gets second. She is the European outdoor champion after winning with 4.80 m in Birmingham, and she also cleared 4.80 m in Rome. Her Lausanne 4.74 m was solid, and she has been remarkably consistent all season: 4.77 m in Paris, 4.74 m in Lausanne, 4.70 m at the World Indoor Championships. The home crowd in Zürich will lift her, but Hana’s 4.84 m in Lausanne is still the single best outdoor result of the group.

**Katie Moon** edges out Sandi Morris for third. Moon is the 2025 world champion and won the 2025 Zürich Diamond League with 4.82 m. She hasn’t quite reached that level in 2026, though she did clear 4.80 m at the Prefontaine Classic. More importantly, she was the better of the two Americans at Lausanne, finishing third at 4.64 m while Morris finished fourth on countback. She is 34, but she still has the big-meet pedigree.

**Sandi Morris** is fourth. She has the most impressive single result of any American this year — a 4.90 m clearance to win the U.S. Championships — plus a 4.85 m win at Prefontaine. But she has also been erratic: 4.45 m in Rabat and only 4.64 m in Lausanne. If this were about peak ability, she could win. But judging by consistency and recent head-to-head form, she lands just off the podium.

**Imogen Ayris** takes fifth. She has quietly become one of the most reliable international vaulters in 2026, with a 4.81 m win at the Paavo Nurmi Games, a 4.75 m win in Ostrava, a World Indoor bronze, and a Commonwealth bronze. She doesn’t have the highest ceiling of the group, but she rarely has a terrible day. That counts for a lot in a field this deep.

**Eliza McCartney** is sixth. She is a Commonwealth champion and former Olympic bronze medallist with a huge 4.94 m personal best. But in 2026 she has been too inconsistent: 4.30 m in Rome and only 4.50 m at Lausanne. She can still beat anyone on talent, but she has not shown the recent form to justify a podium prediction.

**Wilma Heltelä** is seventh. She was brilliant at the European Championships with 4.75 m for silver and also jumped 4.81 m at the Fly Athens meeting in July. But she also finished 11th in Paris and 8th in Lausanne. Her range is wider than the top five, but her floor is lower. I give the edge to the two Kiwis above her because of steadier 2026 results.

**Marie-Julie Bonnin** is eighth. She won the 2025 World Indoor title and took European bronze this year, but her outdoor Diamond League campaign has been mostly in the 4.45–4.60 m range. She did clear 4.72 m at Jockgrim and 4.70 m at the European final, so she is capable of crashing the top five. Still, Zürich is a step up from some of those meetings, and she wasn’t in Lausanne to prove herself against this exact field.

**Emily Grove** is ninth. She has been solid rather than spectacular: 4.70 m at U.S. Championships and Prefontaine, 4.62 m in Monaco. She lacks the 4.80 m ceiling that would move her into the medal conversation. At 32, she is a dependable 4.60–4.70 m vaulter, but that likely isn’t enough to beat the top five in Zürich.

**Tina Šutej** rounds out the field. She is a former World Indoor silver medallist and has been superb indoors, but at 37 she appears to be fading outdoors. The most telling result is the European Championships, where she failed to qualify for the final after only clearing 4.40 m in the qualification round. She followed that with 4.50 m at Lausanne. Her résumé is excellent, but she simply doesn’t look capable of matching the younger athletes over 4.70 m right now.
blurbs.High Jump Women:
Predicted finish and heights (bar progression used: 1.85 – 1.87 – 1.89 – 1.91 – 1.93 – 1.95 – 1.97 – 1.99 – 2.01 – 2.03 – 2.05 m):

2. Nicola Olyslagers (AUS) – 2.03 m  
3. Eleanor Patterson (AUS) – 2.01 m  
4. Iryna Gerashchenko (UKR) – 1.99 m  
5. Angelina Topić (SRB) – 1.97 m (on countback)  
6. Marija Vuković (MNE) – 1.97 m (on countback)  
7. Yuliia Levchenko (UKR) – 1.97 m (on countback)  
8. Maria Żodzik (POL) – 1.95 m  
9. Lamara Distin (JAM) – 1.93 m  
10. Marithe-Thérèse Engondo (SUI) – 1.89 m  

---

**Why this order:**

**Mahuchikh** is the clear favourite. At 24, she is the world-record holder, a three-time Diamond League champion, and the 2026 world indoor and European champion. Her 2026 outdoor season has been controlled rather than spectacular — 2.01 in London, 2.00 in Silesia — but she has repeatedly won when it matters. Her indoor 2.03 in January also shows she has more in reserve than almost anyone here. In a technical, high-stakes Zurich meeting, she should produce the biggest clearance, around 2.05 m.

**Olyslagers** is the most credible challenger. She is the reigning world outdoor champion and 2025 Diamond League winner, and she beat Mahuchikh at London with 2.01. But her late summer has been uneven: 1.93 at the Commonwealth Games and only 1.96 at Silesia. Still, she won Zurich in 2025 with 2.04, so the stage suits her. I expect her to bounce back to 2.03, but Mahuchikh’s consistency and superior season management give the Ukrainian the edge.

**Patterson** has the best late-season form outside the top two. The 29-year-old is a former world champion and Olympic bronze medallist, and in 2026 she has won with 2.00 in Essen and Budapest, taken Commonwealth gold, and finished third in Silesia with 1.98. She has rarely been below 1.95 in recent weeks. That makes 2.01 a realistic Zurich ceiling, just behind the two main contenders.

**Gerashchenko** is harder to trust but capable of a surprise. The Olympic bronze medallist was second in Silesia with 1.98, which is an excellent recent signal. Her 2026 has also included 1.97 in Xiamen. But she has had poor meetings too, including 1.85 in Zagreb and 1.87 at Ukrainian Championships. Still, her Silesia result came just days before Zurich, so I give her fourth place and a 1.99 m clearance.

**Topić** has more natural talent than her placing suggests. The 20-year-old jumped 2.00 indoors this year and was part of the world indoor podium conversation, and she has a 2025 World Championship bronze. But she was only 12th at the 2026 European Championships with 1.83, and her Silesia mark was 1.96. On a high-class Zurich runway, she can reach 1.97, but her inconsistency in major finals keeps her out of the top four.

**Vuković** is the veteran stabiliser. At 33, she showed great resilience with 1.98 in Filothei and 1.98 in Budapest, and she took European bronze in 2026. She has also faded badly at times, including 1.85 in London and 1.93 in Silesia. A 1.97 clearance is a fair middle ground, but her countback record against Topić probably leaves her fifth or sixth.

**Levchenko** is the hardest to read. She won Xiamen with 1.99 in May, which is as good as anyone outside the top two has jumped outdoors this year. But she has been far too erratic since: 1.91 in Rabat, 1.97 in Turku, then a poor 1.89 in Silesia. If she finds her Xiamen rhythm she could beat this prediction, but based on recent form she lands in the 1.97 group.

**Żodzik** has been excellent in European competition — European silver in 2026 and world silver in 2025 — but her outdoor Diamond League ceiling appears lower than the leaders. She has been consistent around 1.95–1.97, with 1.97 in Poznan and 1.95 in Birmingham. I don’t see her jumping 1.99 in this company, so 1.95 is a fair predicted mark.

**Distin** is a Jamaican record holder and Commonwealth champion, but her 2026 outdoor season has mostly stayed in the 1.91–1.94 range. She did clear 1.96 indoors in Banská Bystrica, but outdoors she has not shown the same sharpness. 1.93 is a realistic Zurich outcome.

**Engondo** is the clear outsider. The young Swiss jumper won the national title with 1.89, but her other 2026 results have mostly been 1.80–1.83. She gets a home crowd at Zurich, but against a world-record holder and several global champions, 1.89 is about as high as I can reasonably place her.
blurbs.Shot Put Men:
Predicted finish — 27 August 2026, Zurich Diamond League (marks in metres):

1. **Leonardo Fabbri (ITA)** – 22.38 m  
2. **Jordan Geist (USA)** – 22.07 m  
3. **Rajindra Campbell (JAM)** – 22.03 m  
4. **Joe Kovacs (USA)** – 21.97 m  
5. **Adrian Piperi (USA)** – 21.76 m  
6. **Payton Otterdahl (USA)** – 21.69 m  
7. **Roger Steen (USA)** – 21.55 m  
8. **Chukwuebuka Enekwechi (NGR)** – 21.47 m  
9. **Tom Walsh (NZL)** – 21.38 m  
10. **Uziel Muñoz (MEX)** – 20.91 m  

---

### Why this order?

**1. Leonardo Fabbri**  
Fabbri is the clear favourite in this field. At 28, he is at peak age, and his 2026 results are the strongest of anyone here. He won the European title in Birmingham with 22.31 m, backed that up with 22.08 m at the Silesia Memorial just four days before this race, and owns the best 2026 outdoor mark in the field with his 22.74 m win at the Prefontaine Classic. He has multiple 22-metre competitions this summer and has beaten most of this Zurich field head-to-head. His 21.47 m in Zurich in 2025 looks like an outlier compared to his 2026 consistency.

**2. Jordan Geist**  
Geist has become the most consistent American this season. He won the US outdoor title with 22.32 m, threw 22.44 m in Memphis, 22.24 m at the Iron Wood Classic, and was runner-up to Fabbri at Silesia with 21.96 m. He was also second at the 2026 World Indoor Championships. Compared to Campbell and Kovacs, Geist has fewer poor competitions and has been reliably in the 21.9–22.4 m range since June. That reliability gives him the edge for silver.

**3. Rajindra Campbell**  
Campbell has the highest ceiling outside Fabbri and Geist. He is the Olympic bronze medallist and Jamaican record holder, and his 2026 season includes big wins at Xiamen with 22.34 m and Zagreb with 22.44 m, plus 22.16 m at the Prefontaine Classic. Those are elite-level results. However, he has also thrown 21.04 m in Rabat and 21.61 m at Silesia, so he remains volatile. I still place him on the podium because his peak throws have been better and more frequent than Kovacs’s 2026 output.

**4. Joe Kovacs**  
Kovacs is the most decorated athlete in the field — a two-time world champion, four-time Olympic medallist, and the second-best shot putter in history with 23.23 m. He also won this exact Zurich meeting in 2025 with 22.46 m. But 2026 has been different. His 22.58 m win in Rabat is excellent, but since then he has mostly been stuck at 21.7–21.9 m, with a poor 21.05 m at Prefontaine and only fourth at the US Championships. At 36, he can still peak for a major final, but I don’t think he can out-throw the younger, more consistent form of Fabbri, Geist, and Campbell.

**5. Adrian Piperi**  
Piperi’s 2026 started badly — 20.10 m in Rome and 20.46 m in Los Angeles — but he has clearly been trending upward. He threw 21.70 m at Prefontaine, 21.77 m in Memphis, 21.91 m to finish second at the US Championships, and 21.64 m at Silesia. At 26, he is ascending, and his recent form puts him just ahead of Otterdahl.

**6. Payton Otterdahl**  
Otterdahl had a strong 2025, including 22.35 m at US Championships and 22.07 m in Zurich, but his 2026 has been less convincing. His best outdoor mark this year is only 21.80 m from Silesia, and he had mediocre throws of 20.55 m at Prefontaine and 20.81 m in Budapest. He still has the strength to beat most of the lower group, but he hasn’t shown the 22-metre form needed to crack the top five in this loaded field.

**7. Roger Steen**  
Steen is a very reliable 21.4–21.9 m thrower. He won the 2026 US indoor title, threw 22.07 m indoors in Belgrade, and outdoors has hit 21.93 m at Drake and 21.83 m in Ústí nad Labem. He doesn’t have the same ceiling as the top four, but he has been consistently ahead of Walsh and Enekwechi in most head-to-head meetings this summer. He finished seventh at Silesia with 21.46 m, which seems about right for this race.

**8. Chukwuebuka Enekwechi**  
Enekwechi is the Commonwealth Games champion after beating Walsh in Glasgow, and he has been remarkably consistent in 2026: 21.74 m at Drake, 21.48 m in Budapest, 21.43 m in Ostrava, and a string of 21.3–21.5 m throws. The issue is that he rarely threatens 22 metres outdoors anymore. Against this Zurich field, that consistency gives him a solid mid-pack finish, but not the top five.

**9. Tom Walsh**  
Walsh is a former world champion and Oceanian record holder with 22.90 m, but at 33 he is no longer the 22-metre force he once was. His 2026 outdoor best is only 21.71 m in Madrid, and he could only manage 21.29 m for eighth at Silesia. He did win the World Indoor title in 2026 with 21.82 m, but outdoors he has been stuck in the 21.0–21.7 m range. Enekwechi beat him at the Commonwealth Games, and Steen has generally been ahead of him this summer, so ninth is fair.

**10. Uziel Muñoz**  
Muñoz’s 2025 World Championship silver medal in Tokyo was a massive breakthrough, but his 2026 form has not matched it. His best outdoor throw this year is 21.46 m in Memphis, and he has frequently been in the 20.2–20.9 m range. At 30, he is experienced, but he simply hasn’t shown the consistency to compete with this group in Zurich. He finishes last unless he can recreate his Tokyo magic.
blurbs.100m Hurdles Women:
**Predicted finish – Women’s 100m Hurdles, Zurich Diamond League, 27 August 2026:**

1. **Masai Russell** (USA) – **12.15**  
2. **Tobi Amusan** (NGR) – **12.26**  
3. **Alaysha Johnson** (USA) – **12.38**  
4. **Nadine Visser** (NED) – **12.43**  
5. **Pia Skrzyszowska** (POL) – **12.47**  
6. **Danielle Williams** (JAM) – **12.55**  
7. **Ditaji Kambundji** (SUI) – **12.63**  
8. **Annik Kälin** (SUI) – **12.66**  
9. **Ackera Nugent** (JAM) – **12.69**

---

**Why this order?**

This is one of the deepest 100m hurdles fields of the season, but the 2026 form guide is clear at the top.

**Masai Russell** is the obvious favourite. The 25-year-old American has been the most consistent and explosive hurdler all season. Her **12.14 in Xiamen** is the fastest legal time in the field this year, and she has followed it with **12.24 at Prefontaine**, **12.20 in Monaco**, and **12.27 in Lausanne**. She has a recent head-to-head win over Amusan in Xiamen and has done it repeatedly under Diamond League pressure. Her Olympic gold pedigree from 2024 and her American Record speed make her the woman to beat.

**Tobi Amusan** remains the biggest threat. At 28, she still owns the world record of 12.12, and her 2026 season includes excellent legal marks of **12.28 in Xiamen**, **12.28 in Rabat**, and **12.28 in Paris**. She was right there with Russell earlier in the season, but Russell has pulled ahead in the last two months. Amusan’s **wind-aided 12.19 Commonwealth heat** shows the speed is still there, but her **12.60 wind-aided third place in the Commonwealth final** was a warning sign. She should push Russell hard, but Russell has been better in the big Diamond League finals.

**Alaysha Johnson** gets the bronze medal slot. The 29-year-old American has been exceptionally consistent since June, running **12.38 in Monaco**, **12.39 in Paris**, and **12.42 to finish second at the US Championships**. She also beat the strong European contingent at Lausanne with **12.49**. Johnson doesn’t have Russell’s ceiling, but her rhythm and championship execution are more reliable than most of the field right now.

**Nadine Visser** is the top European in this prediction. The 30-year-old Dutchwoman won the European title in Birmingham with **12.67**, but that was in difficult, windy conditions. More telling are her Diamond League races: **12.41 in Paris** and **12.42 in Lausanne**. She is running with excellent control and should be in the podium fight if Russell or Amusan misfires. Her experience and consistency make her fourth.

**Pia Skrzyszowska** is a tough fifth. The 24-year-old Pole has a season best of **12.44 from Nancy** and won European silver behind Visser. She has also been very competitive in Diamond League company, running **12.46 in Paris** and **12.61 in Lausanne**. She lacks the top-end raw speed of the Americans, but she is technically sharp and should hold off the fading veterans.

**Danielle Williams** is still capable of a big race — her **12.51 at Prefontaine** proved that. But the 33-year-old Jamaican has been too erratic in 2026, with a **DNF in Shaoxing**, **12.90 in Xiamen**, and **12.70 in Silesia**. At this stage of her career, she can still medal on a perfect day, but Zurich’s high-quality field is likely to expose her inconsistency. Sixth feels right.

**Ditaji Kambundji** is the hardest to place. She is only 23 and the reigning 2025 World Champion, with a 12.24 personal best. But her 2026 outdoor season has been puzzlingly below that level: **12.62 in Xiamen** is her best legal time, and she has been slower since, including **12.75 at the European Championships** and **12.71 in Lausanne**. I still give her seventh ahead of the other Swiss woman because of her pedigree and her head-to-head control over Nugent, but she is vulnerable.

**Annik Kälin** is the wild card. The 25-year-old is primarily a heptathlete, but her 2026 hurdle form has been impressive, including a **legal 12.60 in Ratingen** and a **12.67 Swiss title**. That would put her right in this mix, but open Diamond League hurdling against full-time specialists is a different task. She could surprise, but eighth is the sensible call.

**Ackera Nugent** rounds out the prediction. The 23-year-old Jamaican has the talent — her **12.61 in College Station** and her 2025 win in Zürich show that — but her 2026 season has been inconsistent: **12.98 in Shaoxing**, **12.78 in Espoo**, then **12.64 in Silesia**. On form, she is closer to the back of this field than the front. If she finds her old sharpness, she could jump a couple of places, but she starts as the outsider here.

---

**Why this order?**

Emma Zapletalová is the clear favourite. At 25, she is the current European champion and already has a World Championship bronze from 2025. Her 2026 Diamond League form has been outstanding: she won in Rabat, Rome, Oslo, Doha and Lausanne, with a season’s best of 52.30. Her most recent run before Zurich was a commanding 52.41 win in Lausanne, putting her ahead of Anna Cockrell by nearly 0.8 seconds. Even her one poor race — 5th in Zagreb in 55.82 — looks like an outlier after she bounced back to win the European title and then Lausanne. She is the fastest, most consistent and most confident hurdler in the field.

Anna Cockrell is the clear second pick. The 28-year-old Olympic silver medallist has been extremely consistent all season: 52.77 in Rome, 52.94 to win the US title, and 53.15 in Lausanne behind Zapletalová. She has consistently finished ahead of Rushell Clayton whenever they have met, and her ability to run 52.7–53.1 in big races makes her the only woman with a realistic chance of chasing Zapletalová down.

Rushell Clayton gets third. The two-time World bronze medallist from Jamaica has been the model of reliability in 2026, with marks like 53.05 in Doha, 53.14 in Rome and 53.34 in Budapest. She has not matched the very top end of Zapletalová or Cockrell this year, but she has regularly been the best of the rest. Her experience and strength through the final 100m should hold off the rapidly improving Emily Newnham.

Emily Newnham is the difficult one to place. At just 21, she has had a huge breakout year: Commonwealth silver, European silver behind Zapletalová, a 400m flat time of 50.32, and a personal best of 53.33 in the hurdles. That European final was hugely impressive, but she has yet to produce that kind of run against the full American and Jamaican contingent in a stacked Diamond League final. Her momentum could carry her close to Rushell Clayton, but Clayton’s superior season-long consistency and proven 53.0-level speed give her the edge for bronze.

Dalilah Muhammad is the wildcard. At 35, she is a former world-record holder and Olympic champion, and her best 2026 result — 53.39 in Rome — shows she can still mix with some of the best. However, she was disqualified in the US Championships final and has not raced since late July. That lack of sharpness and recent competitive rhythm probably leaves her just outside the top four, though a clean race could push her higher.

Gianna Woodruff follows. The Pan American champion from Panama has been steady rather than spectacular in 2026, running 53.58 in Rome and 53.88 in Doha but also drifting to 54.40 in Lausanne. She is capable of a top-five finish, but she has not shown the sub-53 speed needed to challenge the leading group.

Fatoumata Binta Diallo should take seventh. Her European bronze in 53.55 was excellent, and she is clearly a talented, improving athlete. But her 54.68 in Lausanne after that European Championships shows she can still be inconsistent across back-to-back high-level races. Against this depth, she slots in behind the more seasoned front-runners.

Amalie Iuel rounds out the field. The 31-year-old Norwegian has been respectable all season, with a best of 54.05 in Rome, but she faded to 54.70 in the European final and has not shown the finishing power to challenge the top half of this very strong field. In a Zurich Diamond League final loaded with medal winners, she is likely to finish last unless others falter.

1. **Grant Fisher (USA), 28** — 7:28.91  
2. **Cameron Myers (AUS), 19** — 7:29.26  
3. **Eduardo Herrera (MEX), 28** — 7:29.83

---

**Why this order?**

This should be a genuinely fast 3000m. Mahdi Mahamoud Houssein, 56 and with no listed results, looks like the designated pacemaker, and Boaz Kiprugut’s long string of DNFs over 1500m and 5000m makes him a very unreliable finisher in a Championship-style Diamond League race. That leaves a deep, honest battle over the final two kilometres.

**Grant Fisher** gets the nod for the win. Yes, his 13:07.74 in the Lausanne 5000m on 21 August was a below-par result, but Fisher’s 3000m pedigree is unmatched in this field: he owns the world record for the indoor 3000m (7:22.91) and was runner-up in the 2025 Zurich 3000m in 7:36.81. He also ran 12:49.61 for 5000m in Oslo and won the Paris 5000m in 12:54.80 in June. Fisher is the best mixture of 3000m-specific speed, proven finishing power, and big-race reliability.

**Cameron Myers** is the wildcard. He has the fastest relevant 3000m mark of anyone here besides Fisher’s indoor record: 7:27.57 in Boston in January 2026. Add his 1500m Oceanian record of 3:28.00 and his Commonwealth Games mile silver, and Myers has the best raw speed in the field. The only question is whether he has the outdoor 3000m strength to hold off the 5000m guys, but I think he can sit near the front and unleash a devastating last 300m.

**Eduardo Herrera** is the trickiest call. His 7:27.63 in Shaoxing in May is the fastest outdoor 3000m run by anyone in this field in 2025-26, and he looked excellent as a double CAC Games champion in August. But he also DNF’d in Lausanne in his most recent outing. That inconsistency, combined with a tough turn of schedule, pushes him just behind Fisher and Myers. If he is fresh and fully committed to the 3000m, he could absolutely win; 7:29.83 is a strong, honest projection.

**Dominic Lobalu** and **Biniam Mehary** are the best of the next group. Lobalu’s 7:29.48 career best from 2022 is still a serious marker, and his Monaco 5000m win in 12:52.54 in July shows he is in elite form. His DNF in the Luzern 3000m is a small red flag, but his European 10,000m silver suggests he is fit and tough. Mehary has under-20 world records and an indoor 3000m of 7:29.99, but his 2026 5000m results have been very good rather than spectacular. I expect Lobalu’s superior current endurance to carry him to fourth.

**Graham Blanks** and **Nico Young** are the most reliable American threats after Fisher and Wolfe. Blanks has been remarkably consistent: 7:31.97 indoors, 12:49.99 in Oslo, 12:52.60 in Monaco, 12:59.16 in Lausanne. Young has the American 5000m record from 2025 and a 7:33.32 indoor 3000m, but his 2026 outdoor 5000m form has only been good, not exceptional. Blanks gets sixth ahead of Young because of his superior recent consistency in fast races.

**Santiago Catrofe** is the hardest athlete to rank. He ran 7:29.72 in the same Shaoxing 3000m where Herrera went 7:27.63, which is genuinely world-class. But his track season has been scattered, including a DNF in Lausanne, and he has not produced a high-level 3000m result since May. I’m placing him eighth — not because he lacks talent, but because his late-summer reliability is questionable compared with the Americans around him.

**Parker Wolfe** is next. He won the Prefontaine 2-mile in 8:10.13 and finished second in the Lausanne 5000m in 12:58.20, ahead of Young, Blanks, Sime and Lobalu. That is superb form. However, his 3000m-specific speed is less proven: his 3000m split in that 2-mile was around 7:42, so a dedicated 3000m should be quicker, but I’m not sure he has the raw 3000m range of the top eight. Still, he is clearly ahead of the next group.

**Egide Ntakarutimana** has a solid 7:35.16 from Budapest in 2025 and a strong 12:56.06 5000m in Paris in 2026, but he lacks the finishing speed and consistency of the athletes above him. **Mezgebu Sime** and **Ky Robinson** are both 12:50-level 5000m runners, but neither has shown a standout outdoor 3000m in 2026. Robinson’s Commonwealth 10,000m win is impressive, but 3000m is slightly short for him. **Abdihamid Nur** has 12:57.32 5000m form, but his 2026 season has been too inconsistent to trust for a major 3000m.

**Filip Ostrowski** is a quality 800m/1500m runner — his 3:33.09 1500m in Silesia is strong — but the 3000m is a different game. He should finish, but he is likely to be isolated once the pace lifts. **Boaz Kiprugut** has DNF’d more often than he has finished in recent seasons, so I expect another early exit. And **Mahdi Mahamoud Houssein** should serve as the rabbit: he takes the field through the fast early splits, then steps off as planned.
blurbs.Long Jump Men:
Predicted finish and projected marks for the Zurich Diamond League Men’s Long Jump, 27 August 2026:

1. Miltiadis Tentoglou (GRE) — 8.55 m  
2. Simon Ehammer (SUI) — 8.36 m  
3. Jorge A. Hodelín (CUB) — 8.25 m  
4. Bozhidar Sarâboyukov (BUL) — 8.19 m  
5. Luka Bošković (SRB) — 8.16 m  
6. Wayne Pinnock (JAM) — 8.13 m  
7. Gerson Baldé (POR) — 8.09 m  
8. Tajay Gayle (JAM) — 8.01 m  
9. Francesco Ettore Inzoli (ITA) — 7.95 m  
10. Lester Lescay (ESP) — 7.89 m  

---

**Reasoning:**

Tentoglou is the clear favourite. The two-time Olympic champion and reigning European champion has the strongest 2026 season: 8.66 at the Greek Championships, 8.61 in Monaco, 8.44 to win the European title, and another Diamond League win in Lausanne. Even his “off” winning mark in Lausanne was still better than almost everyone else’s best jump of the night. He is the most reliable big-meet jumper in the world.

Ehammer looks best placed to challenge him. The Swiss decathlete is in career form, with an 8.51 in the Götzis decathlon, a 5th-place 8.32 in Monaco, and European silver with 8.29 into a -2.7 m/s wind. He also won this meeting in 2025, so the Zurich atmosphere suits him. His consistency puts him clearly ahead of the rest, even if Tentoglou is just a step above.

Hodelín is the most exciting young jumper in the field. At only 18, he already has a world U20 record of 8.46, a 3rd-place 8.38 in Monaco, and a CAC Games title. He was only 4th in Lausanne with 8.06, but his season is remarkably consistent for his age. I expect him to outjump the more erratic senior jumpers and take the podium.

Sarâboyukov and Bošković are the next tier. Sarâboyukov has the bigger ceiling — legal 8.49 and 8.48 jumps in July plus a European bronze — but his 7.88 in Lausanne is a real red flag. Still, I give him the edge over Bošković because he has produced multiple 8.2-plus legal marks this summer. Bošković, meanwhile, is improving rapidly: he won national titles, jumped 8.23 in Zagreb, reached the European final and then was 3rd in Lausanne. He may be the future, but Sarâboyukov’s peak is slightly higher right now.

Pinnock has the résumé — Olympic and World silver medals — and his 8.39 in Monaco shows he can beat almost anyone. But he also jumped 7.93 and 7.75 in earlier Diamond League meets and only 8.01 in Lausanne. That inconsistency drops him behind the younger athletes who are peaking more reliably. Baldé is similar: he is the reigning World Indoor champion with an excellent 8.46 indoor mark, but outdoors he has been more solid than spectacular — 8.20, 8.18, 8.02 in his most recent Diamond League-level starts. He is unlikely to threaten the podium unless several others falter.

Gayle is the hardest to place. The 2019 world champion and 2026 Commonwealth champion still has the talent to jump 8.37, as he did at the Jamaican Championships. But his recent form is alarming: 6.80 in Budapest and 7.70 in Lausanne. At 29, he is still capable of a big jump, but he has become too unpredictable to rank above the younger, steadier jumpers.

Inzoli and Lescay are the outsiders. Inzoli won the Italian title with 8.27 and made the European final, but he lacks Diamond League experience against this level of field. Lescay has struggled since his 2025 Euro Indoor bronze; his 7.72 in the European final puts him clearly at the back of this starting list.
blurbs.100m Women:
**Predicted finish – Women’s 100m, Zurich Diamond League, 27 August 2026:**

1. Melissa Jefferson-Wooden (USA) – 10.74  
2. Julien Alfred (LCA) – 10.79  
3. Sha’Carri Richardson (USA) – 10.84  
4. Brianna Lyston (JAM) – 10.92  
5. Amy Hunt (GBR) – 10.96  
6. Tina Clayton (JAM) – 10.99  
7. Zoe Hobbs (NZL) – 11.02  
8. Géraldine di Tizio-Frey (SUI) – 11.06  
9. Jonielle Smith (JAM) – 11.09  

**Why this order?**

The most useful recent form guide is the Silesia Diamond League 100m on 23 August 2026, which featured Melissa Jefferson-Wooden, Julien Alfred, Sha’Carri Richardson, Brianna Lyston, Tina Clayton, and Zoe Hobbs in the same race. Jefferson-Wooden won in 10.78, Alfred was second in 10.83, Richardson and Lyston both crossed in 10.96, Clayton ran 11.01, and Hobbs ran 11.05. That race heavily informs this prediction.

**Jefferson-Wooden** is the clear favourite. She is the reigning world champion in the 100m, has largely been unbeatable in 2026, and has already produced 10.78 wins at both Prefontaine and Silesia. She also has a faster gear from her 10.61 world title run in 2025. I expect her to sharpen slightly to 10.74 in Zurich.

**Alfred** is the strongest challenger. She has the Olympic 100m title from 2024, a consistent 2026 season, and ran 10.83 behind Jefferson-Wooden at Silesia. She also showed brilliant speed endurance with her 21.51 200m in Monaco. Her legal 10.75 from 2025 suggests she can push under 10.80, so 10.79 is a reasonable Zurich prediction.

**Richardson** remains dangerously fast — her 10.77 US title run and 10.79 Prefontaine race prove she can beat almost anyone on her day. But her 10.96 at Silesia, where she finished behind both Jefferson-Wooden and Alfred, is a concern. She also faded relative to the top two at the 2025 World Championships. I still put her third on raw ceiling, but she needs to be sharper than she was in Silesia.

**Lyston** is the pick of the chasing pack. She ran 10.94 earlier in 2026 and backed it up with 10.96 at Silesia, finishing right alongside Richardson and clearly ahead of Clayton and Hobbs. At 21, she is still improving, and in a fast Zurich race she could dip to 10.92.

**Hunt** gets fifth ahead of Clayton and Hobbs because of consistency and championship pedigree. She won the European 100m title in 11.00, ran 10.97 in Stockholm, and took Commonwealth silver in 10.98. She has not yet broken 10.95 this year, which keeps her behind Lyston, but her ability to deliver in big finals gives her the edge over the fading Clayton.

**Clayton** has the fastest season’s best among the non-top-three group — 10.85 in Rabat and again at the Jamaican Championships — but her second half of 2026 has faded. She ran 11.00 at Prefontaine and 11.01 at Silesia, and was beaten by Lyston in their most recent meeting. I think she settles for 10.99.

**Hobbs** is difficult to place. She produced a brilliant 10.93 to win Commonwealth gold and beat Amy Hunt head-to-head in Glasgow. But she followed that with only 11.05 at Silesia, suggesting she may have peaked in late July. Her talent is obvious, but consistency is not quite there. I have her in seventh.

**di Tizio-Frey** is a genuine improver. She won the Swiss title in 10.96 and reached the European 100m final, placing fourth in 11.07. She has been racing and relay sharp through August, and I think she can edge under 11.10 in Zurich. Her 11.06 prediction is based on her being competitive but slightly outrun by the established global names.

**Smith** is the hardest to predict. Her 10.89 at Prefontaine in July shows she still has real speed, and she ran 10.94 at the Jamaican Championships. But she followed that with 11.12 in Budapest and then did not start the Commonwealth Games final. That recent inconsistency and injury doubt put her last here. If fully healthy, she could climb; based on her last completed races, I cannot place her higher.
blurbs.400m Hurdles Men:
**Predicted Finish – Men’s 400m Hurdles, Zürich Diamond League, 27 August 2026**

| Pos | Athlete | Nation | Predicted Time |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Alison dos Santos | BRA | 46.31 |
| 2 | Karsten Warholm | NOR | 46.44 |
| 3 | Matheus Lima | BRA | 47.03 |
| 4 | Ezekiel Nathaniel | NGR | 47.60 |
| 5 | Chris Robinson | USA | 47.93 |
| 6 | Matic Ian Guček | SLO | 48.14 |
| 7 | Abderrahman Samba | QAT | 48.42 |
| 8 | Dany Brand | SUI | 49.21 |

---

**Why this order?**

This is essentially a two-man race at the front, and the evidence points firmly toward **Alison dos Santos** over **Karsten Warholm**.

Dos Santos has been the best 400m hurdler in the world in 2026. He owns the fastest time in the field this season with **46.43** at Silesia on 23 August, where he beat Warholm head-to-head. That followed a strong run of 46.72 in Xiamen, 46.89 in Oslo, and 46.48 at the Brazilian Championships. He is 25, the 2022 world champion, and he already has the best flat 400m speed in the event, having run **44.38** earlier in the season. His rhythm and consistency through the rounds have been exceptional, and he has now beaten Warholm in every 400m hurdles meeting they’ve contested this season, plus the 300m hurdles race in Shaoxing.

Warholm is still a monumental force — a three-time world champion, world record holder, and 2026 European champion. But his 2026 season has been about winning races without quite rediscovering his devastating sub-46 quality. He has run 46.82, 47.40, 46.61, 46.63, and 46.52, with his best being the 46.52 behind dos Santos at Silesia. At 29, he remains a massive big-race performer, and Zürich is one of his favourite stages, but the data says dos Santos has the superior current speed and endurance. A close 1-2 is expected, with dos Santos holding him off.

**Matheus Lima** is the clear third man. The 22-year-old Brazilian has made a massive jump in 2026. He ran 47.37 in Stockholm, 47.64 in Ostrava, 47.74 in Budapest, and then a personal best **47.26** at Silesia, finishing well ahead of Nathaniel and Samba. He also has huge flat 400m ability with 44.90, and his 300m hurdles form (33.75) shows he is comfortable at a fast early pace. He may be the one most likely to dip under 47 seconds if the race is fast, but he still sits below the dos Santos–Warholm level.

**Ezekiel Nathaniel** should take fourth. He is the 2026 Commonwealth Games champion and was fourth at the 2025 World Championships with 47.11. But 2026 has been slightly less spectacular: his season’s best is 47.37 from June, and he posted 47.83 at Silesia. That is respectable but not quite enough to challenge Lima. Still, Nathaniel is a proven championship performer, so he should hold off the chasing pack with a 47.6.

**Chris Robinson** is a fascinating case. He has superb flat 400m credentials — he won the 2026 World Indoor 400m title, ran 44.88 at the Prefontaine Classic, and won the US outdoor 400m hurdles title in **47.61**. But his outdoor 400m hurdles form outside that US final has been inconsistent: 49.09 in Tokyo, 48.66 in Ostrava, and 48.73 in Santo Domingo. He is quick, fearless, and physical, but he hasn’t shown he can run 47.5 or faster against this exact group in a Diamond League setting. Fifth is the right call.

**Matic Ian Guček** has quietly become a very solid 48-second hurdler. He ran 48.03 in the European Championship semi-final and 48.25 in Lausanne just days before Zürich. His Euro final was disappointing — 48.76 — but his overall trajectory is upward at 22. He should outkick the faded Samba, though he lacks the top-end ceiling of the men above him.

**Abderrahman Samba** is the hardest to place because his pedigree is outstanding: he was the second man ever under 47 seconds and won World Championship bronze in 2025 with 47.06. But his 2026 season has fallen off significantly. After a 47.93 in Xiamen in May, he has gone 48.60, 48.31, 48.10, and 48.64. He was seventh at Silesia, and at 30 he appears to be regressing relative to the new generation. His best is still better than Guček’s, but current form favours the younger Slovenian.

**Dany Brand** is the clear outsider. The Swiss athlete reached the European semi-final with a 48.96, but he is generally a 49-second hurdler. He has local familiarity with the Letzigrund track, and he ran a fast flat 400m there in the past, but over the barriers he simply doesn’t have the speed to live with this field. A time around 49.2 would still be a solid effort for him, but last place is expected.
blurbs.Javelin Men:
Predicted finish — Men’s Javelin Throw, Zurich Diamond League, 27 August 2026:

1. Rumesh Tharanga Pathirage (SRI) — 90.22 m  
2. Anderson Peters (GRN) — 87.55 m  
3. Curtis Thompson (USA) — 85.44 m  
4. Keshorn Walcott (TTO) — 83.67 m  
5. Patriks Gailums (LAT) — 83.01 m  
6. Dawid Wegner (POL) — 82.36 m  
7. Thomas Röhler (GER) — 80.92 m  
8. Marc Anthony Minichello (USA) — 80.44 m  
9. Julius Yego (KEN) — 79.68 m  
10. Simon Wieland (SUI) — 76.85 m  

Reasoning:

This is a fascinating field because it mixes the 2025 World champion (Walcott), the 2025 World silver and bronze medallists (Peters and Thompson), and the most in-form thrower in the world in 2026, Rumesh Tharanga Pathirage.

**Pathirage is the clear favourite.** The 22-year-old Sri Lankan has been sensational: he won the 2026 Commonwealth Games title with 89.75 m, threw 92.62 m to win in Rome, and won in Lausanne just six days before Zurich with 88.14 m. He has repeatedly beaten almost everyone in this field head-to-head in 2026, and his combination of youth, momentum, and consistency at 88–92 m makes him the logical winner.

**Anderson Peters should finish second.** Peters has not been at his absolute 2025 World Championship final level, but he has been extremely reliable in 2026: 86.08 m in Rabat, 86.38 m in Doha, and 86.69 m in Lausanne. He has a higher floor than Thompson and Walcott, and he beat Thompson in both of their main Diamond League meetings this year. The 28-year-old former world champion is still elite, but Pathirage has simply been better in every recent encounter.

**Curtis Thompson is the best of the chasing group.** Thompson threw 87.59 m to win the US title in July and also threw 85.99 m in Doha. That shows he still has the highest ceiling of anyone outside Pathirage and Peters. However, his poor outings in Rabat (77.88 m) and Lausanne (78.13 m) are a warning sign. I still trust his 87.59 m national-title form more than Walcott’s 2026 consistency, so I put him third, but he is vulnerable if Zurich exposes the same problems he had in Lausanne.

**Keshorn Walcott is fourth.** Walcott is the 2025 World champion, but his 2026 season has been noticeably below that level. His best mark this year is 83.71 m from Lausanne, and he was only sixth at the Commonwealth Games with 82.55 m. He remains competitive and experienced, but he has not produced the big 86–88 m throws needed to challenge the top three.

**Gailums and Wegner are very close.** Patriks Gailums won the European Championships bronze with 82.97 m, while Dawid Wegner was just one centimetre behind in fourth with 82.96 m. Gailums also threw 83.09 m in Palanga, so I give him a slight edge. Wegner is consistent in the 80–83 m range, but he has not shown a big 85 m-plus throw in 2026. Both are solid mid-field finishers in this loaded Diamond League field.

**Röhler, Minichello, and Yego are the declining or inconsistent group.** Thomas Röhler, at 34, is a former Olympic champion, but his 2026 form peaked at 83.33 m in Nairobi in April and faded badly afterward. He did not even make the European Championships final, throwing only 78.67 m in qualification. Still, his Roma mark of 82.89 m gives him a slight edge over Minichello.

Marc Anthony Minichello threw 84.11 m at Drake Relays in April, but has been erratic since, including 75.98 m at US Championships and 80.06 m at Lausanne. Julius Yego, now 36, had a once-great career, and he did throw 82.22 m in Doha, but his Commonwealth Games qualifying effort of 74.50 m was a clear sign of decline. Simon Wieland is last on current form: after a promising 80.76 m in March, he threw only 73.23 m in Lausanne and failed to make the Euro final.

Ultimately, this is Pathirage’s competition to lose. His 92.62 m in Rome is the best single throw any of these athletes has produced in 2026, and he has been winning against this exact calibre of field all summer.

Predicted finish and marks — Women’s 3000m Steeplechase, Zurich Diamond League, 27 August 2026:

1. Faith Cherotich (KEN) — 8:50.04  
2. Doris Lemngole (KEN) — 8:54.31

16. Emma Coburn (USA) — 9:23.02  

---

**Why this order?**

Faith Cherotich is the clear favourite. She is only 21, but she already has a world title from Tokyo 2025, where she ran 8:51.59 to win, and her 2025 Eugene race produced 8:48.71 — the fastest anyone in this field has run. Her 2026 season has been extremely consistent: 8:51.48 in Shaoxing, 8:52.53 in Xiamen, and 8:51.74 at Prefontaine, where she beat Chemutai and Lemngole. She also won the Commonwealth Games comfortably and then ran 9:01.90 at Lausanne six days out from Zurich. She is tactically sharp, young, and clearly the best steeplechaser entered.

Doris Lemngole is the best of the rest. Her 8:57.89 at Prefontaine in July was the second-fastest steeplechase of her career and put her ahead of Chemutai, Krause, Meyer, and Halladay. She also has a massive flat-speed reserve: her indoor 3000m of 8:31.39 in 2026 is exceptional and suggests that her steeplechase ceiling is higher than 8:57. Her NCAA titles and Bowerman Award support the idea that she is still improving at 23. Lausanne was a step back at 9:07.09, but she still finished ahead of Halladay, Jennings, and Thorner. In Zurich, she is the most likely athlete to follow Cherotich home.

Peruth Chemutai is a two-time Olympic medallist and already a legend of the event, but her 2026 form has been split in two. In May she was magnificent: 8:51.47 in Shaoxing and 8:51.06 in Xiamen, beating Cherotich on both occasions by tiny margins. Since then, however, she has fallen away badly: fifth at Prefontaine in 9:05.39 and third at the Commonwealth Games in 9:09.96. That is a large drop from her early-season level. I still put her third because her pedigree and May performances show that the 8:51-8:56 range is within her, even if her late-summer racing has not matched it. She should be fresher than some of the women who raced Lausanne, and she has the most big-race pedigree of anyone outside Cherotich and Lemngole.

Lexy Halladay gets fourth ahead of Elise Thorner, mainly because of recency and trajectory. Halladay won her second straight US title in 2026 and then ran 9:08.35 at Lausanne, which was the best non-Kenyan performance in that race. She has progressed from 9:13 range earlier in the summer to 9:08 at the end of August. At 24, she is still getting better, and her flat 5000m speed gives her a strong finish. I think she can break into the low 9:05s at Zurich.

Elise Thorner has a faster peak than Halladay — her 9:05.45 Commonwealth silver was excellent and put her clearly ahead of Chemutai in Glasgow. But she has not maintained that level: she was fifth at the Europeans in 9:18.14 and then only eighth at Lausanne in 9:18.29. That looks like a late-season dip. I still have her fifth because her ceiling is proven, but I trust Halladay more right now.

Gesa Felicitas Krause is a veteran with a European title from two weeks ago and a 9:07.50 at Prefontaine. She has the experience to run well at Zurich, but her Lausanne DNF is a real concern. At 33, after that recent DNF, I won’t put her higher than sixth. If she is fit, she could easily beat both Halladay and Thorner, but the data is leaning toward a slightly safer placement.

Gabrielle Jennings is the model of consistency this summer: 9:12.02 in Stockholm, 9:11.72 in Los Angeles, 9:15.29 in Lausanne. She does not have the sudden speed of the top group, but she rarely runs herself out of a race. She should earn seventh with another low-9:10 or high-9:09 performance.

Lea Meyer’s 9:09.13 at Prefontaine shows she can beat several of the women ranked above her, but she has also run 9:17.07 and 9:22.48 in important late-season races. At her best she is a top-six threat; at her worst she fades. Eighth seems right for a athlete with that split between ceiling and floor.

Alemnat Walle is one of the hardest to place. She ran 9:06.88 at the 2025 Prefontaine at only 18/19, and her 9:10.05 in Shaoxing in May 2026 was strong. But her 2026 has been very erratic: 9:15.79 in Xiamen, 9:16.18 in Turku, 9:15.33 in Stockholm, then a poor 9:32.95 at Lausanne. If the 19-year-old version shows up, she can finish top seven. I have her ninth because I do not trust her consistency in a loaded Diamond League final.

Alice Finot is the European record holder and won Euro silver in 9:14.24, but she also ran 9:34.30 in Stockholm this summer. That inconsistency, plus her age of 34, makes her difficult to rank higher. She could beat Gürth and Mononen if she hits a good race, but she can also lose to all of them if she has an off day. Tenth is a middle-ground call.

Olivia Gürth is a promising 23-year-old who won European bronze in 9:15.33, but her Stockholm race was 9:42.35 and she was only ninth at Lausanne in 9:22.47. She is talented, but still not reliable enough against this level. Eleventh.

Ilona Mononen’s 9:15.18 in Stockholm is better than anything Renouard has produced this year, and she is a national record holder who is still only 22. Her European final performance was ordinary, but her flat 3000m speed is genuine. Twelfth.

Flavie Renouard, Cara Feain-Ryan, Gracie Hyde, and Emma Coburn all have strengths, but their recent results are clearly below the rest. Renouard’s 9:21.79 is her best recent mark; Feain-Ryan ran 9:22.07 at the Commonwealth Games; Hyde was 9:22.10 at USAs; Coburn’s 9:29.68 at USAs was a sign of decline at 35. In a fast Zurich race, these four should fill the final places, with Feain-Ryan slightly ahead of Hyde because she has been in 9:21 shape internationally, and Hyde ahead of Coburn because of her US Championship result.

The main storyline is Cherotich vs. the field. She has the best 2026 resume, the best recent form, and the fastest raw speed of anyone in the race. Lemngole is the strongest challenger, and Chemutai can challenge if she rediscovers her May form. After that, the battle is for fourth through sixth, where Halladay, Thorner, and Krause are separated by very little.
blurbs.1500m Men:
Predicted finish for the Men’s 1500 m at the Zurich Diamond League, 27 August 2026:

1. **Yared Nuguse (USA)** – 3:29.31  
2. **Ethan Strand (USA)** – 3:29.42  
3. **Phanuel Kipkosgei Koech (KEN)** – 3:29.54  
4. **Cole Hocker (USA)** – 3:29.63  
5. **Jakob Ingebrigtsen (NOR)** – 3:29.72  
6. **Timothy Cheruiyot (KEN)** – 3:30.05  
7. **Samuel Pihlström (SWE)** – 3:30.20  
8. **Jake Heyward (GBR)** – 3:30.33  
9. **Azeddine Habz (FRA)** – 3:30.48  
10. **Vincent Ciattei (USA)** – 3:30.62  
11. **Anass Essayi (MAR)** – 3:30.76  
12. **Anas Lagtiy Chaoudar (FRA)** – 3:30.91  
13. **Isaac Nader (POR)** – 3:31.08  
14. **Hobbs Kessler (USA)** – 3:31.35  
15. **Robert Farken (GER)** – 3:31.65  
16. **Stefan Nillessen (NED)** – 3:32.10  
17. **Žan Rudolf (SLO)** – 3:34.80  
18. **Ben Claridge (GBR)** – 3:38.50  

---

### Why this order

- **Yared Nuguse** gets the nod for the win. He has the best 2026 1500 m credentials of anyone in the field: wins in Rabat and Stockholm with 3:30.35 and 3:30.11, plus impressive mile results behind fast pace in London and Eugene. He also beat Ethan Strand head-to-head at both the Prefontaine Classic and London meetings. At 26, he is in his prime and has shown the most complete mix of speed and consistency.

- **Ethan Strand** is second because he did what nobody else in this field did in the final run-up to Zurich: he won the loaded Silesia Diamond League 1500 m on 23 August, beating Koech, Hocker, and Ingebrigtsen in 3:30.77. That result is the most relevant recent data point. His age, 23, and his strong mile form back up the idea that this was no fluke.

- **Phanuel Kipkosgei Koech** is only 19, but he is not a prospect anymore — he is already a major player. He owns the world U20 1500 m record of 3:27.72, finished third in Zurich in 2025, won in Budapest this summer, and was second at Silesia just before this race. His youth is a slight risk, but his raw talent and proven ability on the big Diamond League circuit put him above the chasing pack.

- **Cole Hocker** is fourth. He is the Olympic 1500 m champion and 2025 world 5000 m champion, and he was only 0.02 seconds behind Koech at Silesia. His kick is elite, but he has not shown quite the same sustained 2026 1500 m form as Nuguse or Strand. Still, in a fast Zurich race, Hocker is dangerous and should be in the mix.

- **Jakob Ingebrigtsen** is fifth. This may feel low for a two-time Olympic champion and multiple world-record holder, but the 2026 evidence says his focus has been more on 5000 m. He won the European 5000 m title in Birmingham in 13:15.29, then came fourth behind Strand, Koech, and Hocker in Silesia. His pedigree means he cannot be written off, but based on current 1500 m sharpness, the three ahead of him are justified.

- **Timothy Cheruiyot** is next. The 30-year-old former world champion is not the force he was in 2019, but he still won the Oslo Diamond League mile in 3:48.21 and was third in Stockholm in 3:30.67. He is a tough, experienced racer and should be the best of the non-USA/Kenyan-youngster group.

- **Samuel Pihlström** follows. He was the European Championships silver medallist in the 1500 m and then ran 3:31.41 for fifth at Silesia, beating Heyward, Ciattei, Essayi, and Nader. The Swedish record holder is having the best season of his life and looks genuinely reliable.

- **Jake Heyward** is eighth. He was third in the London Diamond League mile in 3:46.73, fourth at the Europeans, and sixth at Silesia in 3:31.47. He is not quite as explosive as the top five, but he is consistent and tough.

- **Azeddine Habz** is the hardest one to place. He owns the fastest flat 1500 m time of the year among these athletes, 3:29.80 in Paris, and he has a 3:27.49 performance from 2025. But he finished 10th in the European final and was only ninth in Stockholm. At 32, he still has the talent, but his late-season form is too inconsistent to put him above Pihlström or Heyward.

- **Vincent Ciattei, Anass Essayi, and Anas Lagtiy Chaoudar** form a tight, reliable group. Ciattei has been excellent in Diamond League races all summer, including 3:30.90 in Rabat and seventh at Silesia. Essayi has a 3:30.17 from Paris and consistently runs 3:30–3:31. Lagtiy, at 21, showed huge potential with 3:30.31 in Paris, but he is less proven at this exact level.

- **Isaac Nader** is lower than his world champion status suggests. He won the world title in 2025, but his 2026 has not gone to plan: he was 12th in the European final and only ninth at Silesia in 3:32.00. His Rabat run of 3:30.43 shows the talent is still there, but he has not put back-to-back races together this summer.

- **Hobbs Kessler** looks more like an 800 m specialist this season after making the US podium over 800 m, and his 1500 m results have been solid but not spectacular. **Robert Farken** is consistent but lacks the late-season spark; he was ninth at the Europeans and his best mile in London was impressive but not quite top-tier. **Stefan Nillessen** is the reigning European champion, but his 14th-place collapse in Silesia in 3:41.72 is a warning sign heading into Zurich.

- **Žan Rudolf and Ben Claridge** are projected last. Rudolf has an alarming number of recent DNFs in Diamond League races, including at Silesia, and Claridge has struggled badly against elite fields. If either finishes at all, it will likely be at the back of the pack.

The top of this race should be very fast. With Nuguse, Strand, Koech, Hocker, and Ingebrigtsen all willing to push, I expect a winning time around 3:29, with the whole top five separated by less than half a second.
blurbs.800m Women:
Predicted finish – Weltklasse Zürich Women’s 800m, 27 August 2026:

1. Audrey Werro (SUI) — 1:54.42  
2. Femke Broeders-Bol (NED) — 1:54.58  
3. Georgia Hunter Bell (GBR) — 1:55.72  
4. Saida Tsehaye (ETH) — 1:56.18  
5. Sarah Billings (AUS) — 1:57.05  
6. Jessica Hull (AUS) — 1:57.48  
7. Eloisa Coiro (ITA) — 1:58.35  
8. Veronica Vancardo (SUI) — 1:58.91  
9. Valentina Rosamilia (SUI) — 1:59.14  
10. Myrte van der Schoot (NED) — 2:02.90  

This is a fascinating race because it mixes a potential all-time great in Werro, a former 400m hurdling world champion in Broeders-Bol, a versatile 800/1500 global medallist in Hunter Bell, and a rapidly rising teenage Ethiopian in Tsehaye.

The clear favourite is Audrey Werro. She is the reigning European 800m champion, she is only 21, and she ran 1:53.80 in Paris in 2026 — the third-fastest time in history. She has also beaten Femke Broeders-Bol in every head-to-head this season, including at Paris, the European Championships and Lausanne. Her Lausanne win over Bol was narrow, 1:55.33 to 1:55.41, but Werro still had the superior finishing strength. On a fast Zürich track, with Bol pushing her, Werro can drop back under 1:55 and should hold on for the win.

Femke Broeders-Bol is the obvious runner-up. Since switching fully to the 800m in 2026, she has been remarkably consistent: 1:55.60 in Paris, 1:55.54 for European bronze, and 1:55.41 in Lausanne. Her 400m speed and 400m hurdles pedigree give her a devastating finish, and she has closed most of the gap to Werro. But she hasn’t yet beaten Werro, and in a championship-style race where Werro controls the pace, Bol may again have to settle for second. She should still run well under 1:55, very close to Werro.

Georgia Hunter Bell is a classy 800m runner, but she arrives in Zürich slightly less 800m-sharp than the top two. She won Commonwealth gold over 800m in 2026 and was the 2025 World Championship silver medallist with 1:54.90. However, her best 800m this year is only 1:55.93 from the UK Championships, and her Commonwealth final was a slow, tactical 1:59.51. She has also been prioritising the 1500m, where she became world indoor and European champion. That means she is fit, but maybe not as specifically explosive over two laps as Werro and Bol. A 1:55.7 from her is strong, but not enough to beat the top two.

Saida Tsehaye is the most exciting outsider. She is just 17, but she has improved enormously through 2026. After running 1:57.96 at Oordegem in early August, she stepped up at Lausanne to run 1:56.92, finishing third behind Werro and Bol and ahead of the Swiss pair. That is a serious time for a teenager, and her upward curve suggests she can go faster still. She might not be consistent enough to beat the established stars yet, but she is clearly the best of the non-Bol/Hunter Bell group.

Sarah Billings is a solid, veteran-level 800m runner. She is the Oceanian record holder and a Commonwealth bronze medallist, and she has run 1:57.01 in Paris this year. That gives her a narrow edge over the chasing pack. However, she hasn’t shown the same rapid improvement as Tsehaye, and her Commonwealth final was only 2:00.61, indicating she may struggle in truly fast, aggressive races. Still, in a paced Diamond League race, Billings should produce another 1:57-class performance.

Jessica Hull is the hardest to predict. She is a world-class 1500m and 3000m runner with an Oceanian-record 800m pedigree, and she made the 800m final at the 2025 World Championships. But she has not run an 800m in 2026 based on her results, and she has spent the season racing 1500s, 3000s, miles and cross country. She also raced a 1500m in Silesia only days before Zürich. That means her endurance is superb, but her 800m sharpness is questionable. A 1:57.4 prediction assumes she uses her strength to stay in contact, but she lacks the recent specific speed to challenge Billings or Tsehaye.

Eloisa Coiro is an interesting case: her bio says she is a 400m specialist, but she has developed into a reliable international 800m runner. She reached the European 800m final in 2026, ran 1:58.42 in Rabat and 1:58.59 in Ostrava. Her 400m speed gives her a good last 200m, but her 800m base is not quite as strong as Hull’s or Billings’s. She should lead the second Swiss/Italian group.

The two Swiss runners, Veronica Vancardo and Valentina Rosamilia, are closely matched. Vancardo ran 1:58.68 in Lausanne and finished fourth there, directly ahead of Rosamilia, who ran 1:58.93. Vancardo also had a slightly stronger European final, though both finished 7th and 8th behind Coiro. Their order should mirror Lausanne: Vancardo ahead of Rosamilia, both in the 1:58-1:59 range.

Finally, Myrte van der Schoot is a 400m specialist and 4x400m relay gold medallist, but she is out of her depth in a world-class 800m. She has already failed to finish 800m races in Paris and Lausanne in 2026, and her event is clearly the flat 400m. If she completes the race, she would likely be last in around 2:02-2:03; if she pushes hard from the start as a pacemaker-style runner, she might again fade and fail to finish. Either way, she is the clear outsider.
blurbs.200m Men:
Predicted finish — Men’s 200m, Zurich Diamond League, 27 August 2026:

1. Kenneth Bednarek (USA) — 19.76  
2. Sinesipho Dambile (RSA) — 19.85  
3. Andre de Grasse (CAN) — 19.93  
4. Makanakaishe Charamba (ZIM) — 20.00  
5. José Figueroa (PUR) — 20.02  
6. Bryan Levell (JAM) — 20.05  
7. Reynier Mena (CUB) — 20.09  
8. Timothé Mumenthaler (SUI) — 20.24  

Why this order:

Bednarek is the clear favourite. He has the best 2026 200m credentials in the field, with a 19.69 win in Rabat and a 19.87 win in Stockholm, and he beat Dambile in both of those races by significant margins. More recently, he ran 9.87 in the 100m at Silesia on 23 August, showing he still has elite speed just days before Zurich. With his 2025 World Championships silver medal and consistent Diamond League form, he should be able to close out this race in the 19.7s.

Dambile is the next safest pick. He has been the most consistent sub-20 performer in the second half of the season, winning Commonwealth gold in Glasgow with 19.96, and following it with a 19.98 run at Lausanne in a headwind. His 19.74 in Doha is the fastest legal mark by anyone in this field behind Bednarek’s 19.69. He also has direct wins over Charamba, Mena, Levell and Mumenthaler this summer. He doesn’t yet have Bednarek’s top-end speed, but he should be firmly second.

De Grasse gets third based on pedigree and his best 2026 marks. His 19.84 in Gaborone is faster than anything Charamba, Figueroa, Levell or Mena have produced this season, and he also ran 19.95 in Zagreb. He was beaten convincingly by Bednarek and Dambile in Rabat, which limits his ceiling in this field, but his 9.96 100m at Silesia suggests he is in good shape. In a high-quality Zurich race, experience should carry him to a podium finish ahead of the younger challengers.

Charamba edges Figueroa for fourth. He has been remarkably consistent in 2026, with 19.88 runs in both College Station and Doha, and he finished ahead of Figueroa at both Prefontaine and Lausanne. He does not have quite the same raw breakthrough speed as Figueroa, but his reliability over 200m makes him the safer pick to run around 20.0 at Zurich.

Figueroa is only fifth, but he is the most dangerous outsider. His 19.87 at the Pan American Championships and 19.98 at the CAC Games are standout results for a 21-year-old, and he has clearly improved from his early-season 20.3s. However, he was 0.02 behind Charamba at Lausanne and was well beaten at Prefontaine earlier in July. He could absolutely overtake Charamba on a good night, but the head-to-head evidence favours Charamba slightly.

Levell is difficult to trust for this race. He was a 2025 World Championship bronze medallist and has a 19.64 personal best, but his 2026 season has been messy. His 19.93 in Nairobi was good, but he followed it with 20.44 in Rabat and 20.20 at Prefontaine, and he hasn’t shown the same late-season form as Dambile, Charamba or Figueroa. He has the talent to finish higher, but based on the data he looks more likely to be in the 20.0–20.1 range in Zurich.

Mena is another athlete whose best marks remain better than his 2026 consistency. The 19.63 runner of 2023 is still capable of an occasional 20.04, which he produced in Doha, but he also ran 20.53 in both Stockholm and Oslo. Against this strong field, that inconsistency probably leaves him in the back half.

Mumenthaler rounds out the prediction. His 20.09 in the European Championship semi-final was a personal best and very encouraging, but his final was 20.26 windy and he could only manage 20.39 at Lausanne. He is clearly a quality European sprinter, but the competition in Zurich is much deeper, and he hasn’t yet shown he can mix with sub-20 runners like Bednarek, Dambile, de Grasse and the rest.

blurbs.Shot Put Women:
Predicted finish — Women’s Shot Put, Brussels Diamond League, 4 September 2026:

1. Chase Jackson (USA) – 21.03 m  
2. Jessica Schilder (NED) – 20.82 m  
3. Sarah Mitton (CAN) – 20.24 m  
4. Yemisi Mabry (GER) – 19.68 m  
5. Fanny Roos (SWE) – 19.35 m  
6. Danniel Thomas-Dodd (JAM) – 18.77 m  

Why this order:

Chase Jackson gets the nod for the win. She has been the most consistent 20.50+ thrower in the world during the late 2026 season, with standout victories at the Prefontaine Classic (20.56 m), Silesia (20.92 m), and ISTAF Berlin (21.02 m). That Berlin throw, just five days before Brussels, shows she is peaking at the right time. She also defeated Jessica Schilder in their three most recent head-to-head meetings — Oslo, Prefontaine, and Silesia — and already has a World Indoor title this year. At 31, Jackson is in the best sustained form of her career.

Jessica Schilder remains the biggest threat. She is the reigning 2025 world champion, the European champion in 2026, and owns the Dutch record of 21.09 m from Shaoxing. She has the highest ceiling in the field, and her wins over Jackson in Shaoxing and Stockholm prove she can beat the American when everything clicks. But her form has been more uneven: 19.88 m in Paris, 20.11 m in Oslo, and 20.20 m in Silesia suggest she is not quite at the 21-metre level heading into Brussels. Still, expect her to push Jackson and finish a clear second.

Sarah Mitton is the clear third favourite. The Canadian is a two-time world indoor champion and Commonwealth champion, and she has thrown 20.66 m this season. She also beat Schilder at the Paris Diamond League in June. However, her results in the biggest Diamond League meetings this year — 19.89 m in Stockholm, 19.89 m in Oslo, 19.61 m at Prefontaine, and a quiet 19.34 m in Silesia — show she lacks the firepower to stay with Jackson and Schilder in a high-quality final. She should still be comfortably ahead of the rest.

Yemisi Mabry is the best of the chasing group. The 2024 Olympic champion has been inconsistent, but she still has clear quality: 20.37 m to win the German Indoor title, 19.93 m in Paris, and 19.73 m at ISTAF Berlin. Those marks are better than anything Fanny Roos or Danniel Thomas-Dodd have produced recently. Mabry’s main issue is reliability — she was only 18.55 m in Shaoxing — but her ceiling is high enough to take fourth.

Fanny Roos should finish fifth. She has been solid throughout 2026, with 19.70 m at Prefontaine, 19.51 m in Helsinki, and a fourth-place finish at the European Championships. She doesn’t have the 20-metre ability of the top four on current form, but she is consistently in the 19.20–19.70 range, which should be enough to hold off Thomas-Dodd.

Danniel Thomas-Dodd rounds out the field. The Jamaican veteran has a national record of 19.77 m and a strong championship pedigree, but at 33 she is clearly past her peak. Her 2026 season has been limited to mostly 18.20–19.30 m efforts, and she struggled badly at Silesia with 18.16 m. Against this level of competition, a low-19 or high-18 metre result is the likely outcome.
blurbs.Long Jump Men:
Predicted finish – Men’s Long Jump, Brussels Diamond League, 4 September 2026:

1. Miltiadis Tentoglou (GRE) – 8.47 m  
2. Tajay Gayle (JAM) – 8.36 m  
3. Wayne Pinnock (JAM) – 8.29 m  
4. Jorge A. Hodelín (CUB) – 8.28 m  
5. Bozhidar Sarâboyukov (BUL) – 8.24 m  
6. Simon Ehammer (SUI) – 8.17 m  
7. Yanni Sampson (BEL) – 7.91 m  

---

**Reasoning:**

**Tentoglou is the clear favourite.** His 2026 season is outstanding even by his own standards: 8.61 in Monaco, 8.66 at the Greek Championships, 8.45 to win in Zürich, and the European title with 8.44. He has also already shown he can win the biggest multi-athlete finals, and his two Olympic golds and four European outdoor titles give him a psychological edge. The only major blip on his record in this timescale was the 2025 World Championships final, but he has rebounded emphatically since then.

**Gayle looks like the main challenger.** His 8.43 in Zürich, just two centimetres behind Tentoglou, shows he is peaking at the right time. He also won the Jamaican title with 8.37 and took Commonwealth gold, while his 2019 World Championship pedigree and 2025 World Championship silver demonstrate his ability to deliver in finals. The worrying 7.70 in Lausanne is a red flag, but he responded immediately with his best jump of the season in Zürich, suggesting he can be trusted to bounce back again in Brussels.

**Pinnock gets the slight edge for third over Hodelín.** Pinnock has been narrowly ahead of Hodelín in their two strongest recent head-to-heads: 8.39 to 8.38 in Monaco and 8.33 to 8.32 in Zürich. That is a tiny margin, but it shows Pinnock’s big-meet experience — Olympic silver and World Championship silver — can help him hold off a younger rival. His inconsistency is a concern, especially after 7.75 in Rome and 8.01 in Lausanne, but his last two Diamond League finals have been solid, and he should make the podium if he produces something similar.

**Hodelín is the most exciting unknown.** At 18, he has already set the world U20 record and jumped 8.46, which is better than Pinnock’s 2026 best. He has also been very consistent in the major Diamond League meetings: 8.38 in Monaco, 8.06 in Lausanne, and 8.32 in Zürich. The only reason he is fourth is that Pinnock has beaten him by one centimetre in two high-level finals. Hodelín is clearly capable of beating anyone except Tentoglou on a good day, and a surprise podium finish would not be shocking.

**Saraboyukov is a strong young jumper but has not matched his best in the biggest DL finals.** He has excellent pedigree — European indoor champion, World Indoor bronze medallist, European outdoor bronze medallist — and his 8.49 in Plovdiv and 8.48 at the Bulgarian Championships show huge raw talent. But in Monaco he was fourth with 8.36, and in Zürich he slipped to fifth with 8.16. He may be hurt slightly by also competing in triple jump and high jump in domestic meetings, so in a one-off Diamond League final against this depth, fifth feels right.

**Ehammer is remarkably consistent but lacks the top-end pop in specialist long jump finals here.** His decathlon long jump of 8.51 in Götzis was superb, and his European silver with 8.29 shows he can medal at major championships. However, in the Diamond League series he has been more workmanlike: 8.32 in Monaco, 8.13 in Lausanne, 8.14 in Zürich. That range is excellent, but probably not enough to beat three or four of the world’s best pure long jumpers in Brussels.

**Sampson is clearly the outsider.** He is a multiple Belgian champion and had a nice breakthrough with a legal 8.02, but his 11th-place finish at the European Championships with 7.59 shows the gap to this field. To be competitive in Brussels he would need a huge personal best, probably around 8.10 or better, and nothing in his recent results suggests he is ready to do that against Tentoglou, Gayle, Pinnock, and Hodelín. A solid 7.91 would still be a respectable showing for him.
blurbs.Discus Throw Women:
Predicted finish — Women’s Discus Throw, Brussels Diamond League, 4 September 2026:

| Place | Athlete | Predicted Mark |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Valarie Sion (USA) | 69.12 m |
| 2 | Jorinde van Klinken (NED) | 68.04 m |
| 3 | Cierra Jackson (USA) | 66.87 m |
| 4 | Shanice Craft (GER) | 65.38 m |
| 5 | Bin Feng (CHN) | 64.42 m |
| 6 | Vanessa Kamga (SWE) | 63.75 m |

---

**Why this order?**

**1. Valarie Sion**  
Sion is the clear favourite. She is the reigning Olympic and World champion, and her 2026 season has been the most consistent of anyone in the field. She has thrown 68–70 metres repeatedly, with a season best of 73.10 m in Oklahoma in April.
