More importantly, she has beaten almost everyone almost every time they have met this year: she won Xiamen, Rabat, Stockholm, Los Angeles, the Prefontaine Classic, and the US Championships. Her only loss came to Cierra Jackson in London, where Sion still threw 68.39 m. Her most recent result, 67.89 m to win ISTAF Berlin on 30 August, shows she is still in strong form heading into Brussels.

**2. Jorinde van Klinken**  
Van Klinken has been the most consistent challenger to Sion. She has finished behind Sion in every direct meeting this season, but she has regularly been the next best thrower. Her 70.99 m in Oklahoma was a Dutch record and just 2.11 m behind Sion’s 73.10 m. Since then she has been remarkably reliable: 66.57 m in Stockholm, 67.99 m in London, 67.67 m to win the European Championships, and 66.86 m to win Bellinzona. She has also beaten Cierra Jackson in most of their 2026 meetings, including by nearly four metres in Oklahoma and by 1.45 metres at Bellinzona. That consistency makes her the strong silver-medal pick.

**3. Cierra Jackson**  
Jackson has the single best performance of the season — her 71.72 m Diamond League record in London was outstanding and shows she can beat anyone on the right day. But that result is the clear outlier in her 2026 season. Away from London she has been uneven: 52.90 m in Stockholm, a no-mark at the Prefontaine Classic, 63.22 m in Los Angeles, 67.40 m at US Championships, and 65.41 m at Bellinzona. She is a serious podium threat because of her huge ceiling, but her reliability is not yet at the level of Sion or van Klinken. A bronze medal with a 66–67 m throw feels right.

**4. Shanice Craft**  
Craft has quietly had a strong late-season push. She threw 66.18 m to win the German Championships in July, then took silver at the European Championships with 65.72 m, finishing ahead of Vanessa Kamga. She also has a 66.03 m mark from May. Her early-season Diamond League results were more modest, but her form has improved since mid-summer. In Brussels, she looks more likely to beat Feng and Kamga than the top three.

**5. Bin Feng**  
Feng is a former world champion and Olympic silver medallist, but her 2026 form has been below her peak. She threw 65.03 m at Xiamen and 64.51 m at Rabat, which placed her comfortably ahead of Craft and Kamga in those meets. However, her late-season results dropped off: she only managed 62.51 m at the Chinese Championships in mid-August. She is capable of a 64–65 m throw, but she has not shown the 66–67 m level that would challenge the top three. She likely finishes fifth.

**6. Vanessa Kamga**  
Kamga has talent and a national record of 66.61 m from the 2025 World Championships, plus a European bronze in 2026. But her 2026 season has been inconsistent. She threw 65.30 m in London, but also 59.78 m in Rabat and just 61.93 m in Stockholm. Her most recent result — 62.87 m in Gothenburg on 24 August — was not the kind of momentum a thrower wants going into a Diamond League final. She could easily outperform this prediction if she finds her best, but on the evidence, she is the weakest link in this particular field.
blurbs.Pole Vault Men:
**Predicted finish / marks — Brussels Diamond League, 4 September 2026 — Men’s Pole Vault**

1. **Armand Duplantis** (SWE, 26) — **6.30 m**  
2. **Emmanouil Karalis** (GRE, 26) — **6.15 m**  
3. **Sondre Guttormsen** (NOR, 26) — **6.00 m**  
4. **Kurtis Marschall** (AUS, 28) — **5.95 m**  
5. **Sam Kendricks** (USA, 33) — **5.90 m**  
6. **Baptiste Thiery** (FRA, 24) — **5.85 m**  
7. **Ben Broeders** (BEL, 30) — **5.75 m**

**Bar progression:** 5.55, 5.60, 5.65, 5.70, 5.75, 5.80, 5.85, 5.90, 5.95, 6.00, 6.05, 6.10, 6.15, 6.20. After Duplantis clears 6.20 and is the only remaining competitor with victory secured, he uses the winner’s option to raise the bar to 6.30 and clears it.

---

**Why this order?**

**Duplantis** is the obvious favourite, and the data backs a statement win. His Wikipedia bio already identifies him as the world-record holder with nine senior global titles, two Olympic golds, and three outdoor World titles. In 2026 alone he went 6.31 indoors, won the World Indoor title with 6.25, won the European outdoor title with 6.15, and then followed with 6.21 in Lausanne, 6.20 in Silesia, and 6.25 in Zurich. He has had two surprising losses — Stockholm (5.80 behind Marschall) and London (5.95 behind Kendricks on countback) — but those look like off-nights, not trend. Brussels is the Diamond League final; I expect him to be locked in, win cleanly at 6.20, then take one celebratory record-height attempt after clearing 6.30.

**Karalis** is clearly the No. 2 in this field. His bio notes he is the only other man alongside Duplantis to have cleared 6.20, and his 2026 results are a constant string of runner-up finishes to Duplantis: 6.05 at the World Indoor, 6.00 at the European final, 6.16 in Lausanne, 6.00 in Silesia, and 6.20 in Zurich. He had a shaky spell in the middle of the summer — 5.70 in Shaoxing and 5.62 in Oslo — but he recovered impressively. In Brussels, I see him pushing Duplantis through 6.15 but failing at 6.20.

**Guttormsen** has arguably been the most improved of the chasing group. His indoor 6.06 in Rouen and 6.00 in Uppsala showed a jump in level, and he carried that into the late summer with 6.00 in both Silesia and Zurich. He was 4th at the World Indoor and 6th at the European final, which suggests he is still a step below Karalis, but he has been consistently better than Marschall and Kendricks in the final part of 2026. I have him clearing 6.00 and then failing at 6.05.

**Marschall** is a two-time World bronze medallist, per his bio, and he has scored some genuine scalps this season — including beating Duplantis in Stockholm, 5.90 to 5.80, and winning Oslo with 5.82. He also cleared 6.00 in Budapest. But his Australian Championships no-height was a reminder that he can still be vulnerable, and in Silesia and Zurich he finished behind Guttormsen. I think he clears 5.95 in Brussels but misses 6.00.

**Kendricks** is a decorated veteran — 2017 and 2019 World champion and 2024 Olympic silver medallist. He even beat Duplantis in London with a 5.95 winner. But at 33, the consistency is not what it was. His late-2026 results include 5.81 in Lausanne, 5.65 in Silesia, 5.80 in Zurich, and 5.62 in Berlin. He can still produce a big jump on a good day, but against this field I think he tops out at 5.90.

**Thiery** is a talented 24-year-old with real upside — his 5.93 in Paris behind Duplantis and European bronze at 5.85 show his ceiling. But he has also shown sharp inconsistency, including 5.51 in Lausanne and 5.50 in Zurich late in the season. I expect a solid but not spectacular 5.85 in Brussels.

**Broeders** is the Euro U23 champion from his bio, but at 30 he is clearly below this level in 2026. His best late-season marks are around 5.70–5.75, and he finished 8th in the European final. In a stacked Diamond League field, 5.75 feels like the realistic ceiling before he fails at 5.80.
blurbs.400m Hurdles Women:
Predicted finish – Women’s 400m Hurdles, Brussels Diamond League, 4 September 2026:

1. Anna Cockrell (USA, 28) – 52.07  
2. Emma Zapletalová (SVK, 25) – 52.43  
3. Dalilah Muhammad (USA, 35) – 53.10  
4. Rushell Clayton (JAM, 33) – 53.18  
5. Paulien Couckuyt (BEL, 28) – 53.31  
6. Fatoumata Binta Diallo (POR, 25) – 53.38  
7. Gianna Woodruff (PAN, 32) – 53.74  
8. Amalie Iuel (NOR, 31) – 54.06  

---

**Why this order?**

**Anna Cockrell** is the clear favourite. She is in her prime at 28, has Olympic silver-medal pedigree from 2024, and has been the most consistent high-end performer in the 2026 Diamond League. Her wins at the US Championships in 52.94 and especially Zürich in 52.13 — beating most of this exact field — make her the athlete to beat. She also ran 51.49 for a flat 400m this season, showing she has the raw speed to close hard off the final hurdle.

**Emma Zapletalová** is the main challenger. The 25-year-old European champion has multiple 2026 Diamond League wins, including 52.30 in Doha and 52.41 in Lausanne, and she beat Cockrell earlier in the season at Rabat, Roma and Lausanne. Her 54.07 in Zürich was a clear outlier and may have been a fatigue blip following her European title and quick turnaround. On form, she is the only woman here who can realistically push Cockrell under 52.5.

**Dalilah Muhammad** gets the nod for third based on late-season momentum and big-race experience. At 35, she is no longer at her world-record level, but her 53.16 at Zürich and 53.36 win in Brescia show she is still highly competitive. Her DQ at the US Championships is a concern, but her Diamond League form since then has been strong, and her championship pedigree gives her an edge in a rapidly assembled high-class final.

**Rushell Clayton** is almost dead-even with Muhammad. She has been exceptionally consistent all season, with marks like 53.05 in Doha, 53.14 in Roma and 53.17 in Zürich. She lacks a true sub-53 breakthrough in 2026, and Muhammad just edged her in Zürich by 0.01, so I keep Clayton just behind. Still, if Muhammad falters, Clayton is the most likely to capitalise.

**Paulien Couckuyt** is a live home-crowd threat. Her 53.28 in Lausanne was a genuine standout, just behind Cockrell and Zapletalová that day, and she has shown she can beat several of the athletes ranked above her on the right day. She was fourth at the European Championships and has been steadily improving through late summer. Running in Belgium could give her an extra push.

**Fatoumata Binta Diallo** has had a strong breakout season, highlighted by European bronze and a 53.30 run in Zürich. But she has also shown inconsistency, with 55-second races in Oslo and Los Angeles earlier in the summer. She is clearly capable of 53.3, but I trust Couckuyt’s late-season consistency slightly more at this point.

**Gianna Woodruff** has been solid but not spectacular in 2026. She has spent most of the season in the 53.5–53.8 range, with her best being 53.58 in Roma. She won CAC gold and has plenty of experience, but she hasn’t shown the speed to threaten the top five in this field.

**Amalie Iuel** rounds out the prediction. She is a strong relay performer and has been consistent in the 54.0–54.2 range, but her individual best this season hasn’t dipped below 54 seconds. Against a field this deep, that leaves her at the back unless others make mistakes.
blurbs.High Jump Men:
Predicted finish — Brussels Diamond League, Men’s High Jump, 4 September 2026:

1. Gianmarco Tamberi (ITA, 33) — 2.34m  
2. JuVaughn Harrison (USA, 26) — 2.32m  
3. Oleh Doroshchuk (UKR, 24) — 2.30m  
4. Romaine Beckford (JAM, 23) — 2.28m  
5. Mateusz Kołodziejski (POL, 23) — 2.26m  
6. Erick Portillo (MEX, 25) — 2.24m  
7. Thomas Carmoy (BEL, 25) — 2.22m  

These marks fit a valid 2cm progression: 2.14, 2.16, 2.18, 2.20, 2.22, 2.24, 2.26, 2.28, 2.30, 2.32, 2.34.

Why this order:

Tamberi gets the narrow nod despite being 33. His age is a storyline, but his 2026 results are those of a man still at championship level: he won the European outdoor title at 2.32m and then went straight to Silesia and beat a very similar field with 2.31m. That Silesia result is the most useful form line here — he finished 5cm clear of Harrison and 3cm clear of Beckford. Tamberi also has the pedigree of a three-time Diamond League champion and knows exactly how to win tactical, high-pressure competitions. A 2.34m clearance would be a small seasonal progression and fits his late-summer momentum.

Harrison has the highest ceiling in the field. His 2.34m at the Monaco Athletics Festival in early August is the best outdoor mark any of these jumpers has produced in 2026. But the flip side is inconsistency: he was only 4th at the US Championships with 2.17m, 9th in Rome with 2.16m, and then 3rd at Silesia with 2.26m. He rebounded to win Bellinzona with 2.28m, which keeps him second, but his failure to back up 2.34m with another big DL result makes him a slight risk against Tamberi.

Doroshchuk is the most consistent 2.30m+ jumper on paper. He won the World Indoor title in 2026, took European outdoor silver behind Tamberi, won Monaco DL with 2.32m, and cleared 2.33m in Berdichev. The worry is his late-summer trend: 2.30m at the European final, 2.26m at Silesia, then 2.24m at Bellinzona. Still, he has the youth and the recent championship credentials to hold off Beckford for third.

Beckford is the biggest threat to break into the top three. He won Commonwealth gold in 2026 and was second at Silesia with 2.29m, finishing ahead of Harrison, Doroshchuk, and Kołodziejski. But that Silesia result is his clear peak; around it he had 2.24m at Monaco, 2.22m at Heilbronn, and several other mid-2.20s. His ceiling is high, but his reliability is a notch below Doroshchuk’s.

Kołodziejski has been quietly very solid through late 2026: 2.27m at Monaco, 2.26m at Silesia, 2.25m at Heilbronn, 2.24m at Bellinzona, plus a 5th-place Euro finish. He does not have Beckford’s raw 2.29-2.30 upside, but he is less likely to fall apart, so fifth at 2.26m feels right.

Portillo’s 2.30m World Indoor silver proves his talent, and he has outdoor wins in Ostrava and at the CAC Games. But his Diamond League form has been too uneven: 2.20m in Silesia, 2.20m in Monaco, and 2.10m in Bellinzona. He can beat almost anyone on a good day, but the data suggests he will be in the 2.24m range in Brussels.

Carmoy rounds out the field. He was an European finalist and cleared 2.24m at Bellinzona, but his other 2026 outdoor marks — 2.18m at Euros, 2.15m in Montreuil — are clearly below this group. In this company, 2.22m is a reasonable ceiling.
blurbs.100m Men:
Predicted finish (Brussels Diamond League, 4 Sep 2026, assuming a legal wind and a fast Brussels track):

1. Oblique Seville (JAM) — 9.81  
2. Kayinsola Ajayi (NGR) — 9.84  
3. Christian Coleman (USA) — 9.92  
4. Gift Leotlela (RSA) — 9.93  
5. Akani Simbine (RSA) — 9.95  
6. Emmanuel Eseme (CMR) — 9.98  
7. Lachlan Kennedy (AUS) — 10.05  
8. Trayvon Bromell (USA) — 10.10  
9. Simon Verherstraeten (BEL) — 10.18  

The most useful guide is the Silesia Diamond League final on 23 August, because it featured most of this exact field in a high-level 100m. There, Seville won convincingly in 9.83, Coleman ran 9.93, Ajayi 9.94, Leotlela 9.95, Simbine 9.96, and Eseme was back in 9.99. That race basically sets the hierarchy for Brussels, with one adjustment: I would flip Coleman and Ajayi based on their broader 2026 seasons.

Oblique Seville is the clear favourite. He is the reigning world champion, ran 9.82 to win the Jamaican title in 2026, won Silesia in 9.83, and has been the most consistent sub-9.90 sprinter in the world this year. At 24, he is in his prime and has the combination of championship experience and late-season form that no one else in this field can match.

Kayinsola Ajayi gets second because of his ceiling. He won both the Prefontaine Classic and London DL in 9.84 legal, and in both races he beat Seville. His NCAA 9.72w was wind-assisted, so it should not be taken literally, but his legal 9.84s are real. The concern is that he was only 9.94 at Silesia and 9.90 at the Commonwealth final, which suggests he can still be exposed when rounds are tougher. But in a one-off Diamond League final, his youth and raw speed make him the biggest threat to Seville.

Christian Coleman is the trustworthy veteran for third. He has not shown 9.8x legal speed this season, but he has been remarkably stable: 9.93 at the US Championships final, 9.93 again at Silesia, plus a wind-assisted 9.90 semi. At 29, he is no longer the 9.76 sprinter he once was, but he still has the start and the competitive reliability to outrun everyone not named Seville or Ajayi.

Gift Leotlela is slightly ahead of Simbine because he ran 9.91 at the Commonwealth final and 9.95 in the Silesia final, while Simbine’s best late-season marks are 9.95 and 9.96. Leotlela is not explosive enough to challenge the top three, but he is solid, and his 9.92 heat in Silesia showed he can run well even when not in a final.

Akani Simbine is still a quality sprinter at 32, but the data says he is now a 9.95-9.97 performer rather than a 9.82-level threat. He has been beaten by younger, sharper finishers all season. He can still beat many of the world’s best on a good day, but he lacks the top-end pop to get on the podium in this particular field.

Emmanuel Eseme is the hardest to place. His 9.83 Commonwealth gold was the standout result of his season, and at his best he can beat anyone in this race. But his 9.99 in the Silesia final, where he finished behind Coleman, Leotlela, and Simbine, is a red flag. At 32, his peak performances are becoming more isolated. I still put him ahead of the fading group because his Commonwealth semi of 9.89 and final of 9.83 show he can produce world-class speed, but he is a risk to run anywhere from 9.85 to 10.00.

Lachlan Kennedy’s Commonwealth silver in 9.85 was brilliant, but his form since then has collapsed. He ran only 10.08 in the Silesia heats and then 10.21 in Brescia five days before this Brussels race. At 22 he has a very high ceiling, but it is hard to predict him higher than seventh when his last two races were so poor.

Trayvon Bromell is also in a late-season slump. His 9.91 win in Paris in June proved he can still run fast, but he has not been close to that since. A 10.26 in the Silesia heats and a 10.16 at Brescia are simply not competitive with the top group. At 30, he looks like he has lost the consistency needed to make a Diamond League final count.

Simon Verherstraeten is a very good Belgian sprinter, and his indoor 60m national record is excellent, but his outdoor 100m has not reached this level. His 10.27 semi and 13.12 final at the European Championships show he was either injured or struggling badly in his most important outdoor race. Even on home soil in Brussels, he looks outclassed against this lineup.
blurbs.Discus Throw Men:
Predicted finish and mark:

1. Mykolas Alekna (LTU) — 72.34 m  
2. Kristjan Čeh (SLO) — 70.22 m  
3. Daniel Ståhl (SWE) — 69.08 m  
4. Roje Stona (JAM) — 68.44 m  
5. Henrik Janssen (GER) — 68.12 m  
6. Matthew Denny (AUS) — 67.16 m  

Why this order:

At the top, this is a two-man duel between Alekna and Čeh. Alekna is the world record holder at just 23 and has been the most consistent 70m+ thrower on the Diamond League circuit in 2026. His Lithuanian title mark of 72.65 m and Silesia win of 72.58 m are the strongest 2026 performances in this field outside Čeh’s Euro final. Čeh beat Alekna head-to-head at the European Championships with 72.51 m, and he also threw 72.61 m earlier in the spring in Oklahoma, so he clearly has the ability to win. But in their two 2026 Diamond League meetings — Prefontaine and Silesia — Alekna came out on top. Čeh’s post-Euro form also dipped slightly to 68.93 m in Silesia and 68.70 m at the Mediterranean Games, while Alekna followed his European silver with 72.58 m and 71.50 m. Alekna is the safer pick for a September Diamond League final.

Ståhl is the best of the chasing group. At 33, he is not the automatic dominant thrower he was in previous years, but he is still the 2025 world champion and a three-time world champion overall. His 2026 season includes 69.60 m in Stockholm, 69.85 m at the Swedish Championships, and 69.06 m in Helsinki. That gives him a higher top-end and more 69m-plus throws than Stona, Janssen, or Denny. He did finish only fourth at the European Championships, behind Čeh, Alekna, and Janssen, but his overall consistency and big-meet pedigree keep him ahead of the others here.

Stona gets fourth because he has the highest ceiling outside the top two and showed late-season life with 68.14 m in Bellinzona. He is an Olympic gold medalist and Olympic record-holder, and he threw 70.66 m in Oklahoma in 2026, which is better than anything Ståhl or Janssen managed this year. But he is also erratic — he had several 62–64 m results in 2026, and he was only sixth in Silesia while the other contenders around him finished higher. His Bellinzona result suggests he is peaking at the right time, but Ståhl’s greater consistency and Stona’s inconsistency make fourth the right call.

Janssen is fifth. His European bronze with 69.53 m was a genuine standout and he beat Ståhl at both the European Championships and in Bellinzona. However, outside that European final, Janssen’s 2026 season has mostly been a string of 65–68 m throws. He lacks Ståhl’s multiple 69m results and Stona’s 70m ceiling. He is a very solid competitor, but in a loaded final he is not quite dangerous enough to break into the top three.

Denny is last, which is harsh given his Olympic bronze and Commonwealth Games gold in 2026. But his form since April tells the story. He threw 74.04 m and 73.58 m in Oklahoma early in the season, which would make him a contender if he reproduced that, but he has not. Since then he has mostly been in the 66–68 m range, with 66.38 m in Silesia and 66.27 m in Bellinzona. Those marks put him behind every relevant rival in this field in their most recent high-level competitions. His Commonwealth win was solid but modest at 67.73 m. Without a return to his April form, Denny is the weakest athlete in this field on current September form.
blurbs.3000m Steeplechase Women:
Predicted finish and marks — Women’s 3000m Steeplechase, Brussels Diamond League, 4 September 2026:

1. **Faith Cherotich (KEN)** — **8:50.12**  
2. **Winfred Yavi (BRN)** — **8:50.68**  
3. **Doris Lemngole (KEN)** — **8:53.27**  
4. **Peruth Chemutai (UGA)** — **8:54.06**  
5. **Marwa Bouzayani (TUN)** — **8:55.89**  
6. **Kena Tufa (ETH)** — **9:02.62**  
7. **Lexy Halladay (USA)** — **9:06.75**  
8. **Elise Thorner (GBR)** — **9:07.90**  
9. **Lea Meyer (GER)** — **9:10.05**  
10. **Gabrielle Jennings (USA)** — **9:13.82**  
11. **Olivia Gürth (GER)** — **9:15.43**

---

**Why this order?**

This is a very deep steeplechase field, but the podium fight comes down to form, consistency, and recent head-to-head results.

**Cherotich ahead of Yavi:** Faith Cherotich is the current world champion and has been the most consistent steeplechaser in the world in 2026. She ran 8:51.48 and 8:51.74 in her two best Diamond League races, and won the Zurich Diamond League on 27 August in 8:55.82, beating Lemngole and Chemutai. She also won the Prefontaine Classic in Eugene in July. Yavi has the superior lifetime pedigree — Olympic champion, world champion, and second-fastest ever — but her 2026 form has not quite reached her 2025 level. She beat Cherotich in Lausanne with 9:00.04, but that was a slower race, and Cherotich bounced back with a much faster win in Zurich. On current form, Cherotich deserves favourite status.

**Lemngole over Chemutai:** Doris Lemngole’s 8:55.94 in Zurich was a breakthrough performance, finishing just 0.12 seconds behind Cherotich and well clear of Chemutai. She also beat Chemutai earlier in Eugene. Lemngole’s NCAA/Bowerman pedigree, her indoor 3000m speed (8:31.39), and her rapid improvement through 2026 make her the most dangerous challenger outside Cherotich and Yavi. Chemutai still has the early-season form — she won in Shaoxing and Xiamen in 8:51.47 and 8:51.06 — but her July and August races were less convincing: 9:05.39 in Eugene, 9:09.96 at the Commonwealth Games, and 8:58.28 behind Lemngole in Zurich. Her class keeps her in the top four, but the trend favours Lemngole.

**Bouzayani fifth:** Marwa Bouzayani has had an excellent 2026, with 8:54.32 in Eugene and a Diamond League win in Stockholm. She was also fourth at the 2025 World Championships. However, she has not beaten the very top trio this season, and Lemngole’s late-summer surge pushes her down one spot. Still, she should be clearly the best of the rest.

**Tufa ahead of the British and American chasers:** Kena Tufa’s 8:59.66 in Shaoxing was a massive breakout, and she is the 2026 Ethiopian champion. She has been inconsistent since, running 9:11–9:12 in Stockholm and Lausanne, but her ceiling is higher than those around her. If race pace is honest, she should finish as the clear first athlete outside the top five.

**Halladay and Thorner:** Lexy Halladay and Elise Thorner are closely matched, but Halladay has the better Diamond League head-to-head record this summer. She finished ahead of Thorner in both Lausanne and Zurich, and her 9:08.35 in Lausanne was a strong statement. Thorner’s Commonwealth silver in 9:05.45 was excellent, but she has not repeated that level in the deeper Diamond League fields.

**Meyer, Jennings, Gürth:** Lea Meyer has the best season mark of this trio with 9:09.13 in Eugene, and she tends to run consistently in the 9:09–9:17 range. Jennings has a faster season best than Gürth (9:11.72 vs 9:15.07), but her Zurich performance was weaker. Gürth’s European bronze and recent 9:15.33 show she is competitive, but her overall ceiling in a fast, high-level Brussels final looks slightly lower than the others.
blurbs.200m Men:
**Predicted Finish — Men’s 200m, Brussels Diamond League, 4 September 2026:**

1. **Kenneth Bednarek (USA)** — 19.66  
2. **Letsile Tebogo (BOT)** — 19.78  
3. **Sinesipho Dambile (RSA)** — 19.84  
4. **Makanakaishe Charamba (ZIM)** — 20.03  
5. **José Figueroa (PUR)** — 20.12  
6. **Timothé Mumenthaler (SUI)** — 20.21  
7. **Courtney Lindsey (USA)** — 20.28  
8. **Reynier Mena (CUB)** — 20.41  

---

### Why this order?

**1. Kenneth Bednarek — 19.66**  
At 27, Bednarek is in the form of his life. His 19.62 (-0.4) in Zürich on 27 August is the peak result of anyone in this field, and it came just over a week before Brussels. He also ran 19.69 in Rabat, 19.87 in Stockholm, and was the 2025 world silver medallist with 19.58. He has consistently outperformed every man here in 2026, including beating Tebogo by 0.27 in Rabat and Dambile by 0.20 in Zürich. His 100m form is also elite — 9.88 at US Championships and 9.87 in Silesia — which supports his top-end speed in the 200m. He is the clear favourite.

**2. Letsile Tebogo — 19.78**  
Tebogo remains the classically dangerous big-race runner. The 22-year-old Olympic champion has not been quite as explosive in 2026 as in 2024-25, but his 200m consistency is still strong: 19.84 in Oslo, 19.93 at Prefontaine, and 19.87 to win Lausanne on 21 August. He beat Dambile in both of their main 2026 200m head-to-heads, in Rabat 19.96 to 20.03 and Lausanne 19.87 to 19.98. Tebogo’s 4th-place 19.65 in the 2025 World Championship final remains a significant pedigree marker. His 400m in Brescia on 30 August is a slight unknown, but he still has the speed reserve to finish second.

**3. Sinesipho Dambile — 19.84**  
Dambile is the most improved 200m runner in this field. The 23-year-old won the 2026 Commonwealth Games title in 19.96, ran 19.74 (+1.8) in Doha, and backed it up with 19.82 in Zürich and 19.98 in Lausanne. He has beaten Charamba comfortably in their recent meetings and pushed Tebogo closely, though he has lost to Tebogo each time they’ve shared a Diamond League 200m in 2026. His consistency at 19.8-20.0 makes him the clear third man here.

**4. Makanakaishe Charamba — 20.03**  
Charamba is dependable but not quite at the level of the top three. The 24-year-old Olympian ran 19.88 in Doha, but his late-season form has settled around 20.10-20.15: 20.14 in Lausanne and 20.10 in Zürich. He is clearly the best of the next group, having finished ahead of Figueroa in both Lausanne and Zürich, but he lacks the sub-19.8 gear shown by Bednarek, Tebogo, and Dambile.

**5. José Figueroa — 20.12**  
Figueroa is only 21 but already a Pan American and CAC Games champion. His 19.87 in Medellín and 19.98 at the CAC Games prove he can run quickly when the field is slightly weaker, but in strong Diamond League company he has struggled to find that same level. He was 20.16 in Lausanne and 20.32 in Zürich — ahead of Mumenthaler and Lindsey in the latter, but still a clear step below Charamba. This is a breakout year, but Brussels may come down too sharply for him.

**6. Timothé Mumenthaler — 20.21**  
Mumenthaler is a genuine championship performer — European champion in 2024 and bronze medallist in 2026 with a 20.09 semifinal — but his Diamond League form has been less convincing. He could only manage 20.39 in Lausanne and 20.34 in Zürich, and he was disqualified in Stockholm. The 23-year-old is solid, but he lacks the late-season sharpness of the men above him.

**7. Courtney Lindsey — 20.28**  
Lindsey’s 2026 season started respectably — 20.21 in Rabat and 20.19 at Prefontaine — but his 200m form has tailed off badly. He was 20.61 in Lausanne and has focused more on the 100m in 2026, where he was fifth at the US Championships. Against this deeper field, his inability to produce a sub-20 in the second half of the season makes it hard to see him moving up.

**8. Reynier Mena — 20.41**  
Mena’s 19.63 personal best from 2022 feels distant. The 29-year-old showed a glimmer with 20.04 in Doha, but his recent results — 20.53 in Oslo, 20.53 in Stockholm, and 20.73 in Zürich — suggest he is no longer at the sharp end. In a race with this much young speed, Mena’s fading late-season form leaves him last.
blurbs.100m Hurdles Women:
Predicted Finish – Women’s 100m Hurdles, Brussels Diamond League, 4 September 2026:

1. Masai Russell (USA) – 12.12  
2. Tobi Amusan (NGR) – 12.24  
3. Nadine Visser (NED) – 12.35  
4. Devynne Charlton (BAH) – 12.38  
5. Alaysha Johnson (USA) – 12.45  
6. Megan Simmonds (JAM) – 12.53  
7. Pia Skrzyszowska (POL) – 12.61  
8. Yanla Ndjip-Nyemeck (BEL) – 12.82  

---

**Why this order?**

Masai Russell is the obvious favourite. Her 2026 season has been extraordinary: 12.14 in Xiamen, 12.20 in Monaco, and then a world record 12.09 in Zürich on 27 August. She has beaten almost every rival in this field multiple times this summer, and she enters Brussels as the dominant force. Even if she does not quite repeat her world-record run, she should control the race from the gun and go under 12.15.

Tobi Amusan is the clear second contender. The former world-record holder has been consistent at 12.28–12.34 for much of 2026, then produced a strong 12.23 behind Russell in Zürich. Her 12.28 wins in Paris and Rabat show she is still elite, but she has not matched Russell’s speed this season. A 12.24 in Brussels is a realistic, high-quality prediction.

Nadine Visser gets third based on late-season momentum. She was 12.41 in Paris, 12.42 in Lausanne, and then ran a season-best 12.34 in Zürich. Her European title in Birmingham in 12.67 was wind-affected, but that does not erase her sharp August form. She has been building well and looks more reliable outdoors than Charlton, who has not raced since the Commonwealth Games in late July.

Devynne Charlton is the toughest call. She has a 12.37 legal season’s best in Xiamen, plus Commonwealth Games gold with 12.33w. She is incredibly consistent and a world-class technician. However, she has not competed in over a month before Brussels, which is a slight concern against Visser, who has raced consistently and was faster in Zürich. I still expect Charlton to beat Alaysha Johnson because of her steadiness: her worst legal outdoor result this year is around 12.62, while Johnson has mixed 12.38 with 12.86 and a DQ.

Alaysha Johnson has genuine speed — 12.38 in Monaco, 12.39 in Paris, 12.42 at US Championships. But she has also been erratic: 12.86 at Prefontaine and a DQ in Zürich. In a loaded Diamond League final, she needs a clean technical race. A 12.45 finish is plausible, but I do not trust her to hold off Charlton over a full championship-style race.

Megan Simmonds is solid and experienced. She won Roma in 12.50, ran 12.52 in Xiamen, and took Commonwealth silver in 12.41w. She has been more consistent in the 12.4–12.6 range than Pia Skrzyszowska in August. Her 12.53 in Bellinzona just before Brussels suggests she is in good shape, and she should beat Skrzyszowska on recent head-to-head form.

Pia Skrzyszowska started the outdoor season strongly with 12.44 in Nancy and 12.46 in Paris, but she has faded late in the summer: 12.64 in Chorzów and 12.70 in Zürich. She is still a fine hurdler, but at this level, 12.61 would be a decent return to form. She does not appear to have the late-season sharpness to challenge the top six.

Yanla Ndjip-Nyemeck is the youngest and least proven in this company. She has improved into a 12.8-level hurdler, with a Belgian record-equalling season, but she finished seventh in the European final in 12.97 and ran 12.87 in Bellinzona. Brussels will be a step up in quality. A 12.82 would be a strong showing, but she is unlikely to crack the top seven against this elite field.
blurbs.400m Hurdles Men:
Predicted finish and marks — Men’s 400m Hurdles, Brussels Diamond League, 4 September 2026:

1. Alison dos Santos (BRA) – 46.21  
2. Matheus Lima (BRA) – 47.18  
3. Ezekiel Nathaniel (NGR) – 47.31  
4. Emil Agyekum (GER) – 47.53  
5. Trevor Bassitt (USA) – 47.69  
6. Caleb Dean (USA) – 47.84  
7. Abderrahman Samba (QAT) – 47.93  
8. Matic Ian Guček (SLO) – 48.06  

### Why this order

**Alison dos Santos is the obvious winner.** He arrives in Brussels as the world-record holder after running 45.80 in Zürich on 27 August. That came on top of a dominant 2026 Diamond League season: 46.72 in Xiamen, 47.11 in Stockholm, 46.89 in Oslo, 46.43 in Silesia, and 46.48 at the Brazilian Championships. Nobody else in this field has shown anything close to that level. Even with a possible post-record letdown, he should still win comfortably in the low-46s.

**Matheus Lima gets 2nd on consistency and late-season PB form.** His 47.26 at Silesia was the best non-Alison time among these athletes in the late season, and he followed it with 47.57 in Zürich. He also ran 47.37 in Stockholm and 47.64 in Ostrava. His August PB, mentioned in his bio, shows he is still improving. He lost to Nathaniel by 0.07 in Zürich, but he beat Nathaniel by 0.57 in Silesia, and his overall rhythm in the 47.2–47.6 range is more reliable.

**Ezekiel Nathaniel is right behind.** The 22-year-old Commonwealth champion has a 47.37 season’s best and ran a sharp 47.50 in Zürich. His flat 400m speed — 45.32 at the Prefontaine Classic — is a big weapon. But his season was a bit more uneven: 48.30 in London and 48.47 in the Commonwealth final show he can still drift off his best. In a fast Brussels race, he should be in the 47.2–47.4 range, but Lima’s extra consistency gives him the nod.

**Emil Agyekum is the best of the next group.** The German record holder and European silver medallist ran 47.45 in London and won Budapest in 47.58, beating several of the same men. However, his most recent results — 47.87 at the European final and 48.18 at ISTAF — suggest he is not quite sharp enough to challenge the 47.2-level men right now. He should still hold off the Americans for 4th.

**Trevor Bassitt has the talent to be higher.** His 47.37 at the USATF Lone Star Grand Prix and 47.59 at Budapest show he can mix with the top challengers. But his 48.71 at Silesia was a real warning sign. In a loaded final, I think he lands just outside the medals in the low-47.7s.

**Caleb Dean is the boom-or-bust pick.** He has real speed: 47.42 at USATF, 47.62 at Budapest, 47.75 in Xiamen. But he also ran 50.45 in London and DNF’d in Silesia. His ceiling is higher than Samba’s, and he beat Samba head-to-head in Budapest (47.62 to 48.31), so I place him 6th. Still, he is the hardest athlete to trust on a week-to-week basis.

**Abderrahman Samba is a faded force.** The 30-year-old former sub-47 star showed a glimpse with 47.77 in Zürich, but that was surrounded by 48.31, 48.60, and 48.64 performances in major races. He no longer looks capable of challenging the top Brazilians or the younger Europeans/Americans. I expect him to run around 47.9-48.0.

**Matic Ian Guček rounds out the field.** The Slovenian record holder ran well with 48.03 in the European semi and 47.80 in Zürich, but he also faded to 48.76 in the European final. He is clearly improving at 22, but he does not yet have the late-season firepower of the athletes above him. A high-47 or low-48 finish seems right.
blurbs.Triple Jump Women:
Predicted finish and marks — Brussels Diamond League, 4 September 2026:

1. **Leyanis Pérez Hernández (CUB)** — **15.01 m**  
2. **Saly Sarr (SEN)** — **14.95 m**  
3. **Davisleydi Velazco (CUB)** — **14.86 m**  
4. **Thea Lafond (DMA)** — **14.72 m**  
5. **Liadagmis Povea (CUB)** — **14.45 m**  
6. **Ackelia Smith (JAM)** — **14.18 m**  
7. **Saliyya Guisse (BEL)** — **13.98 m**

---

**Why this order?**

**Leyanis Pérez Hernández** is the clear favourite. She is the reigning World Champion both outdoors and indoors, and she has repeatedly produced when the pressure is highest: gold at the 2025 World Championships, gold at the 2025 and 2026 World Indoor Championships, and a 15.06 m victory in Monaco this summer. Her 2026 Diamond League form is excellent — 14.91 m in Silesia behind only Sarr, and she won the CAC Games with 14.78 m. In a final-style setting like Brussels, her championship pedigree and consistency should lift her just ahead of the chasing pack.

**Saly Sarr** is the biggest threat. She has been on a sharp upward curve: bronze at the 2026 World Indoor Championships, African Champion again in 2026, and a breakthrough 15.08 m win at Silesia in late August. She also jumped 14.99 m in Monaco, where she finished directly ahead of Lafond and Velazco. Sarr has now beaten Velazco in their most recent high-level meetings and pushed Leyanis harder than anyone in the late season. I expect her to challenge for the win but slightly miss against the more proven Leyanis.

**Davisleydi Velazco** had the strongest early-to-mid Diamond League season of anyone, with 15.13 m in Doha and 14.85 m in Oslo. She also jumped 14.84 m at Silesia and was the best of the rest behind Leyanis and Sarr. However, she finished behind both Sarr and Leyanis in Monaco and Silesia, and she has not matched Sarr’s late-season momentum. Still, she has been more consistent than Lafond and should be a clear third.

**Thea Lafond** remains a major name — Olympic champion and 2025 World Championship silver medallist — and her 15.25 m win in Zagreb is one of the best jumps of the year. But in deep Diamond League fields she has been less reliable: fifth in Oslo, fifth in Doha, third in Monaco, fourth in Silesia. Her 14.58 m in Silesia, directly behind Velazco, shows she is still competitive but slightly below the top three. Her experience and occasional ability to peak make her the best of the rest, but she has not shown the sustained 14.90+ ability needed to beat the younger trio.

**Liadagmis Povea** has had a solid but unspectacular season. She was second at the CAC Games with 14.71 m and fourth in Doha with 14.58 m, but she also slipped to sixth in Oslo and sixth at Silesia. She remains a consistent 14.4–14.7 m jumper on her day, but she has not produced the 14.80+ marks needed to challenge the top four. She should still beat the less-specialist jumpers behind her.

**Ackelia Smith** is talented but is splitting her focus between the long jump and triple jump. Her best triple jump this season was 14.50 m in Oslo, but she dropped to 14.04 m at the Commonwealth Games and 13.97 m at Silesia. Given her inconsistency in the triple jump and the strength of the field, a mid-to-low 14 m mark is realistic.

**Saliyya Guisse** deserves credit for her European Championship silver medal in 2026, but that final result included a wind-assisted 14.46 m; her legal season mark is closer to 14.07 m. At Silesia she finished well down with 13.45 m, and she simply does not have the same triple-jump firepower as the Cubans, Senegalese, or Lafond. Competing in Brussels as a home-region athlete may lift her slightly, but she should still finish last in this elite field.
blurbs.110m Hurdles Men:
Predicted finish and marks:

1. **Ja’Kobe Tharp (USA)** – **12.88**
2. **Jamal Britt (USA)** – **12.97**
3. **Trey Cunningham (USA)** – **13.02**
4. **Kendry L. Menéndez (CUB)** – **13.06**
5. **Cordell Tinch (USA)** – **13.12**
6. **Rachid Muratake (JPN)** – **13.23**
7. **Orlando Bennett (JAM)** – **13.28**
8. **Elie Bacari (BEL)** – **13.37**

This is a loaded Brussels Diamond League field, and the rankings should be driven by 2026 form, recent head-to-head results, and each athlete’s proven ceiling.

Ja’Kobe Tharp is the clear favorite. He is the current world-record holder at 20 years old, with his 12.75 from the 2026 NCAA Outdoor Championships standing as the defining performance of the season. His 2026 résumé is remarkable: he beat the majority of this exact field at Budapest with 12.85, won London in 12.89, and claimed Silesia in 13.05. The one blemish, an 8th-place 14.38 in Lausanne, looks like an anomaly rather than a trend, especially because he bounced back to win Silesia and Bellinzona. Tharp has the best speed, the best recent consistency, and the highest ceiling in the race.

Jamal Britt is the strongest challenger. His 12.86 win at the Prefontaine Classic was the best non-Tharp performance of the year, and he also ran 12.89 in Paris and 12.98 in Zagreb. He beat Tharp head-to-head at Prefontaine, which is more than anyone else in this field can say this season. However, Britt has also thrown in some puzzling races, including a 9th-place 26.75 in Rome and a 8th-place 13.85 in Doha. Those inconsistencies, plus narrow losses to Cunningham at London and Silesia, keep him just behind Tharp. Still, his peak speed and multiple sub-13 performances make him the most credible runner-up.

Trey Cunningham is the safest podium pick. The 2022 World Championship silver medalist has been remarkably consistent in 2026: 12.98 in Rome, 13.03 in Los Angeles, 13.07 in Paris, 13.08 in Silesia, and 13.12 in London. He does not have Britt’s flashy 12.86, but he also does not have Britt’s blow-up races. Cunningham beat Britt in both London and Silesia, and his narrow margin in those races suggests he can push for second on a good day. In this prediction, he lands a deserved third because Britt’s superior ceiling outweighs Cunningham’s steadier floor.

Kendry L. Menéndez is the wild card. At just 19, the Cuban has already shown he belongs with the world’s best, running 13.01 in London and 13.02 in Zagreb. In London, he finished ahead of Cunningham, Britt, and Tinch, which is a massive statement for a teenager. His 13.09 in Budapest and 13.14 in Ostrava add further proof that he is a genuine top-four threat. The concern is his DNF in Silesia and his slight drop to 13.20 in Lausanne. That inconsistency is understandable at 19, but it prevents me from putting him on the podium ahead of more seasoned Americans. Still, he is the most dangerous athlete outside the top three.

Cordell Tinch is the reigning world champion and the 2026 US champion, but he has not looked like the same dominant force this summer. His 13.00 win at the US Championships showed he can still deliver under pressure, and he ran 13.06 in Budapest, 13.07 at Prefontaine, and 13.10 in Shaoxing. However, his late-season form has slipped: 13.17 in both Zagreb and London, 13.22 in Silesia, and 13.25 in Brescia. Tinch also competed in the long jump at the US Championships, placing third, which suggests divided focus. Against this world-class field, that leaves him a step behind the top four.

Rachid Muratake has the credentials and early-season speed to be higher, but his 2026 arc has flattened. The Japanese record-holder ran an excellent 13.05 in Osaka and backed it up with 13.13 in Xiamen, but he faded to 13.21 in Paris and 13.41 in Silesia. He also finished behind Bennett at Silesia and behind most of the American contingent whenever they shared the track. Muratake’s ceiling is clearly top-five, but his recent trend makes sixth the safer projection.

Orlando Bennett is a tough one to place. He was the World Championship silver medalist in 2025 and has genuine sub-13 talent. But in 2026 he has been stuck in the 13.15–13.38 range, with his best showing a 13.15 at Prefontaine. He has been consistently competitive but rarely threatening to beat the top Americans this season. His 13.20 at Shaoxing and 13.20 at Xiamen are solid, yet he was behind Muratake in both of those races. That gives Muratake the edge, and leaves Bennett down in seventh.

Elie Bacari rounds out the field. The Belgian has had a solid season, highlighted by a 13.25 national title and a 13.31 fourth-place finish in Bellinzona. He is a proven European-level hurdler and made the 2025 World Championships, but he simply does not have the same firepower as the international medalists in this lineup. His 13.53 in Lausanne and 13.42 in Madrid show he is a step below the sub-13.10 group. A 13.37 in Brussels would be a respectable, honest performance against an elite field, but it should leave him last.
blurbs.Javelin Throw Women:
**Predicted results — Women’s Javelin Throw, Brussels Diamond League, 4 September 2026**

1. **Ziyi Yan (CHN)** — 69.32 m  
2. **Haruka Kitaguchi (JPN)** — 64.84 m  
3. **Flor Denis Ruiz Hurtado (COL)** — 64.21 m  
4. **Adriana Vilagoš (SRB)** — 62.37 m  
5. **Sigrid Borge (NOR)** — 60.11 m  
6. **Anete Sietiņa (LAT)** — 59.82 m  

### Why this order?

**Ziyi Yan** is the clear favourite. At 17, she has already produced the best throw in the world this season by a wide margin: 71.74 m at Xiamen, a world U20 record and Asian record and the second-best mark in history. Even her “quieter” Diamond League wins this season — 67.11 m in Oslo, 67.44 m in Paris, 68.75 m in Monaco — are better than anything the rest of this field has produced in 2026. She is the most consistent, the most powerful, and the most obvious winner. I expect her to win comfortably, though perhaps not matching her 71.74 m again in a final setting.

**Haruka Kitaguchi** gets second because of her late-season peak. The reigning Olympic champion was poor in the middle of the season: 60.08 m in Xiamen and only 56.24 m in Monaco. But she turned things around dramatically with a 64.90 m win in Lausanne on 21 August, beating both Ruiz Hurtado and Vilagoš head-to-head. That result, plus her proven championship pedigree, gives her the edge for second.

**Flor Denis Ruiz Hurtado** is the biggest threat to Kitaguchi. Her 67.34 m at the CAC Games in early August is outstanding and shows she can still produce a huge throw at 34. But she also had a no-mark in Monaco and a string of 60–61 m Diamond League results before that. She followed her 67.34 m with 64.29 m in Lausanne — excellent, but behind Kitaguchi. I place her third: dangerous, but slightly less reliable than Kitaguchi at the sharp end.

**Adriana Vilagoš** is the clear fourth. She has a big personal ceiling from 2025 — including 67.22 m — but her 2026 season has mostly been in the 59–63 m range. She did win European bronze with 60.93 m and then threw 62.28 m in Lausanne, which is solid. Still, she has not shown the same firepower as Kitaguchi or Ruiz Hurtado this season, and she was behind both in Lausanne. She should be comfortably ahead of the bottom two, though.

**Sigrid Borge** takes fifth, despite a disappointing late season. Her 65.00 m at Xiamen in May was a major standout, and she also threw 61.92 m in Oslo. But after that she faded badly: 56.92 m in Paris, 56.57 m in Monaco, and 54.51 m at the Norwegian Championships. She recovered a bit with 59.98 m in the European final, which is why I still have her ahead of Sietiņa. Her ceiling is higher than anything Sietiņa has shown in 2026, even if she has been inconsistent.

**Anete Sietiņa** is sixth. She has the best championship credential in this group after Kitaguchi — a silver medal at the 2025 World Championships with 64.64 m. But her 2026 form has not matched that level at all. Her best this season is only 60.05 m, she had a no-mark in Paris, and she failed to make the European final after throwing 56.24 m in qualifying. She did beat Borge narrowly at Lausanne, 58.73 m to 58.54 m, but over the full season Borge has shown a higher peak and a better recent championship performance. I give Borge the nod for fifth, with Sietiņa sixth.
blurbs.Shot Put Men:
Predicted finish – Men’s Shot Put, Brussels Diamond League, 4 September 2026:

1. Jordan Geist (USA) – 22.63 m  
2. Rajindra Campbell (JAM) – 22.47 m  
3. Leonardo Fabbri (ITA) – 22.35 m  
4. Joe Kovacs (USA) – 21.82 m  
5. Tom Walsh (NZL) – 21.54 m  
6. Roger Steen (USA) – 21.30 m  

---

**Reasoning:**

This is a deep field, but the most compelling form lines point to a Jordan Geist victory. At 27, Geist is in the prime stretch of his career and has been the most consistent shot putter in the world through the late 2026 season. He arrives in Brussels off a Diamond League win in Zürich with 22.53 m, where he beat Campbell, Fabbri, Kovacs, Steen, and Walsh in the same kind of head-to-head field he’ll see again. Geist also won the US outdoor title with 22.32 m, threw 22.44 m in Memphis, and was consistently above 21.9 m in his final pre-Brussels series. His floor is remarkably high — even his “off” Diamond League meetings in Xiamen and Rabat were 21.52 m and 21.56 m. With the Diamond League final on the line, Geist should be trusted to produce a slight season’s best around 22.6 m.

**Rajindra Campbell** is the biggest threat. The 29-year-old Jamaican Olympic bronze medallist and national record holder has serious late-season momentum, including a 22.59 m victory in Brescia on 30 August and a 22.22 m runner-up effort in Zürich. He has also won Xiamen with 22.34 m and Zagreb with 22.44 m. But Campbell’s pattern is more volatile than Geist’s: he threw only 21.04 m in Rabat, 21.39 m in Rome, and 21.61 m in Silesia. He can absolutely win if he catches one, but Geist has been better at producing big throws when the stakes are highest. Campbell should finish just behind, around 22.47 m.

**Leonardo Fabbri** is still the most credentialed European in the field. At 28, the two-time European champion and 2026 European gold medallist has had a brilliant season. His 22.74 m victory at the Prefontaine Classic in July is the best outdoor mark any of these six athletes has managed in 2026. He has also been extremely reliable: Italian champion with 22.43 m, European champion with 22.31 m, and a consistent run of 22.0–22.2 m late in the season. However, he was third in Zürich behind Geist and Campbell, and second behind Campbell in Brescia. In a final where the top two are peaking, Fabbri might need a perfect series to jump ahead. He should still medal with 22.35 m.

**Joe Kovacs** is the veteran wildcard. At 36, he remains one of the greatest shot putters ever — second on the all-time list with 23.23 m, with multiple world titles and Olympic silvers. But the 2026 season shows his consistency has slipped. He did win Rabat with a superb 22.58 m, but he was eighth at the Prefontaine Classic, fourth at the US Championships, fourth in Zürich, and fifth in Brescia. He still has the power to beat nearly anyone on a given day, but at this age and with this recent form, it is hard to place him above three younger throwers who are throwing 22.2 m or better more regularly. Expect a solid but not spectacular 21.82 m and fourth.

**Tom Walsh** should finish fifth. The 33-year-old New Zealander is a former world champion, Olympic bronze medallist, and the Oceanian record holder with 22.90 m. He also won the 2026 World Indoor title with 21.82 m and took Commonwealth silver in Glasgow. But his outdoor form in 2026 has been stuck in the 21.1–21.7 m range. He was seventh at Prefontaine, eighth in Silesia, and sixth in Zürich. Walsh is competitive but no longer has the pop to challenge the 22.5 m-level throwers outdoors. A 21.54 m mark would be a fair representation of his current level.

**Roger Steen** rounds out the field. The 33-year-old American is a two-time World Indoor medallist and the reigning US indoor champion, but his late 2026 outdoor campaign has faded badly. After a strong indoor season and a 21.93 m Drake Relays win, he had no-mark and 19.81 m efforts at the Ed Murphey Classic, then only 21.06 m at US Championships, 21.46 m in Silesia, and 21.53 m in Zürich. In a field like this, Steen is likely to be chasing the others from the first round. Sixth place with 21.30 m seems the most probable outcome.

Ultimately, this final should come down to Geist and Campbell. Geist gets the edge because he has been sharper in head-to-head competition, more stable across the entire season, and is peaking at exactly the right time for the Diamond League final.
blurbs.Triple Jump Men:
**Predicted finish – Brussels Diamond League, 4 September 2026:**

1. **Andy Díaz Hernández (ITA)** – **18.03 m**  
2. **Pedro Pichardo (POR)** – **17.86 m**  
3. **Yasser Mohammed Triki (ALG)** – **17.72 m**  
4. **Jordan Scott (JAM)** – **17.49 m**  
5. **Lázaro Martínez (CUB)** – **17.21 m**  
6. **Almir dos Santos (BRA)** – **16.98 m**

---

**Why this order?**

This is a very strong field, but the form lines going into Brussels are uneven. Some athletes are peaking, some are fading, and some have been brilliant in lower-level meetings but unable to transfer that to the Diamond League circuit. My prediction is based on 2026 results, head-to-head meetings, and the trajectory of each athlete since the major championships.

**1. Andy Díaz Hernández** – After a wobble at Lausanne, Andy remains the man to beat. His European Championships victory in August was the defining outdoor performance of the year: **18.15 m (+1.7)** is the biggest legal mark on the board for this entire group. He also won the World Indoor title in March with 17.47 m, won in Roma with 17.59 m, repeated 17.59 m in Oslo, and produced 17.87 m to win the Italian title. The only real blemish was a modest 17.20 m at Lausanne, where he finished third behind Pichardo and Triki. That looks like a post-Euro flat spot. At 30 and with his recent championship pedigree, he is the most likely jumper in a loaded final to produce something close to 18 metres. I expect him to bounce back with an 18.03 m winner.

**2. Pedro Pichardo** – The reigning world champion and 2020 Olympic gold medallist is the biggest threat. Pichardo has been remarkably solid in 2026: 17.71 m in Doha, 17.76 m at the European Championships in Birmingham, and a 17.44 m win at Lausanne into a **-1.0 m/s** headwind, which is excellent raw jumping. He also beat Díaz head-to-head in Lausanne, and he has the pedigree to win any final. However, he has not matched Andy’s ceiling this season — Andy beat him convincingly at the European final, 18.15 m to 17.76 m. Pichardo is the safer pick for consistency, but I think Andy still has the higher peak, and Brussels should be a peak performance. Pichardo lands in the low 17.80s, close but second.

**3. Yasser Mohammed Triki** – Triki has been the quietest consistent performer in the world this summer. He has produced a string of high-quality marks: **17.67 m** in Doha, **17.58 m** in Linz, **17.47 m** legal in Madrid, **17.35 m** indoors in Liévin, and a World Indoor bronze. At Lausanne he again finished second, with a wind-assisted 17.43 m, and his legal 17.21 m was still competitive with Andy’s 17.20 m. Triki does not yet have the 18-metre threat of Díaz or Pichardo, but he very rarely has a bad competition. That reliability should lift him to third ahead of Jordan Scott, especially given Scott’s late-season inconsistency.

**4. Jordan Scott** – Scott’s best is right there with the top three. His **17.69 m** in Doha and **17.66 m** in Caguas are serious marks, and he has a World Indoor silver medal and Commonwealth gold in 2026. But his season has been jagged: in Oslo his 17.66 m was wind-assisted and his legal mark was only 16.96 m; he no-marked at Memphis in July; and at Lausanne he could only manage **16.86 m**, finishing behind Triki, Díaz, and Pichardo. Scott has the talent to beat Triki on a good day, but Belgium is late in the season and his form has trended downward since Doha. I have him fourth, still capable of 17.49 m, but not quite consistent enough to hold off Triki.

**5. Lázaro Martínez** – Martínez has a World Championship bronze medal from 2025 and a solid 17.33 m in Oslo in 2026, so the talent is real. But his inconsistency is glaring. He had a disastrous no-contest indoors at the 2025 World Indoor Championships, managed only 15.42 m in Doha in June, and was a subdued sixth at Lausanne with 16.69 m. He did win the CAC Games, but the level there was not comparable to Brussels. In a field this strong, he is more likely to be fighting for fifth/sixth than for the podium. I predict a 17.21 m rebound, but it will not be enough to crack the top four.

**6. Almir dos Santos** – Almir is the oldest of the group at 32 and perhaps the hardest to read. He won the Pan American title with 17.24 m and the Brazilian title with 17.07 m, so he can still jump well in the right setting. But his Diamond League results in 2026 have been poor: 16.22 m in Roma, 15.85 m at Oslo, and 16.20 m at Lausanne. Against this particular field, those marks put him firmly in last. The step up in competition seems to expose technical issues or an inability to get into rhythm in high-pressure DL finals. He could still produce something respectable, but 16.98 m feels like a fair projection, and I don’t see him overtaking any of the five ahead of him.
blurbs.Long Jump Women:
Predicted finish and marks – Brussels Diamond League Women’s Long Jump, 4 Sep 2026:

1. Larissa Iapichino (ITA) – 7.05 m  
2. Alyssa Jones (USA) – 7.01 m  
3. Agate de Sousa (POR) – 6.98 m  
4. Hilary Kpatcha (FRA) – 6.94 m  
5. Monae’ Nichols (USA) – 6.90 m  
6. Claire Bryant (USA) – 6.76 m  
7. Noor Vidts (BEL) – 6.25 m  

---

**Why this order:**

**Larissa Iapichino** gets the nod for the win because she has the best combination of peak mark and big-championship form in 2026. Her 7.12 m legal jump at the Prefontaine Classic was the standout performance of the year among these athletes, and she beat Alyssa Jones head-to-head there. She then delivered when it mattered most, winning the European title in Birmingham with a wind-assisted 7.00 m in the final after producing 6.94 m in qualifying. Although her legal final in Birmingham was modest at 6.80 m, she repeatedly finds a way to win when the pressure is high, and her pedigree as a European champion and World Indoor silver medallist gives her the edge.

**Alyssa Jones** is the clear second favourite. Her 2026 résumé is outstanding: she jumped 7.09 m legal at the NCAA West First Rounds, backed it up with 7.06 m to win the NCAA title, then won the US title with 6.96 m and took the Silesia Diamond League meeting with 6.98 m. She was consistently in the 6.90–7.00 m range through the summer. She lost to Larissa at Prefontaine, but she has been the most consistent challenger and, at only 21, has the strongest upward trajectory. I expect her to push Iapichino closest, but not quite to overtake her.

**Agate de Sousa** is third because she has timed her peak well. She won the World Indoor title in March, then produced the best legal European mark of the late outdoor season with 7.00 m in qualifying at the European Championships. She followed that with 6.98 m at Silesia, narrowly losing to Alyssa Jones on countback. Her consistency through August — 6.89 m legal in the European final, 6.98 m in Silesia — makes her more reliable than Hilary Kpatcha at this stage, even though Kpatcha out-placed her in Birmingham.

**Hilary Kpatcha** is fourth. She had a slow start to the outdoor season, with several jumps in the 6.5–6.7 m range, but she peaked sharply at the right time: 6.98 m legal to win the French title, then a bronze medal at the European Championships with 6.98 m wind-assisted and 6.85 m legal in the final. That late surge is dangerous, but she was less consistent than Agate de Sousa across the full summer and did not follow up Birmingham with another high-level Diamond League result. I still see her as a major threat for the podium, but not quite ahead of de Sousa.

**Monae’ Nichols** is fifth. She has been very solid all year: 6.89 m to win Shaoxing, 6.88 m in Turku, 6.92 m for second at US Championships, and 6.95 m at Silesia. However, she lacks a legal 7-metre jump in 2026 — her 7.05 m at Prefontaine was wind-assisted — and she has lost directly to Alyssa Jones at both the US Championships and Silesia. She also finished behind Agate de Sousa in Silesia. Her consistency is excellent, but her ceiling appears slightly lower than the top four on this occasion.

**Claire Bryant** is sixth. She showed what she is capable of with a strong 6.94 m runner-up finish at the London Diamond League, where she beat Larissa Iapichino, Hilary Kpatcha and Agate de Sousa. But that performance stands apart from an otherwise inconsistent 2026: 6.70 m in Shaoxing, 6.69 m in Stockholm, 6.58 m at Prefontaine, and a poor 6.53 m at Silesia. She is a former World Indoor champion, so she cannot be discounted completely, but her recent form points to a mid-pack finish rather than a podium challenge.

**Noor Vidts** is last. She is a world-class heptathlete, but her long jump marks in 2026 — around 6.21–6.22 m in combined events — are simply not at the level of the dedicated long jumpers in this field. She may use the competition as valuable Diamond League experience, but against this specific group she is unlikely to challenge for a top-six place.
blurbs.1500m Women:
Predicted finish — Women’s 1500m, Brussels Diamond League, 4 September 2026:

1. Georgia Hunter Bell (GBR) — 3:54.79  
2. Tsige Duguma (ETH) — 3:54.95  
3. Jessica Hull (AUS) — 3:55.10  
4. Dorcus Ewoi (KEN) — 3:55.32  
5. Klaudia Kazimierska (POL) — 3:55.49  
6. Abbey Caldwell (AUS) — 3:55.68  
7. Emily MacKay (USA) — 3:55.93  
8. Agathe Guillemot (FRA) — 3:56.06  
9. Birke Haylom (ETH) — 3:56.72  
10. Nikki Hiltz (USA) — 3:59.55  
11. Lorea Ibarzabal (ESP) — 4:04.28  
12. Mariska Parewyck (BEL) — 4:07.85  

I’m treating this as a genuine Diamond League final, so the race should be quick rather than a slow, tactical championship grind. That favours the women who have both 1500m strength and 800m speed, and who have shown they can produce that level in 2026.

Georgia Hunter Bell gets the edge for win No. 1. She is the reigning World Indoor and European 1500m champion and also won the Commonwealth 800m title in 2026. Her Paris Diamond League win in 3:55.63 came directly against Jessica Hull, Abbey Caldwell and Agathe Guillemot, and her 1:54.90 800m from the 2025 World Championships gives her a devastating final kick. Her 1:55.03 run in Zürich five days before Brussels shows she is still sharp.

Tsige Duguma is the obvious challenger. She won the Silesia Diamond League 1500m in a 2026 world-class 3:55.06, beating Hull, Ewoi, Kazimierska, MacKay and Guillemot. Duguma also has a 1:56.64 800m this season, so she has real speed. But Hunter Bell has beaten more of this specific field in 2026 and has a stronger championship record over 1500m specifically, so Duguma takes second.

Jessica Hull is third. She was second at Silesia in 3:55.20, has Olympic and World Championship medals over 1500m, and has been consistently within a few tenths of the very best in 2026. She also ran a strong 800m at the World Championships last year and was competitive over 5000m at the Commonwealth Games, but in this fast 1500m field she may lack just a little of the finishing speed of Hunter Bell and Duguma.

Dorcus Ewoi is fourth. She was the 2025 World Championship silver medallist over 1500m, and her Silesia 3:55.58 was excellent. She has been extremely reliable this season — placing well in Shaoxing, Xiamen and Silesia — but she hasn’t quite shown the same outright win equity as the top three in 2026.

Klaudia Kazimierska takes fifth. Her Silesia 3:55.59 was just 0.01 behind Ewoi, and she was second in Rome behind Hunter Bell in 3:59.24. She also won European 1500m silver in 2026 and has a strong 800m (1:58.11) that helps her finish hard. She is very close to Ewoi, but Ewoi’s greater consistency in the strongest 2026 races gives her the nod.

Abbey Caldwell is sixth. She won the Commonwealth Games mile in 2026 and won the Xiamen Diamond League 1500m in 3:57.26. She also ran 3:56.12 at Shaoxing and finished ahead of Hull there. However, she was well behind Hunter Bell and Guillemot in Paris, and behind Kazimierska in Rome, which drops her just below the podium-chasing group.

Emily MacKay and Agathe Guillemot are nearly inseparable. MacKay was fifth in Silesia in 3:56.24, Guillemot sixth in 3:56.34. MacKay has been the more consistent across the 2026 Diamond League circuit and also won the US 5000m title, while Guillemot is the French record holder and ran 3:56.24 in Paris. MacKay’s head-to-head edge at Silesia gives her seventh.

Birke Haylom is the hardest to place. She won Shaoxing in 3:55.56, the fastest 1500m of her 2026 season, and beat Duguma and Caldwell that day. But she was only eighth at Silesia in 3:56.76 and struggled in the Monaco 3000m in July. She is clearly talented, but the inconsistency and the gap between her best and her recent form pushes her down to ninth.

Nikki Hiltz is tenth. They are the US 1500m champion and won the Prefontaine mile, but their 2026 outdoor 1500m best is only 3:59.26, and they were 10th at Silesia in 4:00.52. In a fast, deep field like this, that isn’t quite enough to contend for the top group.

Lorea Ibarzabal is an 800m specialist and has not shown 1500m form at this level in 2026, including a DNF in Silesia. Mariska Parewyck, at 37, remains competitive domestically but her recent 1500m mark of 4:09.67 is well below the standard of this Diamond League field. So the final two spots go to Ibarzabal and Parewyck, in that order.
blurbs.800m Women:
Predicted finish — Brussels Diamond League, Women’s 800m, 4 September 2026:

1. Audrey Werro (SUI) — 1:53.55  
2. Femke Broeders-Bol (NED) — 1:54.32  
3. Saida Tsehaye (ETH) — 1:56.48  
4. Sarah Billings (AUS) — 1:57.62  
5. Addison Wiley (USA) — 1:57.95  
6. Veronica Vancardo (SUI) — 1:58.36  
7. Prudence Sekgodiso (RSA) — 1:58.76  
8. Oratile Nowe (BOT) — 2:00.18  
9. Rachel Klopfenstein (MRI) — 2:00.92  
10. Camille Laus (BEL) — 2:01.45  

---

This is a deep, end-of-season Diamond League 800m, and the hierarchy is fairly clear at the top. **Audrey Werro** is the overwhelming favourite. At just 21, she arrives as the reigning European champion and has been the dominant force all summer: Euro gold in 1:54.81, DL wins in Paris in 1:53.80, Stockholm in 1:53.98, Ostrava in 1:54.45, and that stunning 1:53.70 in Zürich — the third-fastest 800m in history. Nobody in this field can match her raw strength or her ability to run a genuine 1:53-1:54 pace. I expect another fast, controlled front-run from Werro, possibly a small PB improvement.

**Femke Broeders-Bol** is a clear second. The former 400m hurdles world champion has adapted brilliantly to the 800m in 2026. She was right behind Werro in Lausanne (1:55.41) and Zürich (1:54.71), and she took European bronze in 1:55.54. Her background gives her exceptional speed and race poise, but Werro has simply been better every time they’ve met this season. Bol’s 1:54.71 is far ahead of anyone else in this field, so second place looks locked.

The most interesting battle is for third. I’m giving it to 17-year-old **Saida Tsehaye**. She was third in Lausanne in 1:56.92, ahead of Vancardo, Wiley, Sekgodiso and Nowe, and fourth in Zürich in 1:57.33 behind Werro, Bol and likely another non-field athlete. She also set the Ethiopian U20 record this season. Her youth is remarkable, but her 2026 trajectory is real and rapid. She has the best recent credentials of anyone outside the Werro/Bol top two.

For fourth, I’m taking **Sarah Billings**. Her best 800m this year was 1:57.01 in Paris, where she finished just behind Sekgodiso but ahead of Nowe. She also has great range, shown by her 1500m best of 3:56.73 and Commonwealth bronze over 800m. Billings was a bit flat in Zürich (1:59.67) after a quick turnaround from a strong 1500m, but with a week’s recovery she should be sharper. She has the speed and endurance to lead the chase pack behind Tsehaye.

**Addison Wiley** is next. She has been solid without being spectacular at 800m in 2026, running 1:57.98 in Doha and 1:57.70 in Eugene. She is the American record holder at 1000m and won bronze at the World Indoor 800m in Toruń, so she has proven big-race credentials. Her 3:58.96 1500m in Bellinzona at the end of August shows she is still in excellent shape. Her loss to Vancardo at Lausanne is a concern, but her overall ceiling and recent fitness tip her to edge out the more consistent Vancardo in Brussels.

**Veronica Vancardo** is harder to overlook. She has been remarkably consistent: 1:58.49 in Zürich, 1:58.68 in Lausanne, and sub-1:59 in most major races. She beat Wiley head-to-head in Lausanne and beat Billings in Zürich. But her peak speed is slightly lower than Billings or Wiley, and in a fast Diamond League race, that matters. I see her settling into sixth, just outside the 1:58 barrier.

**Prudence Sekgodiso** is the biggest puzzle. She was the 2025 World Indoor champion and ran 1:56.83 in Paris this year, which would put her right in the top four if that version shows up. But her season has fallen apart since: she was poor at the Commonwealth Games, failed to make the final after a 2:01.57 semifinal, and then ran 1:59.58 in Lausanne. Her talent is clear, but her recent form is too unreliable to rank above Vancardo, Wiley or Billings. I’m putting her seventh, though she could easily be fourth if she recaptures her Paris form.

**Oratile Nowe** has a decent season’s best of 1:57.32 from Rabat, but her late-season results have been troubling: 2:00.89 in Lausanne, 2:01.29 in the Commonwealth final and 2:01.08 in Berlin. She is a nationally record-breaking athlete and has run close to the leaders this year, but she appears to be running out of steam. I expect her to struggle to stay with the 1:58 group.

**Rachel Klopfenstein** set the Mauritian record of 1:58.73 in Ostrava, but her 2026 season has also been defined by DNFs and inconsistency. She was eighth in the Commonwealth final in 2:03.81 and did not finish in Bellinzona at the end of August. If she holds together, she could challenge for seventh or eighth, but I can’t trust her to be sharp in a tough DL race. I have her ninth.

**Camille Laus** is a talented Belgian sprinter/relay athlete, but her 800m still reads like a secondary event. She ran 1:59.43 in a European Championship heat, but then finished only seventh in that heat and didn’t progress. Her Belgian Championships 800m final was 2:06.31, and her focus remains largely on the 4x400m relay. In this field, she lacks the sustained 800m credentials of the others, so I place her last.

Ultimately, Werro and Bol separate themselves early, Tsehaye leads the chasing pack, and the middle depends on who is sharpest late in a long season. Brussels should produce a fast, honest race — and Werro should take another Diamond League scalp in what has already been a historic season.
blurbs.3000m Steeplechase Men:
**Predicted finish – Men’s 3000m Steeplechase, Brussels Diamond League, 4 September 2026:**

1. **Soufiane el Bakkali (MAR)** – 7:57.79  
2. **Gemechu Godana (ETH)** – 8:00.12  
3. **Simon Koech (KEN)** – 8:01.08  
4. **Salah Eddine ben Yazide (MAR)** – 8:03.36  
5. **Edmund Serem (KEN)** – 8:04.05  
6. **Ruben Querinjean (LUX)** – 8:05.58  
7. **Samuel Firewu (ETH)** – 8:06.43  
8. **Karl Bebendorf (GER)** – 8:08.77  
9. **Ryuji Miura (JPN)** – 8:09.42  
10. **Matthew Wilkinson (USA)** – 8:10.89  
11. **Daniel Arce (ESP)** – 8:11.95  
12. **Rémi Schyns (BEL)** – 8:25.46  
13. **Wilberforce Chemiat Kones (KEN)** – DNF  

---

**Why this order?**

El Bakkali remains the man to beat. His 7:57.25 in Rabat in May was the fastest steeplechase of the season by anyone in this field, and his Diamond League wins in Stockholm and Doha confirm consistency. He did lose to Godana at Silesia in August, but in a high-stakes Brussels final I still trust the two-time Olympic champion and former world champion to respond. Godana’s 8:02.74 win at Silesia, plus his African Championships title, make him the clear second favourite; at 20 he is the most rapidly improving athlete in the race.

Simon Koech gets third because his Rabat 7:59.44 and Monaco 8:03.35 are elite-level marks. He has also beaten Edmund Serem several times, notably in Rabat and Monaco. However, his Stockholm 8:13.40 and Commonwealth Games loss to Serem show he can be vulnerable when the race is more tactical. In an honest, fast Brussels race, his Rabat/Monaco form should resurface.

The 4th-7th group is where the toughest calls sit. Salah Eddine ben Yazide gets 4th because of his excellent Silesia run: 8:05.08 in third, directly ahead of Querinjean and clearly ahead of Serem. He also ran 8:09.88 to win Ostrava, and has been far more consistent through August than Serem. Edmund Serem has the higher ceiling — he ran 8:01.61 in Rabat and won Commonwealth gold — but his post-Rabat form has hovered around 8:08-8:18, and he lost ground to ben Yazide at Silesia. I still place him 5th because of that ceiling and his junior-level pedigree.

Ruben Querinjean is the wildcard. His 8:05.36 at Silesia was a genuine breakthrough, and he has already won a Diamond League meeting in Brussels in 2025. That matters. He gets 6th, just ahead of Samuel Firewu, because Querinjean beat Firewu head-to-head at Silesia. Firewu remains a very strong runner — 4th at the 2025 World Championships and 8:06.65 at Silesia — but he has not quite shown the finishing kick of the men directly above him.

Karl Bebendorf is the best of the next group. His Paris win in 8:05.55 was a standout result, and he also finished ahead of Miura, Wilkinson and Arce at Silesia. Ryuji Miura has the strongest raw talent of the remaining runners — his 8:10.30 in Monaco and Japanese record pedigree show that — but his DNF in Hiroshima and 8:23.97 in Stockholm are red flags. Wilkinson is steady rather than spectacular; Arce is still capable of 8:11 but at 33 is unlikely to outrun the younger, sharper steeplechasers.

Rémi Schyns is outclassed at this level based on his European Championships 8:29.25 and lack of Diamond League pedigree. And Wilberforce Chemiat Kones, once a useful Kenyan steeplechaser, has DNFed so often in 2026 — including in Brussels, Paris, Monaco, Stockholm and Ostrava — that I cannot confidently give him a finishing time. He is predicted to drop out.
blurbs.Pole Vault Women:
Predicted finish / clearances (metres) — Brussels Diamond League, 4 September 2026:

1. Hana Moll (USA) — 4.90  
2. Angelica Moser (SUI) — 4.85  
3. Katie Moon (USA) — 4.80  
4. Imogen Ayris (NZL) — 4.75  
5. Tina Šutej (SLO) — 4.70  
6. Emily Grove (USA) — 4.65  
7. Elien Vekemans (BEL) — 4.55  

Bar progression used: 4.40, 4.45, 4.50, 4.55, 4.60, 4.65, 4.70, 4.75, 4.80, 4.85, 4.90 — all raises are 5 cm. Once Hana Moll is the only athlete left at 4.90, I expect her to try 4.95/5.00 for a personal-best attempt, but she misses, leaving the winning mark at 4.90.

Why this order:

Hana Moll is the clear form athlete. At only 20, she already has a 2022 World U20 title and the 2025 NCAA outdoor title, and her late-2026 results are the best in this field: she won Lausanne on 21 August with 4.84 and then beat this exact group in Zurich on 26 August with 4.90. That 4.90 is the highest clearance by anyone in the field this season, and she did it over Angelica Moser and Katie Moon head-to-head. There is no reason to pick against her in Brussels.

Angelica Moser should take second. The 28-year-old Swiss is a two-time European indoor and outdoor champion, and she won the 2026 European title in Birmingham with 4.80. She also jumped 4.85 in Zurich, only 5 cm behind Moll. Moser has been more consistent than Katie Moon in 2026, with multiple 4.80-level clearances, and she looks like the only athlete capable of pushing Moll on the day.

Katie Moon, now 34, remains a massive championship name: 2020 Olympic gold medallist, 2024 Olympic silver medallist, and three-time world champion, including 2025. But her 2026 outdoor form has been solid rather than spectacular. She won Prefontaine at 4.80, but then had 4.62 in Monaco and 4.64 in Lausanne before a 4.75 third place in Zurich behind Moll and Moser. She should bounce back slightly to 4.80, but the top two have more current speed and clearance margin.

Imogen Ayris gets fourth. The 25-year-old New Zealander has had a strong 2026: bronze at the World Indoor Championships in March with 4.70, a 4.81 win in Turku, a 4.75 win in Ostrava, and Commonwealth bronze. She was only sixth in Zurich at 4.75, and she has not shown a 4.85-level ceiling in recent weeks. Still, she has been more reliable at 4.70-4.75 than the veterans below her, so I place her ahead of Šutej.

Tina Šutej is the hardest to rank because her highs are high and her lows are low. The 37-year-old is a World Championships bronze medallist and a multiple World Indoor/European Indoor medallist, and she was second at the 2026 World Indoor Championships with 4.80. But her outdoor 2026 season has been uneven: 4.45 in Rabat, a 4.40 qualifying exit at the European Championships, and 4.50 in Lausanne. She did jump 4.75 in Zurich, but she is more likely than Ayris to have one off round. I give her fifth at 4.70.

Emily Grove is a consistent 4.60-4.70 vaulter in 2026 — she was USA runner-up and jumped 4.70 at Prefontaine and the US Championships — but she lacks the 4.80-4.90 ceiling. Her 4.65 in Zurich, behind Moll, Moser, Moon, Ayris, and Šutej, confirms she is a step below the top five. Sixth at 4.65.

Elien Vekemans, the Belgian record-holder, will have home support in Brussels. She was a very good fourth at the 2026 European Championships with 4.60, but her overall 2026 results are still below the rest of this field. She has not been a regular 4.70-4.75 jumper, and against a Diamond League final field she is likely the first to leave the competition. Seventh at 4.55.
blurbs.Javelin Throw Men:
**Predicted finish – Men’s Javelin Throw, Brussels Diamond League, 4 September 2026**

1. **Rumesh Tharanga Pathirage (SRI)** – **90.74 m**  
2. **Anderson Peters (GRN)** – **87.42 m**  
3. **Dawid Wegner (POL)** – **84.86 m**  
4. **Keshorn Walcott (TTO)** – **83.61 m**  
5. **Julius Yego (KEN)** – **81.88 m**  
6. **Curtis Thompson (USA)** – **80.35 m**  
7. **Timothy Herman (BEL)** – **76.22 m**

---

**Reasoning**

**Rumesh Tharanga Pathirage** is the clear favorite. He has been the most dominant javelin thrower in the world during 2026, with a remarkable run of high-level results: **92.62 m in Rome**, **92.07 m in Zürich**, **89.75 m to win the Commonwealth Games**, and Diamond League wins in Rome, Doha, Lausanne, and Zürich. He has beaten nearly every athlete in this field head-to-head multiple times, including a 5-meter margin over Anderson Peters in Zürich. Even though Peters edged him by 0.11 m in Rabat in May, Pathirage has since overtaken him decisively. At just 22, he is peaking at the right time and should close the Diamond League season with another victory.

**Anderson Peters** remains the strongest challenger. He is not throwing at his 2019/2022 world-champion level, but he is very consistent in the mid-to-high 86–87 m range in August, with **86.93 m in Zürich** and **86.69 m in Lausanne**. He also won the CAC Games and took second in Rome, Doha, and Zürich. Peters is a proven big-meet competitor, but he has not shown the ability to threaten 90 m in 2026. Against Pathirage, he has consistently finished behind since June. A **87.42 m** effort should be enough for second.
