**Dawid Wegner** gets the edge for third. His season has been inconsistent, but he has clearly improved in the late summer. He finished fourth at the European Championships with **82.96 m**, then threw **85.16 m** in Zürich to finish third, ahead of both Walcott and Yego. That Zürich result is the strongest recent form of anyone outside the top two. Wegner is only 25 and seems to be peaking at the end of the season. His main weakness is occasional poor rounds, but if he reproduces his Zürich-level throwing, he should hold off Walcott.

**Keshorn Walcott** is the 2025 world champion and a former Olympic champion, but his 2026 season has been modest. He has not surpassed **83.71 m** this year, and he was only sixth at the Commonwealth Games and fourth in both Lausanne and Zürich. He remains consistent in the low-to-mid 83 m range, which gives him a solid floor, but he lacks the late-season spark shown by Wegner. Fourth place seems realistic.

**Julius Yego** is still competitive at 36, but the results show a clear decline from his 2015 world-title level. He threw **81.66 m** in Zürich and **82.22 m** in Doha, but he also failed to qualify for the Commonwealth final, placing 13th in qualifying. He is no longer a consistent 85+ m thrower. Against this field, fifth is his likely ceiling, unless others falter.

**Curtis Thompson** is difficult to trust. He won the US title in July with **87.59 m**, which shows his talent, but his August form has collapsed: **78.13 m** in Lausanne, **80.31 m** in Zürich, and **74.24 m** in Berlin. That is a brutal late-season fade, and it is hard to predict a sudden reversal in Brussels. Sixth feels harsh for someone who can throw 87 m, but based on recent data, he is the second-worst form athlete in this field.

**Timothy Herman** is clearly last. At 35, he has been stuck around **72–77 m** all season, failed to make the European final, and has no result remotely close to the rest of the field. His national-record ability is in the past. In a Diamond League final against this level of competition, seventh is the only realistic outcome.
blurbs.100m Women:
**Predicted Finish – Women’s 100m, Brussels Diamond League, 4 September 2026**  
*(Assuming fair, legal wind conditions)*

| Place | Athlete | Predicted Time |
|---:|---|---:|
| 1 | Sha’Carri Richardson (USA), 25 | **10.81** |
| 2 | Tina Clayton (JAM), 21 | **10.89** |
| 3 | Amy Hunt (GBR), 23 | **10.96** |
| 4 | Zoe Hobbs (NZL), 28 | **11.00** |
| 5 | Delphine Nkansa (BEL), 24 | **11.04** |
| 6 | Patrizia van der Weken (LUX), 26 | **11.08** |
| 7 | Jonielle Smith (JAM), 29 | **11.14** |
| 8 | Zaynab Dosso (ITA), 26 | **11.15** |
| 9 | Boglárka Takács (HUN), 24 | **11.19** |

---

### Why this order?

**1. Sha’Carri Richardson**  
Richardson is the clear favourite on 2026 form. She is the US champion after running **10.77** at the US Championships, and she also produced **10.79** at the Prefontaine Classic and **10.77** earlier in the season. Those are the fastest legal times any woman in this field has run this year. She was slightly below her best in Silesia and Zürich, but she was still the first of this group home in both races. At 25, she is in her prime, and the 2025 World Championships disappointment — fifth in the 100m final — looks like a blip rather than a trend. She is the one athlete here who can win in 10.8-low even on a so-so day.

**2. Tina Clayton**  
Clayton is the biggest threat. She already has a World Championships silver medal in the 100m from 2025, when she ran **10.76**, and she has twice run **10.85** in 2026 — at Rabat and the Jamaican Championships. That puts her clearly ahead of everyone except Richardson. However, her post-June form has been more mixed: she was fifth at Prefontaine, sixth in Silesia, and fourth in Zürich, while Richardson was ahead of her in the latter races. At 21, Clayton has enormous upside, but on current form she is the clear second-best in this field rather than a genuine favourite to beat Richardson.

**3. Amy Hunt**  
Hunt is the best of the Europeans by some margin. She won the 100m at the 2026 European Championships in **11.00**, and her legal season’s best of **10.97** from Stockholm shows she can threaten 10.9. She also ran **10.98** to take Commonwealth silver behind Hobbs in July. Since then, she has actually closed the gap on Hobbs, finishing ahead of her in Zürich with **11.04** to Hobbs’s 11.18. Hunt is only 23 but already a proven major-final performer. She has the biggest medal haul of any non-American/Jamaican in this race, and her 2026 arc is still upward.

**4. Zoe Hobbs**  
Hobbs is hard to place because her best is clearly better than her recent results. She became the first New Zealand woman to win a Commonwealth Games 100m title, running **10.93** in Glasgow. That remains the fastest time by any non-Richardson/Clayton athlete in this field this season. But her post-Commonwealth form has faded: **11.05** in Silesia, **11.18** in Zürich, and **11.16** in Bellinzona. I still place her fourth because her 10.93 ceiling is better than the Europeans below her, and she has repeatedly shown she can produce on big stages. If she hits her best, she could even challenge Hunt; if she reproduces her late-August form, she could slip further.

**5. Delphine Nkansa**  
Nkansa is the most improved athlete in this field. She was seventh in the 2025 Worlds relay but has since developed into a genuine European medal threat. At the 2026 European Championships she won 100m bronze in **11.06**, having run **11.09** in the semi-final. She also beat both van der Weken and Dosso in that final, which gives her the head-to-head edge here. Her Belgian title in **11.13** and a consistent run of sub-11.2 races suggest she is in career-best shape. The gap to Hunt is real, but Nkansa is the clear next-best European.

**6. Patrizia van der Weken**  
Van der Weken is extremely consistent but lacks the ceiling of the athletes above her. She ran **11.05** in Stockholm, **11.08** at the European Championships semi-final, and **11.10** in the final. She has a strong start — proven by her 60m medals indoors — but over 100m she tends to hold position rather than accelerate past people. She is a reliable 11.05–11.10 performer, which puts her in the middle of this pack but not on the podium.

**7. Jonielle Smith**  
This is a deliberately harsh ranking, but it is based on form and fitness. Smith ran **10.89** at the Prefontaine Classic in July and looked like a top-four threat. Since then, however, she finished sixth in Budapest, missed the Commonwealth final after reaching the semi-final, and ran only **11.14** in Zürich. Withdrawing from a major final is a major red flag, and her subsequent performances suggest she is either carrying a small injury or has lost her sharpness. On pure season’s best she belongs higher, but in Brussels she cannot be placed above healthy athletes who are consistently running 11.0–11.1.

**8. Zaynab Dosso**  
Dosso is a world-class indoor 60m runner — she is the reigning World Indoor champion over 60m — but her outdoor 100m has not matched that level. Her 2026 legal best is only **11.07**, and she ran **11.12** in the European final before closing with **11.26** in Bellinzona. That poor late-season run drops her below van der Weken and Nkansa. Her start will look great for the first 30 metres, but in this field she does not have the top-end speed to convert it into a high finish.

**9. Boglárka Takács**  
Takács is a national record holder and a strong Hungarian champion, but the data says she is outclassed here. Her legal 100m best in 2026 is only **11.16**. She did run **10.93** at the European Championships, but that was wind-aided, and in the semi-final she ran just **11.13**, which was not enough to reach the final. Her recent results — **11.31** in late August — suggest she is not arriving in Brussels in peak form. In a race this strong, she is the likely last-place finisher.

---

**Final takeaway:** Richardson wins from Clayton, with Hunt leading the European challenge. The most interesting battle is behind them, where Hobbs’s ceiling, Nkansa’s momentum, and van der Weken’s consistency will decide places four through six. Smith is the wild card, but her fitness concerns are too serious to ignore.
blurbs.5000m Men:
1. Birhanu Balew (BRN) — 12:48.57  
2. Graham Blanks (USA) — 12:49.03  
3. Grant Fisher (USA) — 12:50.22  
4. Biniam Mehary (ETH) — 12:51.45  
5. Nico Young (USA) — 12:53.18  
6. Cornelius Kemboi (KEN) — 12:55.40  
7. Egide Ntakarutimana (BDI) — 12:56.75  
8. Jacob Krop (KEN) — 12:57.60  
9. Dominic Lokinyomo Lobalu (SUI) — 13:00.85  
10. Reynold Cheruiyot (KEN) — 13:13.40  
11. Tshepo Tshite (RSA) — 13:19.70  
DNF. Mounir Akbache (FRA) — designated pacemaker

The headline battle should be between Birhanu Balew and Graham Blanks. Balew owns the fastest outdoor 5000 m by anyone in this field this year: 12:47.73 at Oslo. He was also the winner at Lausanne in late August, holding off Nico Young and Graham Blanks. That Lausanne win, coming after a string of sub-12:57 races, makes him the most reliable choice to dictate the closing laps. Blanks has been nearly as consistent — 12:49.99 in Oslo, 12:52.60 in Monaco and a sharp 7:27.92 3000 m in Zürich — but he has not yet matched Balew’s highest gear over 5000 m this season.

Grant Fisher is the highest-ceiling American in the race, with his short-track world records and Olympic bronze medals on his bio. But his Lausanne 5000 m was a genuine red flag: 13:07.74, well behind Balew and Blanks. His Paris win and 12:49.61 in Oslo keep him in the top three, but the inconsistency makes him vulnerable. Biniam Mehary remains the best young distance talent in the field, and his 12:54.35 in Oslo plus an impressive 7:28.18 3000 m in Zürich shows he is dangerous. However, in head-to-head meetings with Blanks this summer, Blanks has consistently had the better result in the 5000 m, so Mehary slots just outside the podium.

Nico Young has the American 5000 m record from 2025 and ran a strong 12:58.33 for third in Lausanne. But that remains his only 5000 m of the late summer, and his Zürich 3000 m was not at the same level as Blanks, Mehary or Ntakarutimana. He is the best of the rest, but not yet a medal favourite on current form.

The midpack is where the data gets messy. Cornelius Kemboi has the most reliable sub-13 collection of anyone outside the top five — 12:56.02, 12:57.36, 12:58.10, 12:59.33 — and his 7:27.46 3000 m in Shaoxing shows real range. Egide Ntakarutimana has a strong Paris result at 12:56.06 and was excellent over 3000 m in Zürich, but his 13:07.21 in Lausanne is a caution. Jacob Krop’s pedigree from the 2022 and 2023 World Championships is real, and his 12:53.71 in Monaco proves he can still mix with this group. But his 13:13.29 in Lausanne and 13:01.51 in Oslo are too bad to ignore. Dominic Lokinyomo Lobalu won Monaco in 12:52.54, the best single performance by anyone in this field this summer, but his late-season form collapsed: 13:18.24 at the European Championships and 7:49.51 in the Zürich 3000 m. That volatility drops him behind the more consistent Africans.

Reynold Cheruiyot and Tshepo Tshite are essentially middle-distance men stepping up. Cheruiyot’s 7:26.11 3000 m from Shaoxing is far better than Tshite’s, and his 13:16.40 5000 m from 2025 gives him a clear edge. Tshite’s only 5000 m of note this year was 13:20.92 in Oslo, so he should finish at the back of the finishers. Mounir Akbache is almost certainly the rabbit: at 39, with a string of DNFs, his job is to set a fast pace and step off, not to contest a finishing position.
blurbs.800m Men:

|-------|----------------------|---------|-----|----------------|
| 1 | Emmanuel Wanyonyi | KEN | 21 | 1:41.89 |
| 2 | Djamel Sedjati | ALG | 26 | 1:42.08 |

| 9 | Gabriel Tual | FRA | 27 | 1:44.38 |
| 10 | Jan Vukovič | SLO | 25 | 1:46.44 |

---

**Why this order?**

**Emmanuel Wanyonyi** is the clear favourite. He is the Olympic and World champion, and his 2026 season has followed an upward curve: after a slower Rabat opener, he ran 1:42.09 in Oslo, then went to Monaco and broke the 1000 m world record with 2:11.83. His most telling form marker is the 1:41.76 win in Zürich on 27 August—the best time by anyone in this field this season. The only concern is his 4th place in London in July, but he answered that immediately by winning Lausanne and Zürich. At 21, and with a 1:41.11 lifetime best, he is the most complete and dangerous 800 m runner here.

**Djamel Sedjati** looks the biggest threat. The 2024 Olympic bronze medallist and 2025 World silver medallist is built for championships and late-season finals. His 2026 résumé includes a 1:42.31 in Lausanne, a 1:41.83 in Zürich, and a 1:43.19 win in Budapest. He finished directly behind Wanyonyi in Zürich and beat Marco Arop fairly comfortably in Lausanne. Sedjati’s easy runs at the Mediterranean Games—1:46.00 and 1:46.25—look like controlled efforts rather than a loss of form. At 26, he is in his physical prime and has the most reliable blend of speed and endurance after Wanyonyi.

**Marco Arop** is harder to place. On paper, he has the fastest personal best of anyone other than Wanyonyi: his 1:41.20 from Paris 2024 makes him the fourth-fastest man in history, and his 2023 world title shown in his bio proves he knows how to win major races. His Paris Diamond League win in 2026 was excellent, 1:41.84, and he also ran 1:42.13 in Edmonton. However, he was only 4th in Lausanne in 1:43.18 and skipped Zürich, meaning he arrives less battle-sharpened than Wanyonyi and Sedjati. His raw ability is enough for third, but he has not shown the same late-summer consistency as the two men ahead of him.

**Slimane Moula** is the best of the next group. He has not quite rediscovered his 2022 African Championship level, but his 2026 season is solid: 1:43.73 in Rabat, 1:43.41 in Stockholm, and 1:43.52 in Zürich. His Paris DNF is a worry, and his Mediterranean Games final was flat, but he has repeatedly been competitive in Diamond League fields. He does not have the top-end pure speed of Arop or Sedjati, but his consistency earns him fourth.

**Eliott Crestan** is a slightly difficult projection because his 2026 outdoor season has been mixed. His indoor form was exceptional—he took silver at the World Indoor Championships, matching his bio’s reputation as a medal contender—and he has a Belgian record of 1:42.43 from 2024. Outdoors he ran 1:43.85 in Oslo and 1:44.23 in Paris, then ran fast 400 m times in July, suggesting good fitness. The absence of a late-August 800 m is a risk, but as the Belgian athlete in Brussels, and with a proven ability to run well on the Memorial van Damme stage, I still place him fifth.

**Ben Pattison** has shown he can run very well, including 1:43.34 in London in July, but he has also been frustratingly inconsistent. His 2026 highlights include 4th in Stockholm and 4th in Paris, but his Commonwealth and European Championship finals were disappointing—4th in 1:46.25 and 6th in 1:46.14 respectively. That suggests he can produce a 1:43.3 on a good day in a fast race, but he is less reliable than the four above him. Sixth feels right.

**Tobias Grønstad** deserves respect after a breakthrough spell in mid-2026: he ran 1:43.61 in Oslo and 1:43.63 in Paris, finishing ahead of several bigger names. However, he faded badly in London with 1:44.58 and struggled in the European semi-final. He is young and improving, but he is not yet consistent enough to out-kick Moula, Crestan, or Pattison in a deep final. Seventh.

**Yanis Meziane** is another consistent but slightly unspectacular 800 m runner. His European U23 title shows pedigree, but his 2026 outdoor results are mostly in the 1:43.9–1:44.4 range. He ran 1:43.96 in Budapest and 1:44.26 in Brescia, but has not threatened the low-1:43 or 1:42 territory that the top group occupies. Eighth is a reasonable ceiling for him here.

**Gabriel Tual** is the toughest to judge. His bio reminds us that he is a European champion and has run 1:41.61, so he is clearly capable of winning in this field. But his 2026 form has been poor by his standards: he was 7th in Oslo, 8th in Paris, failed to make the European final, and only ran 1:43.89 in Zürich. His best recent result was 1:43.66 in Rome in June, but he has not shown the sharpness to compete with the leaders. Ninth.

**Jan Vukovič** is clearly outclassed here. His 2026 outdoor best of 1:46.11, combined with multiple DNFs across various distances, makes him the clear outsider. He has some solid domestic results, but nothing in this field suggests he can run under 1:44. Last place is expected.
blurbs.200m Women:
Predicted finish and marks — Women’s 200m, Brussels Diamond League, 4 September 2026:

1. **Julien Alfred (LCA)** — **21.58**  
2. **Kayla White (USA)** — **21.97**  
3. **Amy Hunt (GBR)** — **22.23**  
4. **Cambrea Sturgis (USA)** — **22.35**  
5. **Anavia Battle (USA)** — **22.41**  
6. **Audrey Leduc (CAN)** — **22.52**  
7. **Success Eduan (GBR)** — **22.58**  
8. **Jenna Prandini (USA)** — **22.67**

---

**Reasoning:**

**Julien Alfred** is the clear class of the field. Her 21.51 in Monaco is the fastest 200m any of these women has run in 2026, and she followed it with 21.66 in London. She also arrives off a stunning 10.70 100m in Zürich, showing she is peaking at the end of the season. As Olympic 100m champion and Olympic 200m silver medallist, she has the biggest pedigree and the best current speed. I expect her to control the race and go under 21.70.

**Kayla White** looks like the clear second-fastest 200m runner in this field. Her 21.92 in Budapest and 22.04 in Monaco are well ahead of everyone except Alfred. She also beat Amy Hunt head-to-head in Lausanne, 22.18 to 22.32, and her 100m form — US runner-up in 10.90 — shows she has real speed. She hasn’t reproduced Alfred’s 21.51 level, but she is the only other woman here with a realistic shot at breaking 22 seconds in Brussels.

**Amy Hunt** should slot in third. She is the reigning world silver medallist over 200m and had a historic 2026 European Championships, winning four golds including the individual 200m in 22.19. That is a genuinely elite result. But her head-to-head loss to Kayla White in Lausanne and her slower season’s best make her third here. Still, her big-championship pedigree means she should be trusted to run well in a high-pressure Diamond League final.

**Cambrea Sturgis** is the most difficult call after the top three. She has shown elite-level ability this season, including 22.09 at Waco, 21.93 at altitude in Nairobi, and a strong runner-up finish in 22.22 at the US Championships. That US final performance is better than anything Battle has produced this season. However, she has also been erratic, with 22.57 in London and 22.84 in Brescia. I’m giving her fourth on ceiling and national-level form, but she is the highest-variance pick.

**Anavia Battle** has been more consistent than Sturgis at a slightly lower level. She ran 22.21 in Budapest and has multiple 22.2–22.4 performances, including 22.29 in Xiamen and 22.39 in Rome. She was fourth at the 2025 World Championships in 22.22, so she knows how to perform in finals. She doesn’t have Alfred, White, or Hunt’s top-end speed, but she should hold off the next group.

**Audrey Leduc** is a very solid sixth. She owns the Canadian records in both sprints, including 22.36 over 200m, and her 2026 season includes 22.38 and 22.41. But she has not been as sharp late in the season, missing the Commonwealth 200m final and running 22.95 in Szczecin. That suggests she is not quite at her record-breaking level, and the faster Americans and Hunt will be too much.

**Success Eduan** is young and improving. She won the UK title in 22.43, ran 22.53 in London, and reached the European final with 22.66. That is a promising season, but she is still a step behind the established international 200m medallists. She should beat the fading Prandini, but not the athletes above her.

**Jenna Prandini** is the veteran of the field, and her past achievements — two Olympics, relay gold and silver, multiple national titles — are far bigger than her current form. But at 33, the results this season have trended downward. After a fine 22.36 in May, she ran 22.46, 22.46, 22.68, 22.91 in the US final, and 22.75 in Brescia. Without a recent sub-22.5 performance, she is the weakest 200m runner in this particular race and should finish last.
blurbs.400m Men:
Predicted finish and marks – Men’s 400m, Brussels Diamond League, 4 September 2026:

| Place | Athlete | Predicted Time |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Busang Collen Kebinatshipi (BOT) | 43.45 |
| 2 | Jacory Patterson (USA) | 43.92 |
| 3 | Zakithi Nene (RSA) | 44.05 |
| 4 | Matthew Hudson-Smith (GBR) | 44.10 |
| 5 | Chris Bailey (USA) | 44.14 |
| 6 | Jereem Richards (TTO) | 44.52 |
| 7 | Khaleb McRae (USA) | 44.66 |
| 8 | Daniel Segers (BEL) | 45.08 |

---

**Why this order?**

**Kebinatshipi** is the clear favourite. He is the reigning world champion, won the 2025 world title in 43.53, and in 2026 he has been outstanding: 43.92 in Xiamen, 43.54 in Paris, 43.44 in Monaco, 43.59 in Silesia. He has the best speed reserve in the field, shown even by his 9.89s 100m run earlier in 2026. He finished 6th in Brussels in 2025 in 45.09, but that was before he exploded at the World Championships. Twelve months later, he is a different athlete.

**Patterson** gets second. He won this exact meeting in 2025 in 44.05 and then ran 43.85 in Zürich. His 2026 campaign includes 44.11 in Rabat and 43.96 in Monaco, making him the fastest man in the field this year after Kebinatshipi. He can be inconsistent at global championships, but Diamond League one-off races suit him.

**Nene** is the big threat to Patterson. His 43.89 in Paris was the best 400m of 2026 by anyone not named Kebinatshipi. He has also been very consistent: 44.40 Xiamen, 44.41 Rabat, 44.37 Silesia. But his championship finals have tended to be slightly below his one-off Diamond League peaks — 5th at the 2025 World Championships and 3rd at the 2026 Commonwealth Games. I think he runs well but just misses Patterson.

**Hudson-Smith** is still elite, just not at his 2024 best. He became European champion again in 2026 with 44.17, and he has run 44.09 in Paris and 44.18 in London. The 31-year-old clearly knows how to race and compete, but the 43.44-level form from the Paris Olympics has not returned. He gets fourth because he has been more consistent recently than Bailey, and he edged Nene in Monaco, but Nene’s Paris and Silesia runs are slightly stronger overall.

**Bailey** has a strong case to be higher: his 44.06 in Paris was excellent, and he won the 2026 US title in 44.39. But he was only 7th in Silesia in 44.77, and he has struggled to translate strong Diamond League form into global individual finals. He is very good, but the top four have shown more consistent individual 400m sharpness.

**Richards** has the pedigree — World Championships silver in 2025 in 43.72 — but his 2026 form is a step below that. His best 400m this season is 44.44, and he ran 44.82 in the Commonwealth Games final. He still beat McRae head-to-head in Stockholm and London, so sixth feels right.

**McRae** is dangerous because of his indoor world record 44.52 and his outdoor 44.40 in Rabat. But he has also produced too many 44.90-plus races, including 44.91 in Eugene and 45.39 in Santo Domingo. He is capable of beating Richards on a good day, but his recent consistency is not quite there.

**Segers** is a very solid European sprinter, but this is a world-class field. His best 2026 marks are 44.81 and 44.82, and he was 8th at the European Championships in 45.48. Running at home in Brussels may lift him, but he would need a personal best just to challenge for 7th. I see him finishing last in around 45.08.
blurbs.400m Women:
**Predicted finish – Women’s 400m, Brussels Diamond League, 4 September 2026**

1. **Marileidy Paulino** (DOM) – **48.61**  
2. **Henriette Jæger** (NOR) – **49.12**  
3. **Nickisha Pryce** (JAM) – **49.25**  
4. **Natalia Bukowiecka** (POL) – **49.52**  
5. **Aaliyah Butler** (USA) – **49.78**  
6. **Lurdes Gloria Manuel** (CZE) – **49.91**  
7. **Roxana Gómez** (CUB) – **50.18**  
8. **Helena Ponette** (BEL) – **50.62**

---

### Why this order?

**Marileidy Paulino is the clear No. 1.**  
Paulino is the Olympic champion, the world No. 1, and has been the most dominant woman in the event for years. Her 2026 season is a string of sub-49 performances: **48.48 in Paris**, **48.67 in Monaco**, **48.87 in Silesia**, **48.94 at the CAC Games final**, and **48.97 in London**. No one else in this field can match that consistency or that ceiling. She also ran 47.98 at the 2025 World Championships final, showing a championship gear no one here possesses. The only question in Brussels is not whether she wins, but by how much.

**Henriette Jæger gets the nod for silver, despite a rough Silesia.**  
Jæger’s standout result is her **49.04 European Championship win** in Birmingham in August. That is the fastest 400m of anyone in this race outside Paulino and Aaliyah Butler’s 48.84. More importantly, Jæger has repeatedly beaten Nickisha Pryce head-to-head in 2026: she was ahead of Pryce in Roma, Oslo, and London, including a strong **49.15 to 50.09** win in London. Her seventh-place 49.85 at Silesia is a blip, likely a post-championship flat spot after her European title. If she is anywhere near her 49.04 form, she is the second-best runner in this field.

**Nickisha Pryce is the most dangerous late-season riser.**  
Pryce has been excellent in the closing weeks of the season. Her **49.27 win in Brescia** was her best of 2026, and she followed her **49.49 at Silesia** by beating Jæger, Bukowiecka, Butler, and Gómez there. She may not have Jæger’s championship peak, but she has been more consistent recently. The concern is that in their earlier 2026 meetings, Jæger usually beat her by a clear margin. Pryce has genuine podium potential, and if Jæger repeats her Silesia performance, Pryce could easily take second. But based on overall ceiling and head-to-head form, she settles for third.

**Natalia Bukowiecka is the reliable veteran.**  
Bukowiecka rarely runs badly. The Polish record-holder and Olympic/World medallist delivered **49.57 in the European semi-final** and **49.60 at Silesia**, both strong late-season marks. She has a lower ceiling than Butler or Manuel, but a much higher floor. Her European silver with 50.04 was solid, and she has the experience to execute in a deep Diamond League field. She is the clear fourth pick ahead of the younger, more erratic talents.

**Aaliyah Butler is the wild card, and the toughest ranking decision.**  
Butler’s **48.84 in Monaco** is the fastest anyone has run this season apart from Paulino. It is a genuinely elite mark, and she is the US champion. But she has not reproduced anything close to that since: **49.93 at US Championships** and **50.38 at Silesia**. That is a worrying trend. She could absolutely win or take second if she rediscovers Monaco form, but a prediction should weigh consistency, not just a single brilliant performance. I place her fifth, ahead of Manuel because of her superior peak, but behind Bukowiecka due to reliability.

**Lurdes Gloria Manuel has talent but is hard to trust after her European final.**  
Manuel is the world indoor champion and ran **49.37 in Paris** and **49.44 in Monaco**, so the ability is there. But at the European Championships final, she faded hard to **50.86**, which was a major missed opportunity. She then skipped the 400 at Silesia, running a fast 300m instead. That suggests her 400m rhythm may be off at the back end of the season. I expect her to be competitive and maybe split the difference, but she is not quite as strong a bet as Bukowiecka or the top three.

**Roxana Gómez and Helena Ponette round out the field.**  
Gómez has been a reliable 50-second runner in 2026, with a best of **49.99 at the CAC Games final**, but her Diamond League form has slipped to **50.37, 50.14, and 50.88**. She was a 49.48 runner at the 2025 World Championships, but this year she has not shown enough sustained speed to challenge the top five. Ponette is a solid European-level competitor, with a season’s best of **50.31 in the Euro semi-final**, but her **51.43 in the Euro final** shows she is still a step below the top group. Both are likely fighting for seventh and eighth rather than the podium.
blurbs.High Jump Women:
Predicted finish — Brussels Diamond League women’s high jump, 4 September 2026:

| Place | Athlete (Age) | Predicted Successful Mark |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Nicola Olyslagers (AUS, 29) | 2.02 m |
| 2 | Yaroslava Mahuchikh (UKR, 24) | 2.00 m |
| 3 | Eleanor Patterson (AUS, 29) | 2.00 m |
| 4 | Iryna Gerashchenko (UKR, 30) | 1.98 m |
| 5 | Lamara Distin (JAM, 25) | 1.96 m |
| 6 | Angelina Topić (SRB, 20) | 1.94 m |
| 7 | Merel Maes (BEL, 20) | 1.90 m |
| 8 | Nafissatou Thiam (BEL, 31) | 1.84 m |

Valid bar progression used: **1.80 – 1.84 – 1.88 – 1.90 – 1.92 – 1.94 – 1.96 – 1.98 – 2.00 – 2.02 – 2.04**. The increments are 4cm, 4cm, then 2cm, so they never increase. Mahuchikh is placed 2nd over Patterson on countback at 2.00m.

---

**Why this order?**

**Nicola Olyslagers** is the strongest current form jumper in the field. She is the reigning world champion and Diamond League holder, and she has already won the 2026 edition of the Zürich Diamond League meeting with **2.02m**, beating a field that included Mahuchikh, Gerashchenko, Patterson and Distin. She also beat Mahuchikh head-to-head in London in July with **2.01m** versus **2.01m** on countback. Her Oceanian record and 2025 Zürich win at **2.04m** show she still has the ceiling to win a big meeting. At 29, she is in her prime and her consistency over the last two seasons is unmatched.

**Yaroslava Mahuchikh** is the highest-profile jumper in the world and the world record holder, but her 2026 outdoor form has been slightly below her best. She won the World Indoor title with **2.01m** and the European outdoor title with **1.97m**, and she won Silesia in August with **2.00m**. However, she was only 4th in Zürich with **1.96m** — a real blip — and she lost to Patterson in Heilbronn with **2.00m** against Patterson’s **2.02m**. Still, her consistency across the season, plus her clear wins at Silesia and the European Championships, makes her the best pick for 2nd, assuming she is cleaner than Patterson on countback.

**Eleanor Patterson** deserves serious respect after her **2.02m** win in Heilbronn on 30 August, just days before Brussels. That is the best outdoor mark any of these women has produced in the very immediate lead-up. She is also a former world champion and Olympic medallist, with big-meet pedigree. But she has also had flat days this season: 7th at the World Indoor Championships with **1.93m** and 6th in Zürich with **1.96m**. I expect her to be in the mix at **2.00m**, but Mahuchikh’s superior consistency gives her the edge.

**Iryna Gerashchenko** has had a very strong late-summer surge. She was 2nd in Silesia with **1.98m** and then 2nd in Zürich with **2.00m**, ahead of Mahuchikh, Patterson, Distin and Topić. That run is better than almost anyone outside the top three, and her Olympic bronze from 2024 shows she can handle big stages. The question is whether she can repeat 2.00m against a stronger front group. I think she settles just below that in Brussels with **1.98m**.

**Lamara Distin** has the talent and the Jamaican record, plus a Commonwealth title from 2022, but her 2026 season has been erratic. She jumped **1.98m** in Heilbronn, which is a strong late-season mark, and she matched **1.96m** in Zürich. But she also had a poor Silesia where she only managed **1.89m**, and her 2025 World Championships ended in a no-mark. She could push Gerashchenko, but I expect **1.96m** to be her final clearance.

**Angelina Topić** is only 20 and clearly the future of the event. She has a **2.00m** indoor Serbian record and was world indoor silver medallist in 2026. But her outdoor 2026 season has not matched that indoor level. She was 12th at the European Championships with a poor **1.83m**, and she was only 7th in Zürich with **1.93m**. She has multiple **1.96m** outdoor jumps this summer, so she is still dangerous, but I think **1.94m** is the realistic Brussels outcome.

**Merel Maes** is a talented Belgian jumper with a **1.97m** national title from 2025, but her 2026 outdoor season has been very thin. She qualified for the European final with **1.91m**, then finished 13th with **1.83m**. Against this stronger Diamond League field, **1.90m** is a fair predicted finish, though she could sneak higher if she catches a good day.

**Nafissatou Thiam** is one of the greatest multi-event athletes ever, but this is not her primary event, and her 2026 high jump form is well below the specialists. She cleared **1.84m** in the Ratingen heptathlon and **1.81m** in Eindhoven. Her heptathlon season was disrupted by DNFs, and even home support in Brussels is unlikely to lift her above **1.84m** in this field.
blurbs.1500m Men:
Predicted order and marks for the Brussels Diamond League Men’s 1500m – 4 September 2026:

1. **Cole Hocker (USA)** – 3:28.84  
2. **Phanuel Kipkosgei Koech (KEN)** – 3:28.93  
3. **Yared Nuguse (USA)** – 3:28.99  
4. **Cameron Myers (AUS)** – 3:29.15  
5. **Jakob Ingebrigtsen (NOR)** – 3:29.34  
6. **Ethan Strand (USA)** – 3:29.68  
7. **Timothy Cheruiyot (KEN)** – 3:30.05  
8. **Vincent Ciattei (USA)** – 3:30.30  
9. **Hobbs Kessler (USA)** – 3:30.43  
10. **Robert Farken (GER)** – 3:30.60  
11. **Jake Heyward (GBR)** – 3:30.78  
12. **Ruben Verheyden (BEL)** – 3:31.20  
13. **Christian Jackson (USA)** – 3:39.10  
14. **Boaz Kiprugut (KEN)** – 3:43.20  

---

### Why this order

**Hocker looks like the man to beat.** His late-2026 form is the strongest in the field: he won the Zürich Diamond League 1500m in 3:31.71, beating Koech and Nuguse directly, and was only 0.02 seconds behind Koech at Silesia after finishing third. Add his 2024 Olympic 1500m gold, his 2025 world 5000m title, and the fact that he owns the fastest PB in the field (3:27.65), and he becomes the obvious favourite.

**Koech gets second on consistency and head-to-head results.** The 19-year-old Kenyan was second in both Silesia and Zürich, ran 3:31.09 to win Budapest in July, and already owns a world U20 record of 3:27.72 from 2025. He beat Hocker at Silesia and edged Nuguse in Zürich by one hundredth. He is still young, but he is no longer just a promising junior — he is one of the best 1500m runners in the world.

**Nuguse is the model of consistency.** He won Rabat and Stockholm earlier in the summer, split 3:29.36 en route to second in the London Mile, and was right behind Hocker and Koech in Zürich. His only issue is that he has not quite had the late-season edge over Hocker or Koech in direct 1500m meetings. Still, with his 2024 Olympic bronze and 3:27.80 PB, he is the clear third pick.

**Myers is the biggest wildcard.** He ran 3:28.00 in Paris, won the Prefontaine Classic Mile, and won in Berlin on 30 August in 3:30.96 just days before Brussels. He also ran 7:27.97 for 3000m in Zürich, showing he has the endurance and speed. He hasn’t raced Hocker/Koech/Nuguse in a 1500m this late in the season, so I’ve placed him just off the podium, but he could easily medal if the race is fast and honest.

**Putting Ingebrigtsen fifth feels drastic, but the recent evidence is hard to ignore.** In 2025, Ingebrigtsen was shockingly eliminated early in the World Championship 1500m and then finished 10th in the 5000m final. In 2026, he won the European 5000m title, but in his two late-season 1500m Diamond League appearances he was fourth in Silesia and fifth in Zürich, behind Hocker, Koech, and Nuguse both times. He remains world-class, but his 1500m sharpness is not currently matching his 5000m strength.

**Strand showed he can beat everyone, but also showed he can disappear.** His Silesia win in 3:30.77 was the best individual 1500m result of the late season, ahead of Koech, Hocker, and Ingebrigtsen. But he followed it with 10th place in Zürich in 3:32.95. That sort of swing makes him dangerous but unreliable, so sixth is a fair middle ground.

**Cheruiyot is still a factor, but no longer a podium certainty.** He ran 3:30.67 in Stockholm and won the Oslo Mile, but he faded to 11th in Zürich. At 30, he can still beat most of the field on a good day, but the younger Americans and Koech have clearly moved past him in head-to-head matchups.

**The second tier is led by Ciattei.** He has been remarkably consistent: fourth in Stockholm, seventh in Silesia, seventh in Zürich. Kessler had a fine sixth in Zürich but a poor 11th in Silesia. Farken is in strong form and was second in Berlin, but his Zürich and Stockholm finishes were behind both Ciattei and Kessler. Heyward had a good sixth in Silesia but dropped to ninth in Zürich. Verheyden has had a disappointing late season, including failing to make the European final, so he rounds out the main contenders.

**Jackson and Kiprugut are clear outsiders.** Jackson is a strong 800m runner — fourth at US Championships and a 1:44.74 performer — but his 1500m PBs are nowhere near this level. Kiprugut’s 2025–2026 record is littered with DNFs, including a DNF in the Zürich 3000m, and his only recent 1500m finishes have been around 3:46 in Kenyan trials. If he finishes at all, he should be last.
blurbs.5000m Women:
Predicted finish — Women’s 5000m, Brussels Diamond League, 4 September 2026:

1. Freweyni Hailu (ETH) — 14:17.12  
2. Likina Amebaw (ETH) — 14:17.56  
3. Senayet Getachew (ETH) — 14:19.72  
4. Medina Eisa (ETH) — 14:20.18  
5. Hirut Meshesha (ETH) — 14:21.46  
6. Marta Alemayo (ETH) — 14:26.83  
7. Maureen Koster (NED) — 14:33.24  
8. Rose Davies (AUS) — 14:40.58  
9. Linden Hall (AUS) — 14:41.35  
10. Francine Niyomukunzi (BDI) — 14:42.08  
11. Jana van Lent (BEL) — 14:44.20  
12. Georgia Griffith (AUS) — 14:45.65  

This is a fast, paced Diamond League race rather than a slow championship final, so the runners’ best 5000m times and their ability to handle honest pace matter more than pure tactical finishing speed.

Freweyni Hailu gets the nod for the win. Her bio shows major global indoor titles over 1500m and 3000m, and she has translated that strength outdoors in 2026. In Roma she ran 14:18.94, within half a second of Likina Amebaw’s 14:18.41, then she won the Oslo 3000m in 8:24.22 and was second in the Silesia 5000m with 14:54.62. Likina, by contrast, was only eighth in Silesia with 14:56.42. Freweyni’s superior 1500m speed should decide a late-race kick between two very evenly matched Ethiopians.

Likina Amebaw is the clear silver-medal candidate based on pure numbers. Her Roma win in 14:18.41 is the fastest 5000m any woman in this field has run in 2026. She also has outstanding road credentials, including a 1:04:44 half marathon and a 14:23 road 5km, which give her tremendous aerobic strength. But her disappointing Silesia run and her lack of Freweyni’s finishing punch make her slightly vulnerable at the sharp end.

Senayet Getachew is the most consistent of the next group. She ran 14:24.71 in Shaoxing and 14:22.37 in Roma, and she has a 3000m best of 8:24.02 from Monaco. Her 30:36.67 10,000m from 2025 and her U20 cross-country pedigree show real endurance. She has simply been more reliable than Medina Eisa and Hirut Meshesha in 2026, so she takes third.

Medina Eisa has the talent and the résumé to win on a good day, including a 2025 London Diamond League win and a road 10km of 29:25. She also won in Doha in 14:53.91. However, her 2025 World Championships final collapse, her Nagoya Marathon DNF, and a 2026 season that has been good but not dominant keep her behind Senayet. Her 14:22.51 in Roma was excellent, but she was still behind Senayet in both Shaoxing and Roma.

Hirut Meshesha is the riskiest pick in the top five. She has the pedigree, with a World Indoor 1500m bronze on her bio, and her 14:22.56 in Roma shows she can run with the best. But she also DNF’d in Shaoxing and finished 15th in Silesia. I am giving her the benefit of the doubt because her best 5000m time is far superior to anyone outside the top four, and she has the 3000m strength to stay with the early pace if healthy.

Marta Alemayo, at just 17, is the most exciting young talent in the field. Her two U20 world cross-country titles and her 14:15 road 5km this year are outstanding. But her track 5000m best remains 14:32.84, and she was about eight seconds behind the top Ethiopian pack in Shaoxing. In a genuinely fast race she should run a big personal best, but she is not yet ready to bridge the gap to the 14:20 women.

Maureen Koster is the best of the non-Ethiopians. Her 14:33.56 in Roma and her 30:50.31 10,000m in Ostrava show she is in strong shape. She also won European 10,000m silver in 2026, which speaks to her endurance. Rose Davies beat her in a tactical Silesia race, but on a paced night in Brussels, Maureen’s faster raw 5000m credentials should come out on top.

Rose Davies had a fantastic 2026, winning the Commonwealth double over 5000m and 10,000m. Her 14:40.83 Australian record also shows she is a legitimate international-level runner. But in this company, her 5000m ceiling is still around 14:40, while the top Ethiopians are at 14:17–14:22. She can lead the second chase group and perhaps dip under her own record, but a medal would require a much slower, more tactical race.

Linden Hall remains a strong 1500m runner, and her 14:40.81 in Roma proves she can run a good 5000m. But she is not primarily a 5000m specialist, and at 34 she may lack the closing strength of the dedicated 5000m/10,000m runners around her. She slots in just behind Rose Davies.

Francine Niyomukunzi has been competitive in 2026, including 14:41.46 in Roma and 14:57.34 in Silesia, but she has not shown the same consistency as the runners above her. Her 2025 Brussels DNF in the 5000m is also a slight concern on this specific track.

Jana van Lent is a solid Belgian distance runner with national records and a home crowd behind her, but her 2026 track 5000m form has been modest. Georgia Griffith has a faster personal best from 2025, but her 2026 season has been inconsistent, and she was 16th in Silesia. In the end, I expect the home favourite to outkicks Georgia for 11th, with Griffith rounding out the field.
